examples: Press the return key to enter the information.
You can use the arrow keys on the keyboard instead.

definitions.description: any of the wooden or metal parts that you press to play a piano and some other musical instruments
examples: His hands flew over the piano keys.

definitions.description: a set of related notes, based on a particular note. Pieces of music are usually written mainly using a particular key.
examples: a sonata in the key of E flat major

definitions.description: a set of answers to exercises or problems
examples: Check your answers in the key at the back of the book.

definitions.description: an explanation of the symbols used on a map or plan
examples: You can find the symbols in the key at the bottom of the page.

definitions.description: a unit for measuring distance; 1 000 metres
examples: The industrial estate is 6 kilometres from the city centre.
She had been driving at 110 kilometres per hour.

definitions.description: consisting of goods or services, not money
examples: As well as his salary, he gets benefits in kind.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: with the same thing
examples: She insulted him and he responded in kind.

definitions.label: (especially British English)
definitions.description: a room in which meals are cooked or prepared
examples: We ate at the kitchen table.
the kitchen floor/window/door
a stainless steel kitchen sink
He stabbed her with a kitchen knife.
The house has a fully fitted kitchen with custom-built units.

definitions.label: (informal, humorous)
definitions.description: a very large number of things, probably more than is necessary
examples: We seem to take everything but the kitchen sink when we go camping.

definitions.label: (informal)
definitions.description: used to tell somebody to stop trying to do something if they find it too difficult, especially in order to suggest that they are less able than other people

definitions.label: (informal)
definitions.description: to have information in your mind as a result of experience or because you have learned or been told it
examples: No one knows the answer.

definitions.description: to realize, understand or be aware of something
examples: As soon as I walked in the room I knew (that) something was wrong.

This case is hopeless and he knows it (= although he will not admit it).

examples: He knew (that) he could trust her.

definitions.description: to be familiar with a person, place, thing, etc.
examples: I've known David for 20 years.

Do you know the play (= have you seen or read it before)?

definitions.description: to have learned a skill or language and be able to use it
examples: Do you know any Japanese?

definitions.description: to think that somebody/something is a particular type of person or thing or has particular characteristics
examples: He has become widely known as an expert in child psychology.

examples: Iran was formerly known as Persia.

definitions.description: to be able to recognize somebody/something
examples: I couldn't see who was speaking, but I knew the voice.

definitions.description: to understand the difference between one person or thing and another

definitions.description: to have seen, heard or experienced something

definitions.description: the surface of the earth that is not sea
examples: The new project will reclaim the land from the sea.

definitions.label: (North American English)
definitions.description: an area of ground, especially of a particular type or used for a particular purpose
examples: agricultural/arable/fertile land

a piece/plot of land

definitions.label: formal
definitions.description: the area of ground that somebody owns, especially when you think of it as property that can be bought or sold
examples: public/private land
to own/buy/purchase/sell land

The college owns vast tracts of land.

definitions.description: used to refer to the countryside and the way people live in the country as opposed to in cities
examples: At the beginning of the 20th century almost a third of the population lived off the land (= grew or produced their own food).

definitions.label: (literary)
definitions.description: used to refer to a country or region in a way that involves the emotions or the imagination

faraway lands beyond the sea
America is the land of freedom and opportunity.
the land of the fairies/elves/giants

definitions.description: the system of communication in speech and writing that is used by people of a particular country or area
examples: the English language

definitions.description: a particular style of speaking or writing
examples: spoken/written language
literary/poetic language

the language of science

definitions.description: a way of expressing ideas and feelings using movements, symbols and sound
examples: the language of mime
the language of dolphins/bees

definitions.description: a system of symbols and rules that is used to operate a computer

definitions.description: big in size or quantity

examples: My mother's dead; she died in 2017.
a dead person/animal
dead leaves/wood/skin
Catherine's dead body lay peacefully on the bed.
He was shot dead by a gunman outside his home.
A high school shooting has left six students dead.
She was pronounced dead at the scene of the accident.
The poor child looks more dead than alive.
He was missing, presumed dead.
He dropped dead (= died suddenly) last week.
One short year later, Fred would be dead from a heart attack.
In ten years he'll be dead and buried as a politician.

definitions.description: not working because of a lack of power
examples: a dead battery
Suddenly the phone went dead.
John's mobile was completely dead.

definitions.description: no longer believed in or aimed for
examples: Many believe the peace plan is dead.
Unfortunately racism is not yet dead.
Though the idea may be dead, it is far from being buried (= people still talk about it, even though there is nothing new to say).

definitions.description: belonging to the past; no longer practised or fashionable
examples: Is the Western a dead art form?
a dead language (= one that is no longer spoken, for example Latin)

definitions.label: (informal)
definitions.description: finished; not able to be used any more
examples: dead matches
There were two dead bottles of wine on the table.

definitions.label: (informal, disapproving)
definitions.description: very quiet, without activity or interest
examples: There were no theatres, no cinemas, no coffee bars. It was dead as anything.

definitions.label: (informal, disapproving)
definitions.description: without activity; with nobody buying or selling anything
examples: ‘The market is absolutely dead this morning,’ said one foreign exchange trader.
Winter is traditionally the dead season for the housing market.

definitions.label: (informal)
definitions.description: extremely tired; not well
examples: half dead with cold and hunger
She felt dead on her feet and didn't have the energy to question them further.

definitions.description: unable to feel because of cold, etc.
examples: My left arm had gone dead.

definitions.description: unable to feel or understand emotions
examples: He was dead to all feelings of pity.

definitions.refer: (especially of somebody’s voice, eyes or face)
definitions.description: showing no emotion
examples: She said, ‘I'm sorry, too,’ in a quiet, dead voice.
His usually dead grey eyes were sparkling.

definitions.label: (informal)
definitions.description: complete or exact
examples: a dead silence/calm
the dead centre of the target
The car gave a sudden jerk and came to a dead stop.
Her face was a dead giveaway (= made it very obvious) that something was going on.
This horse is a dead cert for (= will certainly win) the race tomorrow.
She crumpled to the floor in a dead faint (= completely unconscious).

definitions.description: never having been alive
examples: dead matter (= for example rock)
a dead planet (= one with no life on it)

definitions.description: outside the playing area
examples: There was a dead ball with five seconds to go in the game.

definitions.description: to give cards to each player in a game of cards
examples: Whose turn is it to deal?
Start by dealing out ten cards to each player.
He dealt me two aces.

definitions.description: to buy and sell illegal drugs
examples: You can often see people dealing openly on the streets.
He was sent to jail for dealing drugs to his friends.

definitions.description: the fact of somebody dying or being killed
examples: the anniversary of his wife’s death
his sudden/untimely/premature death
the tragic death of a child
The jury returned a verdict of accidental death.
It is believed she died a violent death.
He suffered a slow and painful death.
an increase in deaths from cancer

definitions.description: the end of life; the state of being dead
examples: Police are trying to establish the cause of death.
The disease can cause death unless the patient is treated promptly.
Do you believe in life after death?
He was sentenced to death (= to be executed).
Millions of people starved to death (= were killed by lack of food).
He's drinking himself to death (= so that it will kill him).
to beat/kick/stab somebody to death

definitions.description: the stopping of biochemical processes of life in a cell or tissue, in a way that cannot be reversed
examples: This process becomes irreversible and leads to cell death.

definitions.description: the permanent end or destruction of something
examples: the death of all my plans
the death of fascism

definitions.label: (literary)
definitions.description: the power that destroys life, imagined as human in form
examples: Death is often shown in paintings as a human skeleton.
Death marched in and took him away.

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: a choice or judgement that you make after thinking and talking about what is the best thing to do
examples: I think I've made the right decision.
No decisions have yet been taken.
We need a decision on this by next week.
I will consult colleagues before making a final decision about how to proceed.
We must come to a decision about what to do next.
We finally reached a decision (= decided after some difficulty).
Who made the decision to go ahead with the project?
Choosing a college is a big decision for students and their families.
a difficult/tough/hard decision
It is almost impossible for the average person to make an informed decision (= one based on evidence).
The government plans to appeal against the decision in the High Court.
to appeal the decision
to reverse/overturn a decision on appeal
The editor's decision is final.

definitions.description: the process of deciding something
examples: The moment of decision had arrived.
The power of decision remained with the directors.
The most persuasive talker often dominates the decision process.

definitions.description: the ability to decide something clearly and quickly
examples: This is not a job for someone who lacks decision.

definitions.label: (figurative)
definitions.description: having a large distance from the top or surface to the bottom
examples: a deep hole/well/river
deep water/snow
The water looks quite deep there.
Around the world, the deep oceans are heating.
Sunflowers have deep roots.
The custom has deep roots in the community.

definitions.description: having a large distance from the front edge to the furthest point inside
examples: a deep cut/wound
deep space

definitions.description: used to describe or ask about the depth of something
examples: The water is only a few centimetres deep.
How deep is the wound?

definitions.description: as far up or down as the point mentioned
examples: The water was only waist-deep so I walked ashore.
She stood knee-deep in the water.
We were walking in ankle-deep water.

definitions.description: in the number of rows mentioned, one behind the other
examples: They were standing three-deep at the bar.

definitions.description: taking in or giving out a lot of air
examples: She took a deep breath.
He gave a deep sigh.

definitions.description: a person in a deep sleep is difficult to wake
examples: She fell into a deep sleep.
to be in a deep trance/coma

definitions.description: strong and dark
examples: a rich deep red

definitions.description: low
examples: I heard his deep warm voice filling the room.
We heard a deep roar in the distance.
He gave a deep groan.

definitions.description: strongly felt
examples: a very deep feeling of love
I felt a deep sense of loss when I heard of her death.
They expressed deep concern.
We extend our deepest sympathies to his family.
It was with deep regret that I accepted his resignation.
They have a deep respect for tradition.

definitions.description: extreme or serious
examples: He's in deep trouble.
a deep economic recession
The affair had exposed deep divisions within the party.
a place of great power and of deep significance

definitions.description: showing great knowledge or understanding
examples: She had reached a deep understanding of the local culture.
We will need a deeper analysis of this problem.

definitions.description: difficult to understand
examples: This discussion's getting too deep for me.
He always sought for a deeper meaning in everything.
They spent hours discussing deep philosophical issues.

definitions.description: fully involved in an activity or a state
examples: to be deep in thought/conversation
He is often so deep in his books that he forgets to eat.
The firm ended up deep in debt.

definitions.description: if a person is deep, they hide their real feelings and opinions
examples: She's always been a deep one, trusting no one.

definitions.description: to or from a position far down or across the field
examples: a deep ball from Brown

definitions.description: a way of emphasizing that something is true and that there is no doubt about it
examples: I definitely remember sending the letter.
‘Was it what you expected?’ ‘Yes, definitely.’
‘Would you like to go back there?’ ‘Definitely not!'
She most definitely did not want my help.
The claim is definitely true.
If you want to know more I'd definitely recommend checking out this guide .

definitions.description: in a way that is certain or that shows that you are certain
examples: The date of the move has not been definitely decided yet (= it may change).
Please say definitely whether you will be coming or not.

definitions.description: a unit for measuring temperature
examples: Water freezes at 32 degrees Fahrenheit (32°F) or zero/nought degrees Celsius (0°C).
Temperatures are expected to drop below 2 degrees.
Last weekend temperatures reached 40 degrees.

definitions.description: a unit for measuring angles
examples: an angle of ninety degrees (90°)

definitions.description: the amount or level of something
examples: Her job demands a high degree of skill.
The story has been staged several times before, with varying degrees of success.
I agree with you to a certain degree.
The reaction to his decision has been, to some degree, predictable.
These criticisms are, to a degree (= to some extent), well founded.
To what degree can parents be held responsible for a child's behaviour?
Most pop music is influenced, to a greater or lesser degree, by the blues.

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: the qualification obtained by students who successfully complete a university or college course
examples: My brother has a degree from Harvard.
She's pursuing a degree in biochemistry.
a four-year degree course
an undergraduate/graduate/doctoral degree
a law/medical degree

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: a university or college course, normally lasting three years or more
examples: I'm hoping to do a chemistry degree.
He completed a degree in law then joined a law firm.

definitions.description: a level in a scale of how serious something is
examples: murder in the first degree (= of the most serious kind)

definitions.label: formal
definitions.description: a person whose job is to take care of people’s teeth
examples: to see/visit/consult your dentist
the dentist's chair/drill

definitions.description: a place where a dentist sees patients
examples: I hate going to the dentist.
an appointment at the dentist’s
She couldn’t get treatment because she wasn’t registered with the dentist.

definitions.description: a section of a large organization such as a government, business, university, etc.
examples: the Department of Health
He is a lecturer in the department of psychology at Trinity College, Dublin.
the Treasury Department
a government/university, etc. department
the marketing/sales, etc. department
The children's department (= in a large store) sells a wide range of good quality clothes.
the English department
She used to work in the IT department.
He later served as head of the art history department.

definitions.label: (informal)
definitions.description: to be something that somebody is responsible for or knows a lot about
examples: Don't ask me about it—that's her department.

definitions.label: (informal)
definitions.description: in a particular aspect or quality
examples: He doesn't have much going for him in the brains department, to be honest.
Movies lacking in the story department can still succeed.

definitions.description: according to
examples: Starting salary varies from £26 000 to £30 500, depending on experience.
He either resigned or was sacked, depending on who you talk to.

definitions.description: used to say that you are not certain about something because other things have to be considered
examples: ‘Is he coming?’ ‘That depends. He may not have the time.’
I don't know if we can help—it all depends.
I might not go. It depends how tired I am.
‘Your job sounds fun.’ ‘It depends what you mean by “fun”.’
I shouldn't be too late. But it depends if the traffic's bad.

definitions.label: (figurative)
definitions.description: a large area of land that has very little water and very few plants growing on it. Many deserts are covered by sand.
examples: the Sahara Desert
Somalia is mostly desert.
They travelled many miles across burning desert sands.
Occasionally, we passed a desert oasis surrounded by small tracts of grass and shrub.
The town has become a cultural desert (= a place without any culture).

definitions.description: a person whose job is to decide how things such as clothes, furniture, tools, etc. will look or work by making drawings, plans or patterns
examples: a web/game designer
She works as a set designer for the Royal Opera House.
the company's chief jewellery designer

definitions.description: to damage something so badly that it no longer exists, works, etc.
examples: The building was completely destroyed by fire.
The earthquake damaged or destroyed countless homes.
Some of the habitat has already been totally destroyed.
They've destroyed all the evidence.

definitions.description: to take all the value and pleasure from somebody's life; to ruin (= completely damage) somebody's life or reputation
examples: Failure was slowly destroying him.
She threatened to destroy my reputation.
He wanted revenge on the man who had destroyed his life.
Their lives have been virtually destroyed by this tragedy.

definitions.description: to kill an animal deliberately, usually because it is sick or not wanted
examples: The injured horse had to be destroyed.

definitions.description: a person, especially a police officer, whose job is to investigate crimes and catch criminals
examples: a police/homicide/undercover detective
Several objects were taken away by detectives from the anti-terrorist squad.
Detective Inspector (Roger) Brown
a detective constable/sergeant/superintendent

definitions.description: a person employed by somebody to find out information about somebody/something
to gradually grow or become bigger, more advanced, stronger, etc.; to make something do this
examples: From birth to age 5, a child's brain develops rapidly.
Some children develop more slowly than others.
Gradually these settlements developed into cities.
Human beings developed from earlier species of animals.
The place has rapidly developed from a small fishing community into a thriving tourist resort.
The aim is to develop your personal skills.
She developed the company from nothing.
The competition helps entrants develop ideas into business concepts.

definitions.description: to start to have a skill, ability, quality, etc. that becomes better and stronger; to become better and stronger
examples: He's developed a real flair for management.

definitions.description: to think of or produce a new idea, product, etc. and make it successful
examples: The company develops and markets new software.
It takes time to develop new technology.
We are developing products for different parts of the industry.
to develop a strategy/system/programme
to develop a method/model/technique
A new type of painkilling drug has recently been developed.

definitions.description: to begin to have something such as a disease or a problem; to start to affect somebody/something
examples: She developed lung cancer at the age of sixty.
Her son developed asthma when he was two.
The car developed engine trouble and we had to stop.
If symptoms develop, seek help quickly.
Problems can develop unexpectedly.

definitions.description: to start to happen or change, especially in a bad way
examples: A crisis was rapidly developing in the Gulf.
We need more time to see how things develop before we take action.
The conflict quickly developed into full-scale war.
The situation is developing into a crisis.

definitions.description: to build new houses, factories, etc. on an area of land, especially land that was not being used effectively before
examples: The site is being developed by a French company.

definitions.description: to build or improve a building or other facilities
examples: The company is developing a chain of hotels.
He is enthusiastic about plans to develop the leisure facilities at the site.

definitions.label: (economics)
definitions.description: to become economically and socially more advanced
examples: For a country to develop, a good road network is essential.
Their economy was developing at an incredible pace.

definitions.description: to add further explanation or details to an idea, story or musical theme
examples: She develops the theme more fully in her later books.
The piano then takes up the melody and develops it.
He began to develop these ideas in a series of paintings.

definitions.description: to treat film that has been used to take photographs with chemicals so that the pictures can be seen
examples: When Lewis developed the film, he was astonished by what he saw.

definitions.description: an object or a piece of equipment that has been designed to do a particular job
examples: a tracking/recording/listening device
The new devices will be installed at US airports.
electrical labour-saving devices around the home

definitions.description: a piece of computer equipment, especially a small one such as a smartphone
examples: You can store thousands of photos on your device.
a portable/wireless device
The waiter takes orders on a hand-held device.
Now connect the device to your computer.

definitions.description: a bomb or weapon that will explode
examples: A powerful device exploded outside the station.
It was the world's first atomic device.
Two bombers detonated their devices in the busy shopping centre.
The device failed to detonate.

definitions.description: a method of doing something that produces a particular result or effect
examples: Targeted advertising on social media is very successful as a marketing device.

definitions.description: a plan or trick that is used to get something that somebody wants
examples: The report was a device used to hide rather than reveal problems.
This device can be seen as somewhat dishonest.

definitions.description: a form of words that is intended to produce a particular effect in speech or writing

definitions.description: in a different way from somebody/something
examples: Boys and girls may behave differently.
He didn't like being treated differently.
What will you do differently next time?
Eddie comes from an older generation that thought differently than we do.
The male bird has a differently shaped head.

definitions.description: using a system of receiving and sending information as a series of the numbers one and zero, showing that an electronic signal is there or is not there
examples: a digital camera
digital media/content/platforms
These figures include digital downloads in addition to retail sales.
He quickly realized that all film and video production would go digital.
The system is fully digital, with no analogue components.

definitions.description: connected with the use of computer technology, especially the internet
examples: communication in the digital age
Digital technology continues to evolve rapidly.
Advertisers are putting more and more money into digital marketing.

definitions.description: showing information by using figures, rather than with hands that point to numbers
examples: a digital clock/watch
The instrument panel has an easy-to-read digital display.

definitions.description: going in the straightest line between two places without stopping or changing direction
examples: the most direct route
This door allows direct access from the kitchen to the garage.
a direct flight (= a flight that does not stop)
There's a direct train to Leeds (= it may stop at other stations but you do not have to change trains).
a direct hit (= a hit that is accurate and does not touch something else first)

definitions.description: happening or done without involving other people, actions, etc. in between
examples: She has been in direct contact with the prime minister.
Clinical depression is thought to have a direct link to brain chemistry.
There is a direct connection between these two phenomena.
This information has a direct bearing on (= is closely connected with) the case.
He died as a direct result of his employer's actions.
a direct effect/consequence
Many farmers are developing direct access to consumers.
He was cleared of any direct involvement in the case.
Participation in sport brings many benefits, both direct and indirect.

definitions.description: with nothing between something and the source of the heat or light
examples: The plant should not be placed in direct sunlight.
Grilling involves subjecting the food to direct heat.

definitions.description: saying exactly what you mean in a way that nobody can pretend not to understand
examples: I asked him a direct question: ‘Did you do it?’
He would not give a direct answer.
Her response is refreshingly direct.
Their message is simple and direct: obesity kills.
You'll have to get used to his direct manner.
I prefer a more direct approach.

definitions.description: clearly showing something
examples: There is no direct evidence for the beneficial effects of these herbs.

definitions.description: exact
examples: That's the direct opposite of what you told me yesterday.
a direct quote (= one using a person’s exact words)

definitions.description: related through parents and children rather than brothers, sisters, aunts, etc.
examples: a direct descendant of the country’s first president
With his death, the direct male line of the House of Capet came to an end.

definitions.description: the general position a person or thing moves or points towards
examples: They headed in the direction of the village.
She pointed in my direction.
They hit a truck coming in the opposite direction.
The road was blocked in both directions.
The aircraft was flying in a northerly direction.
in the right/wrong direction
When the police arrived, the crowd scattered in all directions.
Has the wind changed direction?
I lost all sense of direction (= I didn't know which way to go).

definitions.description: instructions about how to do something, where to go, etc.
examples: Let's stop and ask for directions.
A farmer gave us directions to the town.
With all pesticides, follow the directions for use carefully.
Simple directions for assembling the model are printed on the box.

definitions.description: the general way in which a person or thing develops
examples: The exhibition provides evidence of several new directions in her work.

The industry will continue to move in the direction of more automation.
Do you think this represents a radical change of direction for the president?

definitions.description: the general position a person or thing comes or develops from
examples: Support came from an unexpected direction.
Let us approach the subject from a different direction.

definitions.description: a purpose; an aim
examples: We are looking for somebody with a clear sense of direction.
Once again her life felt lacking in direction.

definitions.description: the art of managing or guiding somebody/something
examples: She was entrusted with the direction of the project.
All work was produced by the students under the direction of John Williams.

definitions.description: the instructions given by somebody directing a film or play
examples: There is some clever direction and the film is very well shot.

definitions.description: one of a group of senior managers who run a company
examples: a non-executive director
He's on the board of directors.

definitions.description: a person in charge of a film or play who tells the actors and staff what to do
examples: a famous film director
He remained active in the theatre as a playwright and director.
the writer and director of the movie ‘Wind River’

definitions.description: a person who is in charge of a particular activity or department in a company, a college, etc.
examples: She was artistic director of the city's photography festival.
He was musical director at the National Theatre.
the deputy/assistant/associate director
the finance/marketing/technical director
the director of marketing/operations/communications
He is assistant director of market research for IDFA.
She recently served as director of the Longwood Arts Project in the Bronx.
the company's regional director in North America
an eminent museum director and curator

definitions.description: if two people disagree or one person disagrees with another about something, they have a different opinion about it
examples: Even friends disagree sometimes.
No, I disagree. I don't think it would be the right thing to do.
I must respectfully disagree with my colleague.
Victoria and I obviously disagree on this issue.
He disagreed with his parents on most things.
I'm afraid I disagree with you on that point.

Jack and Robert disagree about everything.
I strongly disagree with this decision.
to disagree with a statement/view/conclusion/policy
Some people disagree with this argument.

definitions.description: if statements or reports disagree, they give different information
examples: The results of the two approaches disagree.
The two reports disagree on the number of people who will be affected by this change.
Clinical diagnoses have frequently been reported to disagree with autopsy results.

definitions.description: to become impossible to see
examples: With that, Matt promptly disappeared.
The mirror made the ceiling seem to disappear.
The plane disappeared behind a cloud.
Lisa watched until the train disappeared from view.
Lucy watched his tall figure disappear into the cafe.

definitions.description: to stop existing
examples: Her nervousness quickly disappeared once she was on stage.
The problem won't just disappear.
Our countryside is disappearing at an alarming rate.
Wildlife is fast disappearing from our countryside.
These fish have virtually disappeared from their traditional waters.

definitions.description: to be lost or impossible to find
examples: I can never find a pen in this house. They disappear as soon as I buy them.
Then one day he simply disappeared.
The plane mysteriously disappeared over the Indian Ocean.
The child disappeared from his home some time after four.

definitions.description: if a person is disappeared, they are arrested or captured and kept in prison without trial or killed, usually for political reasons
examples: 10 000 people have been disappeared and over 160 000 displaced.
One month later, he was disappeared by the regime.

definitions.description: to remove something secretly or illegally so that it cannot be found
examples: In the last five years, nearly 5 000 companies have been disappeared from the registry.
Soon after the blog post went up, someone disappeared it.

definitions.description: an unexpected event, such as a very bad accident, a flood or a fire, that kills a lot of people or causes a lot of damage
examples: the world's worst humanitarian disaster
an environmental/ecological disaster
a rail/mining/tsunami disaster
Thousands died in the disaster.
They provided more than $2.3 billion in disaster relief.
It was taking years for disaster victims to settle and rebuild.
Given the threat of earthquake, we recognized the need for disaster recovery centres.

definitions.description: a very bad situation that causes problems
examples: Losing your job doesn't have to be such a disaster.
Disaster struck when the wheel came off.
Archie has to act quickly to avert disaster.
They could think of no way to avoid the impending disaster.
Many business partnerships end in disaster.
The discovery of the disease among sheep spells financial disaster for farmers.
Letting her organize the party is a recipe for disaster (= something that is likely to go badly wrong).

definitions.label: (informal)
definitions.description: a complete failure
examples: As a teacher, he's a disaster.
The play's first night was a total disaster.
a complete/total/absolute/unmitigated disaster

definitions.description: to be the first person to become aware that a particular place or thing exists
examples: Cook is credited with discovering Hawaii.
Scientists around the world are working to discover a cure for the disease.
a newly discovered snake species
They first discovered this protein about five years ago.
She recently discovered two fungi that were new to science.

definitions.description: to find somebody/something that was hidden or that you did not expect to find
examples: Police discovered a large stash of drugs while searching the house.
We discovered this beach while we were sailing around the island.
His body was discovered in the lake near his house.
He was discovered hiding in a shed.
She was discovered dead at her home in Leeds.

definitions.description: to find out about something; to find some information about something
examples: She was determined to discover the truth about her neighbours.
to discover a secret
I've just discovered hang-gliding!
Discover the joys of yoga!
It was a shock to discover (that) he couldn’t read.
We never did discover why she gave up her job.

definitions.description: to be the first person to realize that somebody is very good at singing, acting, etc. and help them to become successful and famous
examples: The singer was discovered while still at school.
There's great talent out there just waiting to be discovered.

definitions.description: an act or the process of finding somebody/something, or learning about something that was not known about before
examples: Researchers in this field have made some important new discoveries.

the discovery of antibiotics in the twentieth century

the discovery of new talent in the art world

definitions.description: a thing, fact or person that is found or learned about for the first time
examples: The drug is not a new discovery—it's been known about for years.
one of the most important scientific discoveries of all time
potentially the biggest archaeological discovery in Norway for fifty years
recent discoveries about sleep

definitions.description: a conversation about somebody/something; the process of discussing somebody/something
examples: I discovered something interesting during a family discussion.
We'll continue this discussion some other time.

A lively discussion followed about whether he should be allowed to join the club.
The pair held informal discussions on a number of topics.

The plans have been under discussion (= being talked about) for a year now.
a list of topics for discussion
to stimulate/provoke discussion
to initiate/start/spark a discussion
a panel/group/round-table discussion

definitions.description: a speech or a piece of writing that discusses many different aspects of a subject

definitions.description: more with one person, thing, etc. than with others, or more in particular circumstances than in others
examples: In some countries, especially poorer ones, healthcare systems are struggling to cope.
I love Rome, especially in the spring.
The car is quite small, especially if you have children.

definitions.label: British English
definitions.description: for a particular purpose, person, etc.
examples: I got up early especially.
I made it especially for you.
The vehicle was designed especially for use in the desert.

definitions.description: very much; to a particular degree
examples: A plentiful supply of water is especially important in summer.
especially useful/interesting
Many websites display the date of publication within the URL for the page. This is especially true of blogs and news sites.
I wasn't feeling especially happy that day.
‘Do you like his novels?’ ‘Not especially.’

definitions.description: a short piece of writing by a student as part of a course of study
examples: I have to write an essay this weekend.
an essay on the causes of the First World War
Have you done your essay about Napoleon yet?
He made some very good points in his essay.

definitions.description: a short piece of writing on a particular subject, written in order to be published
examples: a collection of essays by prominent African American writers
The book contains a number of interesting essays on women in society.
Pierce contributes a long essay about John F. Kennedy.
I discuss this in a forthcoming essay.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: an attempt to do something
examples: His first essay in politics was a complete disaster.

definitions.description: used or happening every day or regularly; ordinary
examples: Change is a part of everyday life in business.
plates and dishes for everyday use
Using everyday objects, basic scientific principles can be explained to young children.
Violent crime is part of the everyday experience of the people in these neighbourhoods.

definitions.description: in, to or at every place; all places
examples: I've looked everywhere.
He follows me everywhere.
We'll have to eat here—everywhere else is full.
Everywhere we went was full of tourists.

definitions.label: (specialist)
definitions.description: the facts, signs or objects that make you believe that something is true
examples: Researchers have found clear scientific evidence of a link between exposure to sun and skin cancer.
There is a growing body of evidence for the existence of black holes that are ten times as massive as the Sun.
There is not a shred of evidence that the meeting actually took place.
Have you any evidence to support this allegation?
The study provides empirical evidence (= based on experiments or experience) to prove that the drug has no long-term side effects.
Anecdotal evidence (= based on personal accounts) suggests that drivers over the age of 70 find it difficult to get insurance.
On the evidence of their recent matches, it is unlikely the Spanish team will win.
In the absence of evidence to the contrary, it should be assumed that proper procedures were followed.

definitions.label: (especially North American English)
definitions.description: the information that is used in court to try to prove something
examples: I was asked to give evidence (= to say what I knew, describe what I had seen, etc.) at the trial.
The defence accused the prosecution of withholding several key pieces of evidence.
circumstantial/forensic evidence
Despite a lack of evidence against him, Burton will appear in court next week.
He was released when the judge ruled there was no evidence against him.
The emails were presented as evidence of his involvement in the fraud.
The police officer took a statement which was later used in evidence.

definitions.label: (informal)
definitions.description: correct in every detail
examples: The new palace is an exact replica of the original building.
It is an exact copy of the original document.
The model is exact in every detail.
For now they are keeping the exact date and location of the wedding a secret.
The exact nature of her illness (= precisely what her illness is) has not been made public.
Her second husband was the exact opposite of her first (= completely different).
The colours were an almost exact match.
She's in her mid-thirties—thirty-six to be exact.
I had the exact same problem as you when I first started.
What were his exact words?
A clear definition requires very exact wording.
Nobody knows the exact number of people affected, but it is over 10 000.
He started to phone me at the exact moment I started to phone him (= at the same time).

definitions.description: very accurate and careful about details
examples: He was very exact about everything he did.

definitions.description: using accurate measurements and following set rules
examples: Assessing insurance risk can never be an exact science.

definitions.description: used to emphasize that something is correct in every way or in every detail
examples: It's exactly nine o'clock.
It happened almost exactly a year ago.
Your answer is exactly right.
It was a warm day, if not exactly hot.
I know exactly how she felt.
It's impossible to say exactly what happened.
Do exactly as I tell you.
You haven't changed at all—you still look exactly the same.
His words had exactly the opposite effect.

definitions.label: (informal)
definitions.description: used to ask for more information about something
examples: Where exactly did you stay in France?
Exactly what are you trying to tell me?

definitions.description: used as a reply, agreeing with what somebody has just said, or emphasizing that it is correct
examples: ‘You mean somebody in this room must be the murderer?’ ‘Exactly.’

definitions.description: extremely good
examples: an excellent book/article
excellent results/work
The meal looked and tasted excellent.
Both the food and the service were truly excellent.
The performances of the cast are uniformly excellent throughout.
She has done an excellent job of adapting the novel for the screen.
It is an excellent example of how a farm can work in harmony with nature.
The party provided an excellent opportunity to meet new people.
The apartment is in excellent condition and is ready to move into.
He was great at sport and excellent at art.
Our staff are excellent at advising small businesses.
The experience was excellent for students' self-confidence.
Ferns are excellent for planting in shady parts of the garden.

definitions.description: used to show that you are very pleased about something or that you approve of something
examples: You can all come? Excellent!
It's excellent to see so many people at today's event!

definitions.description: to be real; to be present in a place or situation
examples: Does life exist on other planets?
Few of these monkeys still exist in the wild.
Major differences continue to exist between the two countries.
A solution has been found and the problem no longer exists.
On his retirement the post will cease to exist.
Adequate facilities already exist to serve the needs of people visiting the town.
It is an art gallery that exists only on the internet.
Evidence of their relationship exists in the form of a series of letters.
I didn't think people like that existed any more.
The charity exists to support victims of crime.

definitions.description: to live, especially in a difficult situation or with very little money
examples: We existed on a diet of rice.
We can't exist on the money I'm earning.

definitions.description: to think or believe that something will happen or that somebody will do something
examples: The company is expecting record sales this year.
Change often happens when you least expect it.
Don't expect sympathy from me!
That's not the sort of behaviour I expect of you!
They never expected to find their dream home.
I looked back, half expecting to see someone following me.
Analysts expect the company to announce growth of at least 5 per cent.
I fully expected her to refuse my offer.
House prices are expected to rise sharply.
Do you really expect me to believe you?
Many people were expecting (that) the peace talks would break down.
It is widely expected that interest rates will rise.

definitions.description: to be waiting for somebody/something to arrive, as this has been arranged
examples: to expect a visit/call/letter from somebody
We were expecting him yesterday.
They are not expected until tomorrow.
Are you expecting visitors?
I'm expecting an important call.
We were expecting him to arrive yesterday.

definitions.description: to demand that somebody will do something because it is their duty or responsibility
examples: It is reasonable to expect changes in the way we work.
No one has a right to expect good results without working hard.
These are the high standards that hotel guests have come to expect.
He's still getting over his illness, so it's unrealistic to expect too much from him.
Are you clear what is expected of you?
You can't reasonably expect people to pay such high taxes.
We are expected to work on Saturdays.
It would be unreasonable to expect them to do all that work for free.
I expect to be paid promptly for the work.

definitions.label: (especially British English, informal)
definitions.description: used when you think something is probably true
examples: ‘Will you be late?’ ‘I expect so.’
‘Are you going out tonight?’ ‘I don't expect so.’
‘Who’s eaten all the cake?’ ‘Tom, I expect/I expect it was Tom.’

definitions.description: the knowledge and skill that you have gained through doing something for a period of time; the process of gaining this
examples: My lack of practical experience was a disadvantage.
Do you have any previous experience of this type of work?
This new approach draws on years of experience of teaching children to read.
a doctor with experience in dealing with patients suffering from stress
He gained extensive experience in the field of artificial intelligence whilst working on the project.
I have over ten years’ experience as a teacher.
The course provides hands-on experience with various systems.
She didn't get paid much but it was all good experience.
We all learn by experience.
The new player will bring a wealth of experience to the team.

definitions.description: the things that have happened to you that influence the way you think and behave
examples: Experience has taught me that life can be very unfair.
Experience shows that this strategy does not always work.
The book is based on personal experience.
It is important to try and learn from experience.
She knew from past experience that Ann would not give up easily.
In my experience, very few people really understand the problem.
He had first-hand experience of poverty.
the collective experience of everyday life

definitions.description: an event or activity that affects you in some way
examples: a unique/positive/wonderful experience
Share your experiences of parenthood by emailing the address below.
We aim to give our guests the experience of a lifetime.
It was her first experience of living alone.
The play is based loosely on his own life experiences.
He found the whole experience traumatic.
Losing four matches in a row proved a valuable learning experience (= it showed the players what they need to improve).
Living in the Arctic was very different from home and quite an experience (= unusual for us).

definitions.description: what it is like for somebody to use a service, do an activity, attend an event, etc.
examples: We are continually looking for ways to improve the customer experience.
Enjoy a fine dining experience with quality service.

definitions.description: events or knowledge shared by all the members of a particular group in society, that influences the way they think and behave
examples: musical forms like jazz that emerged out of the Black American experience

definitions.description: a scientific test that is done in order to study what happens and to gain new knowledge
examples: to do/perform/conduct an experiment
laboratory experiments
The results of the experiment were inconclusive.
The 30 subjects in each experiment were divided into two groups.
The temperature was kept constant during the experiment.
Many people do not like the idea of experiments on animals.
The experiment with cells from other species was unsuccessful.
Facts can be established by observation and experiment.

definitions.description: a new activity, idea or method that you try out to see what happens or what effect it has
examples: I've never cooked this before so it's an experiment.
the country’s brief experiment in democracy
His experiments with narrative form were very influential.
The system was installed four years ago as an experiment.

definitions.description: a person with special knowledge, skill or training in something
examples: a legal/security/medical/computer expert
Police consulted their own team of forensic experts.
According to our panel of leading industry experts, a downturn is inevitable.
Experts believe/predict/say…
Experts in the field of child psychology warn of the dangers of social media.
I don't pretend to be an expert on the subject .
Nobody can be an expert at everything.
You will need to become an expert in analysing data.
an expert on managing change in the workplace
He's an expert at getting his own way.
Don't ask me—I'm no expert!

definitions.description: a statement, fact, or situation that tells you why something happened; a reason given for something
examples: The most likely explanation is that his plane was delayed.
It's the only explanation that makes any sense.
a plausible/an alternative explanation
to offer/provide an explanation
I can't think of any possible explanation for his absence.
I'm sure there's a perfectly simple explanation for this.
She didn't give an adequate explanation for being late.
The book opens with an explanation of why some drugs are banned.
an explanation as to why he had left early
She left the room abruptly without explanation.
‘I had to see you,’ he said, by way of explanation.

definitions.description: a statement or piece of writing that tells you how something works or makes something easier to understand
examples: Other parts of the book contain unnecessarily lengthy explanations.
For a full explanation of how the machine works, turn to page 5.
The teacher gave the children a detailed explanation of the story.
He entered into a technical explanation about software and programming.

definitions.description: to show or make known a feeling, an opinion, etc. by words, looks or actions
examples: Teachers have expressed concern about the changes.
to express a view/an opinion
to express a hope/desire
to express fears/doubts
Customers expressed interest in trying the product.
I'd like to express my gratitude to everyone who helped us.
Words cannot express how pleased I am.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: to speak, write or communicate in some other way what you think or feel
examples: Some teenagers have difficulty expressing themselves.
Perhaps I have not expressed myself very well.
She expresses herself most fully in her paintings.
He expressed himself freely on the subject of immigration.
They expressed themselves delighted.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: to become obvious in a particular way
examples: Their pleasure expressed itself in a burst of applause.

definitions.label: (mathematics)
definitions.description: to represent something in a particular way, for example by symbols
examples: The figures are expressed as percentages.
Educational expenditure is often expressed in terms of the amount spent per student.

definitions.description: to remove air or liquid from something by pressing
examples: Coconut milk is expressed from grated coconuts.

definitions.label: (North American English)
definitions.description: to send something by express post
examples: As soon as I receive payment I will express the book to you.

definitions.label: (informal)
definitions.description: a word or phrase
examples: What's the meaning of the expression ‘on cloud nine’?
She uses a lot of slang expressions that I've never heard before.
Keep a list of useful words and expressions.
He's a pain in the butt, if you'll pardon the expression.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: things that people say, write or do in order to show their feelings, opinions and ideas
examples: Freedom of expression (= freedom to say what you think) is a basic human right.
The poet's anger finds expression in (= is shown in) the last verse of the poem.
Only in his dreams does he give expression to his fears.
He describes drawing as a very personal form of artistic expression.
Words, as a means of expression, can be limiting.
the expression of emotion/feelings
expressions of concern/sympathy/support
We are calling for expressions of interest from people wanting to take part in the project.
laws which aim to restrict free expression of opinion

definitions.description: a look on a person’s face that shows their thoughts or feelings
examples: The actors' gestures and facial expressions are perfect.
He had a pained expression on his face.
The blank expression in her eyes showed that she hadn't understood.
He looked down at the tiny child and his expression softened.
His expression changed from surprise to one of amusement.
Her expression betrayed nothing of her thoughts.
She wore an expression of anger.

definitions.description: a strong show of feeling when you are playing music, speaking, acting, etc.
examples: Try to put a little more expression into it!
She plays the violin with great expression.

definitions.description: a group of signs that represent an idea or a quantity
very great in degree
examples: We are working under extreme pressure at the moment.
people living in extreme poverty
extreme heat/cold/temperatures
The heat in the desert was extreme.

definitions.description: not ordinary or usual; serious or severe
examples: extreme weather events such as floods and heatwaves
Children will be removed from their parents only in extreme circumstances.
It can cause nausea and, in extreme cases, death.
The ship got into difficulties in extreme conditions.
She was forced to take extreme measures.
Don't go doing anything extreme like leaving the country.
It was the most extreme example of cruelty to animals I had ever seen.

definitions.description: far from what most people consider to be normal, reasonable or acceptable
examples: extreme left-wing/right-wing views
Fascism was basically an extreme form of nationalism.
an extreme nationalist organization
Their ideas are too extreme for me.
She didn't like the idea—it sounded too extreme.

definitions.description: as far as possible from the centre, the beginning or in the direction mentioned
examples: Kerry is in the extreme west of Ireland.
She sat on the extreme edge of her seat.
politicians on the extreme left of the party

definitions.description: to a very high degree
examples: It is extremely important to follow the directions exactly.
extremely useful/valuable
extremely dangerous/serious/complex
extremely popular/successful
She found it extremely difficult to get a job.
It's still an extremely rare occurrence.
The risks involved are extremely high.
extremely low temperatures
I would be extremely grateful if you could have a word with her.
Their new tablet is selling extremely well.
He works extremely hard.

definitions.description: one of several things that cause or influence something
examples: Obesity is a major risk factor for heart disease.
the key/crucial/deciding factor
Criminality is associated with a range of individual, family and environmental factors.
The result will depend on a number of different factors.
The closure of the mine was the single most important factor in the town's decline.
We have identified a few key factors in the project's success.

definitions.label: (mathematics)
definitions.description: a number that divides into another number exactly
examples: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12 are the factors of 12.

definitions.description: the amount by which something increases or decreases
examples: The real wage of the average worker has increased by a factor of over ten in the last 70 years.

definitions.description: a particular level on a scale of measurement
examples: a suntan lotion with a protection factor of 10
The wind-chill factor will make it seem colder.

definitions.label: (medical)
definitions.description: a substance in the blood that helps the clotting process. There are several types of this substance.
examples: Haemophiliacs have no factor 8 in their blood.

definitions.description: a building or group of buildings where goods are made, mainly by machine
examples: a car factory
The factory closed down ten years ago.
She works in the local textile factory.
factory workers

definitions.label: (disapproving)
definitions.description: a person or organization that continuously produces a large quantity of a particular thing
examples: This record label has become a real hit factory (= one that produces a lot of successful songs).
These universities are becoming colourless degree factories, with no sense of what higher learning is really about.

definitions.description: to not be successful in achieving something
examples: Many diets fail because they are boring.
Ultimately all their efforts failed.
a policy/plan fails
I failed in my attempt to persuade her.
He failed in his bid for the presidency.
The department failed to meet its sales targets.
They promised a lot, but utterly failed to deliver.
The song can't fail to be a hit (= definitely will be a hit).

definitions.description: to not pass a test or an exam; to decide that somebody/something has not passed a test or an exam
examples: What will you do if you fail?
He failed his driving test.
Students who fail the exam can retake it.
She was disqualified after failing a drugs test.
The restaurant failed a hygiene inspection.
The examiners failed over half the candidates.

definitions.description: to not do something
examples: People failed to recognize her talent.
His article fails to mention that he actually supported this change.
If you fail to comply, you can be fined.
The government has failed to provide the needed resources.
Such comments never failed to annoy him.
I fail to see (= I don't understand) why you won't even give it a try.
She cannot fail to (= must) be aware of the situation.
They failed in their duty to protect the public.

definitions.description: to stop working
examples: The brakes on my bike failed half way down the hill.
The air-conditioning system failed on the hottest day of the year.
Sadly, his kidneys had failed.

definitions.description: to become weak
examples: Her eyesight is failing.
The light began to fail.

definitions.label: (figurative)
definitions.description: to disappoint somebody; to be unable to help when needed
examples: When he lost his job, he felt he had failed his family.
She tried to be brave, but her courage failed her.
Words fail me (= I cannot express how I feel).

definitions.description: to not be enough when needed or expected
examples: The crops failed again last summer.
The rains had failed and the rivers were dry.

definitions.description: to be unable to continue
examples: Several banks failed during the recession.

definitions.label: (especially British English)
definitions.description: acceptable and appropriate in a particular situation
examples: a fair deal/wage/price
The punishment was very fair.
In the end, a draw was a fair result.
I give you fair warning, I’m not always this generous.
We wanted to resolve this matter in a way that would be fair to her.
Was it really fair to him to ask him to do all the work?
Moving to a new city wouldn't have been fair on the kids.
It's not fair on the students to keep changing the timetable.
It's only fair to add that they were not told about the problem until the last minute.
I think it is fair to say that they are pleased with this latest offer.
It's fair that they should give us something in return.
To be fair, she behaved better than we expected.
‘You should really have asked me first.’ ‘Right, okay, fair comment.’

definitions.description: treating everyone equally and according to the rules or law
examples: She has always been scrupulously fair.
They are fair and decent employers.
demands for a fairer distribution of wealth
his vision of a fairer, kinder society
The new tax is fairer than the old system.
We have to be fair to both players.
to receive a fair trial
For the first time, free and fair elections will be held.
It's not fair! He always gets more than me.

definitions.description: pale in colour
examples: a fair complexion
Kate had dark hair and fair skin.
She has long fair hair.
All her children are fair (= they all have fair hair).

definitions.description: quite large in number, size or amount
examples: A fair number of people came along.
There's been a fair amount of research on this topic.
a fair-sized town
We've still got a fair bit (= quite a lot) to do.
My birthday’s still a fair way off (= it’s still a long time until my birthday).

definitions.label: (especially British English)
definitions.description: quite good
examples: There's a fair chance that we might win this time.
It's a fair bet that they won't turn up.
I have a fair idea of what happened.
His knowledge of French is only fair.
Scoring twenty points was a fair achievement.

definitions.description: bright and not raining
examples: It was a fair and breezy day.
The day was set fair with the spring sun shining down.

definitions.label: (literary)
definitions.description: not too strong and blowing in the right direction
examples: They set sail with the first fair wind.

definitions.label: (literary or old use)
definitions.description: beautiful
examples: a fair maiden

definitions.description: a person who admires somebody/something or enjoys watching or listening to somebody/something very much
examples: sports/music fans
Movie fans will be familiar with his work already.
Crowds of football fans filled the streets.
I like his films, but I wouldn't say I'm a diehard fan (= one who strongly admires somebody/something in all circumstances).
I'm a big fan of her books.
I'm a huge fan of Rihanna.
I'm not a great fan of bushy beards (= I don't like them).

definitions.description: a machine that creates a current of air
examples: to switch on the electric fan
a fan heater
a fan blowing cold air

definitions.description: a thing that you hold in your hand and wave to create a current of cool air

definitions.label: (North American English)
definitions.description: the business of managing or working on a farm
examples: to take up farming
organic farming
sheep/fish/salmon farming
modern farming methods
a farming community
the British farming industry

definitions.label: (North American English also)
definitions.description: a popular style of clothes, hair, etc. at a particular time or place; the state of being popular
examples: the latest fashion trends
the new season’s fashions
Jeans are always in fashion.
Long skirts have come into fashion again.
Some styles never go out of fashion.

definitions.description: the business of making or selling clothes in new and different styles
examples: They all want to work in fashion.
household names in the world of fashion and design
a fashion magazine
the fashion industry

definitions.description: a popular way of behaving, doing an activity, etc.
examples: This theory, though recent, is more than a passing fashion.
Fashions in art and literature come and go.
He seemed to endorse the current fashion for neoliberal economics.
The fashion at the time was for teaching mainly the written language.

definitions.description: the bad feeling that you have when you are in danger or when a particular thing frightens you
examples: Her eyes showed no fear.
The child was shaking with fear.
I suddenly felt gripped by fear.
We were living in a perpetual state of fear and anxiety.
The attacks created a climate of fear.
Terror attacks are a tool to instil fear in the public.
He managed to overcome his fears.
Fear of crime can affect people's lives.
We lived in constant fear of losing our jobs.
Women should be able to work without fear of harassment.

definitions.description: a feeling of concern about somebody's safety or about something bad that might happen
examples: The doctor's report confirmed our worst fears.
Police tried hard to allay the fears of local residents.
her fears for her son’s safety
Alan spoke of his fears for the future.
the fear that he had cancer
The announcement sparked fears that interest rates will rise.
The government announced the new measures amid growing security fears.

definitions.description: to give food to a person or an animal
examples: Have you fed the cat yet?
The baby can't feed itself yet (= can't put food into its own mouth).
It's important to feed children a well-balanced diet.
He has to be fed liquids through a tube in his stomach.
The cattle are fed (on) barley.
The barley is fed to the cattle.
The animals are fed with hay and grass.

definitions.description: to eat food
examples: Slugs and snails feed at night.

definitions.description: to provide food for a person or group of people
examples: They have a large family to feed.
There's enough here to feed an army.
Have they been feeding you well?
They struggled to feed and clothe the children.
Having another mouth (= person) to feed can be a strain.

definitions.description: to give a plant a special substance to make it grow
examples: Feed the plants once a week.

definitions.description: to give advice, information, etc. to somebody/something
examples: We are constantly fed gossip and speculation by the media.
The media were being fed with accusations and lies.
Gossip and speculation are constantly fed to us by the media.

definitions.description: to supply something to somebody/something
examples: The lake is fed by a river.
The electricity line is fed with power through an underground cable.
Power is fed into the electricity line through an underground cable.

definitions.description: to put or push something into or through a machine
examples: He fed the meter with coins.
He fed coins into the meter.
The information was fed into the data store.
The fabric is fed through the machine.

definitions.description: to satisfy a need, desire, etc. and keep it strong
examples: For drug addicts, the need to feed the addiction takes priority over everything else.

definitions.description: being a woman or a girl
examples: a female student/employee/artist/athlete
She has written brilliant roles for strong female characters.
a predominantly female audience
Two of the candidates must be female.

definitions.description: belonging to the sex that can lay eggs or give birth to babies
examples: a female cat
female reproductive organs

definitions.description: of women; typical of women; affecting women
examples: female characteristics
the female role
a female preserve (= an activity that only women do)
Weaving was a traditionally female occupation.

definitions.label: (biology)
definitions.description: that can produce fruit

definitions.label: (specialist)
definitions.description: having a hole that another part fits into
examples: a female plug

definitions.label: (US English)
definitions.description: a type of literature that describes imaginary people and events, not real ones
examples: a work of popular fiction
historical/romantic/crime fiction
to write/read fiction
a crime fiction writer

definitions.description: a thing that is invented or imagined and is not true
