to score a goal/try/touchdown/victory/point/run
Brazil failed to score a win, leaving their further progress in the competition in doubt.
the only man to score a hat-trick in a World Cup final
On his debut at Old Trafford he scored 154 against Australia.
She scored 20 points in 36 minutes.
He scored 30 goals in 20 games.

definitions.description: to keep a record of the points, goals, etc. won in a game or competition
examples: Who's going to score?

definitions.description: to gain marks in a test or an exam
examples: She scored 98 per cent in the French test.
Girls usually score highly in language exams.
Women consistently scored higher than men in this test.
Some studies show that low-income Latino adolescents tend to score low on self-esteem.

definitions.description: to give something/somebody a particular number of points
examples: The tests are scored by psychologists.
Score each criterion on a scale of 1 to 5.
a scoring system

definitions.description: to be worth a particular number of points
examples: Each correct answer will score two points.

definitions.description: to succeed; to have an advantage
examples: The army continued to score successes in the south.
Lewis scored a win with a hugely funny sketch about a car salesman.
She's scored again with her latest blockbuster.
Bicycles score over other forms of transport in towns.

definitions.description: to arrange a piece of music for one or more musical instruments or for voices
examples: The piece is scored for violin, viola and cello.
The director invited him to score the movie (= write the music for it).

definitions.description: to make a cut or mark on a surface
examples: Score the card first with a knife.

definitions.label: (slang)
definitions.description: to have sex with a new partner
examples: Did you score last night?

definitions.label: (slang)
definitions.description: to buy or get illegal drugs
the flat surface at the front of a television, computer, or other electronic device, on which you see pictures or information
examples: a computer screen
a monitor with a 21-inch screen
They were staring at the television screen.
Move your cursor to the top of the screen.
Tessa glanced at the phone's little screen.
an LCD/plasma screen
Hundreds of fans watched on giant television screens.
The image came up on the screen for a few seconds.
The birds appear as red dots on the radar screen.
Information can be viewed on screen or printed out.
the screen display
The system was designed with a menu bar at the bottom of the screen.

definitions.description: the large flat surface that films or pictures are shown on
examples: a cinema/movie screen
an eight-screen cinema
The movie will be coming to your screens shortly.
This film should keep you glued to the screen (= unable to stop watching) for two hours.
The film hits cinema screens in November.
The film demands to be seen on a big screen.

definitions.description: films or television in general
examples: He has adapted the play for the screen.
Some actors never watch themselves on screen.
His face never appears on screen.
She was a star of stage and screen (= plays and films).
a screen actor
She has great screen presence (= she makes a good impression on screen).
He made his screen debut in 1954 as a stable boy.
the screen adaptation (= film) of John Steinbeck's novel East of Eden

definitions.description: the data or images shown on a computer screen
examples: Press the F1 key to display a help screen.
Can you do a printout of this screen for me?
I posted the screen grab online.

definitions.description: a tall, flat piece of furniture or equipment that is fixed to a wall, etc. or that can be moved to divide a room or to keep one area hidden or separate
examples: The nurse put a screen around the bed.
A wooden screen hid one corner of the room.
She went behind the screen and changed into the ballet costume.

definitions.label: (figurative)
definitions.description: something that prevents somebody from seeing or being aware of something, or that protects somebody/something
examples: We planted a screen of tall trees.
A screen of bodyguards protected the President.
All the research was conducted behind a screen of secrecy.

definitions.label: (especially North American English)
definitions.description: a wire or plastic net that is held in a frame and fastened on a window, or a door, to let in air but keep out insects
examples: Do you have screens on your windows?

definitions.description: a wood or stone structure in a church, that partly separates the main area from the altar or choir
a system of checking a person or thing to find out whether or not something, typically a disease, is present
examples: You should get a health screen every couple of years.
Candidates for this position must be able to pass a drug screen.

definitions.description: an attempt to find somebody/something, especially by looking carefully for them/it
examples: a long search for the murder weapon
She began a search for new premises
The search for a cure goes on.
The search is on (= has begun) for someone to fill the post.
Detectives carried out a thorough search of the building.
Police conducted a fingertip search of the garden.
She went into the kitchen in search of (= looking for) a drink.
Eventually the search was called off.
a search and rescue team

definitions.description: an act or the activity of looking for information on a computer or on the internet
examples: I've just done a search on the internet and came up with this website.
I did an image search for ‘vinyl record’.
A Google search on her name yielded nothing.
Our site is found on the first page of search results.

definitions.description: any of the four main periods of the year: spring, summer, autumn and winter
examples: the changing seasons
Autumn is my favourite season.

definitions.description: a period of the year in tropical countries when it is either very dry or it rains a lot
examples: In this climate there are no real changes of temperature, just a wet and a dry season.
Next month is the start of the rainy season.

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: a period of time during a year when a particular activity happens or is done
examples: the cricket/football/hunting/shooting season
He scored his first goal of the season on Saturday.
They achieved their first win of the season.
He will not be offered a new contract at the end of the season.
The team have had a dream start to the season.
The female changes colour during the breeding season.
The growing season for these trees varies depending on species.
We're in the middle of the roughest hurricane season we've seen in quite some time.
The hotels are always full during the peak season (= when most people are on holiday).
the holiday season
the tourist season
the holiday season (= the time of Thanksgiving, Hanukkah, Christmas and New Year)
the festive season (= Christmas and New Year)
the summer blockbuster season

definitions.description: a period of time in which a play is shown in one place; a series of plays, films or television programmes
examples: The play opens for a second season in London next week.
a season of films by Alfred Hitchcock

definitions.description: a period of time during one year when a particular style of clothes, hair, etc. is popular and fashionable
examples: This season's look is soft and romantic.
The fashion magazines are full of the new look for the spring season.

definitions.label: (especially North American English)
definitions.description: a set of television or radio programmes that have the same characters or deal with the same subject
examples: The show begins its second season next week.
I binge-watched an entire season of ‘Succession’ (= watched all of the episodes on one occasion) on Sunday.
I can't wait to see the season finale (= last episode in the season).
the season opener (= the first episode in the season)

definitions.description: a place where you can sit, for example a chair
examples: She sat back in her seat.
He put his shopping on the seat behind him.
Please take a seat (= sit down).
Ladies and gentlemen, please take your seats (= sit down).
the front/passenger seat (= in a car)
the back/rear seats
a child seat (= for a child in a car)
a window/an aisle seat (= on a plane or train)
a window/corner seat (= one near a window/in a corner)
a car/toilet seat
We used the branch of an old tree as a seat.
We all filed back to our seats in silence.

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: with the number of seats mentioned
examples: a ten-seater minibus
an all-seater stadium (= in which nobody is allowed to stand)

definitions.description: the part of a chair, etc. on which you actually sit
examples: a steel chair with a plastic seat

definitions.description: a place where you pay to sit in a plane, train, theatre, etc.
examples: Call the theatre box office to book your seats.
To reserve a seat, visit our website.
There are no seats left on that flight.
Airlines often give great deals to fill empty seats.
We had excellent seats for the show, on the third row.

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: an official position as a member of a parliament, council, committee, etc.
examples: a seat on the city council/in Parliament/in Congress
Republicans currently hold 51 seats in the Senate.
The majority of seats on the board will be held by business representatives.
The party won 32 seats in the recent elections.
Several ministers are in danger of losing their seats.
to take your seat (= to begin your duties, especially in Parliament)
One vote could make all the difference in the highly marginal seat of Crawley.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: a place where people are involved in a particular activity, especially a city that has a university or the offices of a government
examples: Washington is the seat of government of the US.
a university town renowned as a seat of learning

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: a large house in the country that belongs to a member of the upper class
examples: For the first two years of her life she lived at Ickworth, the family seat in Sussex.

definitions.label: (especially formal)
definitions.description: the part of the body on which a person sits
the part of a pair of trousers that covers a person’s seat
used to introduce the second of a list of points you want to make in a speech or piece of writing
examples: Firstly, it's expensive, and secondly, it's too slow.
First of all, there's no time to do all this, and secondly, it's the wrong thing to be doing anyway.
Secondly, and importantly, cultural influences on behaviour are discussed.

definitions.description: known about by only a few people; kept hidden from others
examples: secret information/meetings/talks
They belong to an age-old secret society.
He tried to keep it secret from his family.
Details of the proposals remain secret.
a secret passage leading to the beach
The two candidates were chosen by a secret ballot (= in which nobody knows how you voted) of MPs.
He's a natural salesman, whose secret weapon is the sheer confidence and optimism that he exudes.
The group is on a highly secret mission.
Secret police documents were leaked to the press.
The scandal was kept secret from the French public for 18 years.
What could be so secret that it had to stay hidden?

definitions.description: used to describe actions and behaviour that you do not tell other people about
examples: He's a secret drinker.
I didn't know you were a secret football fan.
her secret fears
Perhaps he has secret hopes that she'll go back to him.

definitions.description: liking to have secrets that other people do not know about; showing this
examples: They were so secret about everything.
Jessica caught a secret smile flitting between the two of them.

definitions.description: a person who works in an office, working for another person, dealing with mail and phone calls, keeping records, arranging meetings with people, etc.
examples: a legal/medical secretary
the mayor's press secretary
Please contact my secretary to make an appointment.
He is secretary to the board of governors.

definitions.description: an official of a club, society, etc. who deals with mail, keeping records and making business arrangements
examples: the membership secretary
She served as club secretary for 25 years.
The union's branch secretary said he hoped a solution would be found.
secretary to the Jockey Club

definitions.description: (in the UK) the head of an important government department
the head of a government department, chosen by the president
examples: Secretary of the Treasury
She was deputy secretary of agriculture.

definitions.description: an assistant of a government minister, an ambassador, etc.
examples: Ms Watson is a former parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Education.

definitions.description: to give the impression of being or doing something
examples: You seem happy.
Do whatever seems best to you.
This may seem obvious to you.
It seems clear that there has been a mistake.
It seems likely that they will lose the election.
Strange as it may seem, exactly the same thing happened to me.
He seems a nice man.
She seems to be a smart woman.
You seem to be nervous.
People aren’t always what they seem to be.
It seemed like a good idea at the time.
It always seemed as though they would get married.
‘He'll be there, then?’ ‘So it seems (= people say so).’
It seems to me that teachers have to work pretty hard.
It must have seemed to him that he was safe.
It seems that they know what they're doing.
They seem to know what they're doing.

definitions.description: used to make what you say about your thoughts, feelings or actions less strong
examples: I seem to have left my book at home.
I can't seem to (= I've tried, but I can't) get started today.

definitions.description: used to suggest that something is true when you are not certain or when you want to be polite
examples: It would seem that we all agree.
This last point, it seems to me, is particularly important.
It seems only reasonable to ask students to buy a dictionary.

definitions.label: (figurative)
definitions.description: an understanding about something; an ability to judge something
examples: One of the most important things in a partner is a sense of humour (= the ability to find things funny or make people laugh).
He has a very good sense of direction (= finds the way to a place easily).
She has lost all sense of direction in her life (= the idea of what she should do in her life).
Always try to keep a sense of proportion (= of the relative importance of different things).
a sense of rhythm/timing
a sense of fun/adventure
Readers gain a real sense of what life was like in the camp.
Alex doesn't have any dress sense (= does not know which clothes look attractive).

definitions.description: good understanding and judgement; knowledge of what is sensible or practical behaviour
examples: You should have the sense to take advice when it is offered.
There's no sense in (= it is not sensible) worrying about it now.
Can't you talk sense (= say something sensible)?
There's a lot of sense in what Mary says.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: the meaning that a word or phrase has; a way of understanding something
examples: That word has three senses.
The word ‘love’ is used in different senses by different people.
Globalization in the broadest sense is nothing new.
The word ‘perspective’ is being used here in a technical sense.
He was a true friend, in every sense of the word (= in every possible way).
In a sense (= in one way) it doesn't matter any more.
In some senses (= in one or more ways) the criticisms were justified.
In no sense can the issue be said to be resolved.
I am using ‘cold’ in the sense of ‘unfriendly’.
I don't mean that the press ought to be free in the sense that no one ought to pay for it.
There is a sense in which we are all to blame for the tragedy.

definitions.description: one of the five powers (sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch) that your body uses to get information about the world around you
examples: the five senses
Dogs have a keen sense (= strong sense) of smell.
the sense organs (= eyes, ears, nose, etc.)
I could hardly believe the evidence of my own senses (= what I could see, hear, etc.).

definitions.description: a feeling about something important
examples: His career was guided by a strong sense of duty.

My parents instilled a strong sense of responsibility in me.
Clubs try to create a sense of community.
Helmets can give cyclists a false sense of security.
He felt an overwhelming sense of loss.
I had the sense that he was worried about something.
I got the sense that she wasn't very pleased to see us.

definitions.label: (old-fashioned)
definitions.description: a normal state of mind; the ability to think clearly
examples: If she threatens to leave, it should bring him to his senses.
I waited for them to come to their senses and return.
No one in their right senses would give him the job!
Are you out of your senses? You'll be killed!

definitions.description: forming a unit by itself; not joined to something else
examples: They have begun to sleep in separate rooms.
Raw meat must be kept separate from cooked meat.
The school is housed in two separate buildings.
Write a list of names on a separate piece of paper.

definitions.description: different; not connected
examples: a separate incident/issue
The companies now exist as two separate entities.

This is a completely separate matter.
It happened on three separate occasions.

to merge the two previously separate businesses
species from widely separate parts of the world

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: a set of television or radio programmes or podcasts that deal with the same subject or that have the same characters
examples: The first episode of the new series is on Saturday.

the hit comedy series ‘The Big Bang Theory’

definitions.description: several events or things of a similar kind that happen one after the other
examples: The incident sparked off a series of events that nobody had foreseen.

definitions.label: (sport)
definitions.description: a set of sports games played between the same two teams
examples: the World Series (= in baseball)

definitions.label: (specialist)
definitions.description: an electrical circuit in which the current passes through all the parts in the correct order
examples: batteries connected in series

definitions.description: bad or dangerous

definitions.description: thinking about things in a careful and sensible way; not silly

definitions.label: (informal)

examples: Believe me, I'm deadly (= extremely) serious.

definitions.description: needing to be thought about carefully; not only for pleasure
examples: a serious article
a serious newspaper
an appreciation of serious music
serious drama/fiction

definitions.description: that must be treated as important
examples: a serious matter
serious questions/concerns/doubts
serious allegations/charges

definitions.label: (informal)
definitions.description: used to emphasize that there is a large amount of something
examples: You can earn serious money doing that.

definitions.description: to give somebody food or drink, for example at a restaurant or during a meal

Shall I serve?

The quiche can be served hot or cold.

definitions.description: to be enough for somebody/something
examples: This dish will serve four hungry people.

definitions.label: (especially British English)
definitions.description: to help a customer or sell them something in a shop
examples: Are you being served?

definitions.description: to be useful to somebody in achieving or satisfying something

definitions.description: to provide an area or a group of people with a product or service

definitions.description: to work or perform duties for a person, an organization, a country, etc.; to spend a period of time in a particular job
examples: He served as a captain in the army.

definitions.description: to be suitable for a particular use, especially when nothing else is available

definitions.description: to have a particular effect or result
examples: The judge said the punishment would serve as a warning to others.

definitions.description: to spend a period of time in prison
examples: prisoners serving life sentences

definitions.label: (law)

examples: to serve a writ/summons on somebody

definitions.description: to start playing by throwing the ball into the air and hitting it
examples: Who's serving?

definitions.description: an organization or a company that provides something for the public or does something for the government

the Foreign Service

the development of new goods and services

definitions.label: (especially British English)
definitions.description: the serving of customers in hotels, restaurants, and shops
examples: The food was good but the service was very slow.
I complained about the poor service.
10% will be added to your bill for service.

definitions.description: the work that somebody does for an organization, etc., especially when it continues for a long time or is admired very much
examples: She has just celebrated 25 years' service with the company.

definitions.description: the army, the navy and the air force; the work done by people in them
examples: Most of the boys went straight into the services.

definitions.description: the use that you can get from a vehicle or machine; the state of being used
examples: That computer gave us very good service.

examples: a service engineer

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: the particular skills or help that a person is able to offer
examples: You need the services of a good lawyer.

definitions.label: (North American English)
definitions.description: a religious ceremony
examples: a funeral/memorial service

to go to morning/evening service

definitions.description: a bus, train, etc. that goes regularly to a particular place at a particular time

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: a place next to a motorway where you can stop for petrol, a meal, the toilets, etc.
examples: motorway services
It's five miles to the next services.
The next services is/are five miles away.

definitions.description: an act of hitting the ball in order to start playing; the way that you hit it
examples: It's your service (= your turn to start playing).
Her service has improved.

definitions.description: a complete set of plates, dishes, etc. that match each other
examples: a tea service (= cups, saucers, a teapot and plates, for serving tea)

definitions.label: (old-fashioned)
definitions.description: the state or position of being a servant
examples: to be in/go into service (= to be/become a servant)
a job in domestic service

definitions.label: (law)
definitions.description: the formal giving of an official document, etc. to somebody
examples: the service of a demand for payment

definitions.description: to move or make somebody/something move with short quick movements from side to side or up and down
examples: The whole house shakes when a train goes past.

She shook her hair loose.

definitions.description: to move something in a particular direction by shaking
examples: She bent down to shake a pebble out of her shoe.

definitions.description: to take somebody’s hand and move it up and down as a way of saying hello or to show that you agree about something
examples: Do people in Italy shake hands when they meet?

Our host shook each of us warmly by the hand.
They shook hands on the deal (= to show that they had reached an agreement).
They shook on the deal (= shook hands to show the deal was agreed).
Let's shake on it.

definitions.description: to turn your head from side to side as a way of saying ‘no’ or to show that you are sad, feel doubt, etc.
examples: ‘Drink?’ he offered. She shook her head.

She shook her head in disbelief.
He shook his head at the thought.

definitions.description: to show that you are angry with somebody; to threaten somebody by shaking your fist (= closed hand)
examples: The man shook his fist at the court after he was sentenced.

definitions.description: to make short quick movements that you cannot control, for example because you are cold or afraid
examples: Her hands had started to shake.
He was shaking with fear.
He saw his mother turn away, her shoulders shaking with laughter.
His whole body shook with rage.
I was shaking like a leaf.

definitions.description: to sound unsteady, usually because you are nervous, upset or angry
examples: ‘Who are you?’ he asked, his voice shaking.

definitions.description: to shock or upset somebody very much
examples: He was badly shaken by the news of her death.

Shaken up by the early goal against them, the team began to fight back.

definitions.description: to make a belief or an idea less certain
examples: The incident had shaken her faith in him.

definitions.description: to get rid of something
examples: I can't seem to shake off this cold.

definitions.label: (figurative)

examples: a rectangular/spherical/cylindrical shape

fantastic creatures that can change shape and be either visible or invisible

Candles come in all shapes and sizes.
Glass is blown or moulded into many shapes.

It was a pretty stupid thing to do.
You've been warned, so don't do anything stupid.
I was stupid enough to believe him.
It was stupid of you to get involved.
That was just plain stupid!
We made some incredibly stupid business mistakes.

definitions.label: (sometimes offensive)
definitions.description: not clever or intelligent; slow to learn or understand
examples: He'll manage—he isn't stupid.
Forgetting my notes made me look stupid.
She always makes me feel really stupid.

definitions.label: (informal)
definitions.description: used to emphasize that you are annoyed with somebody/something
examples: I can't get the stupid thing open!
Get your stupid feet off the chair!

definitions.description: to achieve something that you have been trying to do or get; to have the result or effect that was intended
examples: Our plan succeeded.
Whether we succeed or fail depends on ingenuity and luck.
He succeeded in getting a place at art school.
I tried to discuss it with her but only succeeded in making her angry (= I failed and did the opposite of what I intended).

definitions.description: to be successful in your job, earning money, power, respect, etc.
examples: You will have to work hard if you are to succeed.
She doesn't have the ruthlessness required to succeed in business.
He had hoped to succeed as a violinist.

definitions.description: to come next after somebody/something and take their/its place or position
examples: Who succeeded Kennedy as President?
Their early success was succeeded by a period of miserable failure.
Strands of DNA are reproduced through succeeding generations.

definitions.description: to gain the right to a title, property, etc. when somebody dies
examples: She succeeded to the throne (= became queen) in 1558.
He had no right to succeed to the tenancy when his father died.

definitions.description: achieving your aims or what was intended
examples: The experiment was entirely successful.
We congratulated them on the successful completion of the project.
He's always been highly successful in his work.
They were successful in winning the contract.
No one can be successful at everything.
I wasn't very successful at keeping the news secret.

definitions.description: having become popular and/or made a lot of money
examples: The play was very successful on Broadway.
a successful actor/businessman
She has had a long and successful career in television.
The company has had another successful year.

definitions.description: quickly and unexpectedly
examples: I suddenly realized what I had to do.
I suddenly became aware of just how late it was.
She took ill and died suddenly at her home.
You might suddenly find yourself in dire need of cash.
A pedestrian suddenly appeared in front of the taxi.
I tried to sit up but I suddenly felt dizzy.

definitions.label: (British English also)
definitions.description: to put forward an idea or a plan for other people to think about
examples: I'd like to suggest a different explanation for the company's decline.
The designer is known for suggesting innovative ideas to her clients.
He thought long and hard, but no answer suggested itself.
A solution immediately suggested itself to me (= I immediately thought of a solution).
I strongly suggest (that) you don't get involved.
I suggested going in my car.
It has been suggested that bright children take their exams early.
It has been suggested that bright children should take their exams early.
‘We could go for a drive,’ Nate suggested hopefully.

definitions.description: to tell somebody about a suitable person, thing, method, etc. for a particular job or purpose
examples: Who would you suggest for the job?
She suggested Paris as a good place for the conference.
She suggested John as chairman.
Can you suggest a better way of doing it?
May I suggest a white wine with this dish, Sir?
There is a suggested donation of $5 to attend the show.
Can you suggest how I might contact him?

definitions.description: to put an idea into somebody’s mind; to make somebody think that something is true
examples: All the evidence suggests (that) he stole the money.
Recent studies suggest the possibility of a cure for the disease.
Some believe that organic foods offer no health benefits, but this research suggests otherwise.
The symptoms suggest a minor heart attack.
The stage lighting was used to suggest a beach scene.
What do these results suggest to you?

definitions.description: to state something indirectly
examples: Are you suggesting (that) I’m lazy?
I’m not suggesting (that) she was responsible for the accident.
I would never suggest such a thing.
It is not far-fetched to suggest a connection between them.
You're not seriously suggesting that is a plausible explanation?
I do not mean to suggest that the poem is purely biographical.
I am merely suggesting that there is more than one way to view this matter.

definitions.description: an idea or a plan that you mention for somebody else to think about
examples: Can I make a suggestion?
Do you have any suggestions?
I would like to offer a suggestion.
He rejected my suggestion as impractical.
The report offers suggestions for improvement to policy.
I'd like to hear your suggestions for ways of raising money.
We welcome any comments and suggestions on these proposals.
Are there any suggestions about how best to tackle the problem?
He agreed with my suggestion that we should change the date.
We are open to suggestions (= willing to listen to ideas from other people).
We need to get it there by four. Any suggestions?

definitions.description: a reason to think that something, especially something bad, is true
examples: A spokesman dismissed any suggestion of a boardroom rift.
There is no suggestion of any impropriety.
There was no suggestion that he was doing anything illegal.

definitions.description: putting an idea into people’s minds by connecting it with other ideas
examples: Most advertisements work through suggestion.
the power of suggestion

definitions.label: (formal or literary)
definitions.description: a slight amount or sign of something
examples: She looked at me with just a suggestion of a smile.
He spoke English with a suggestion of a French accent.
Her eyes contained a strong suggestion of mischief.

definitions.description: a set of clothes made of the same cloth, including a jacket and trousers or a skirt
examples: She was wearing a grey business suit.
He is dressed in a formal black suit.
They won't let men into the restaurant without a suit and tie.
a two-/three-piece suit (= of two/three pieces of clothing)
a pinstripe suit

definitions.description: a set of clothing worn for a particular activity
examples: a diving suit
a suit of armour
His parents had bought him a new suit of clothes for the occasion.

definitions.description: any of the four sets that form a pack of cards
examples: The suits are called hearts, clubs, diamonds and spades.

definitions.description: a claim or complaint against somebody that a person or an organization can make in court
examples: to file/bring a suit against somebody
a divorce suit

definitions.label: (informal)
definitions.description: a person with an important job as a manager in a company or organization, especially one who is thought to work mainly with financial matters or to have a lot of influence
examples: We can leave the detailed negotiations to the suits.
He’s a ‘suit’, not a ‘creative’.

definitions.description: to help or encourage somebody/something by saying or showing that you agree with them/it
examples: to support an idea/a view
The party fully supports new welfare reform bill.
Efforts to reduce waste are strongly supported by environmental groups.
The majority of ordinary citizens did not support the war.
If you raise it at the meeting, I'll support you.
The government supported the unions in their demand for a minimum wage.

definitions.description: to give or be ready to give help to somebody if they need it
examples: an organization that supports people with AIDS
She supported her husband through many difficult times.
The company will support customers in Europe (= solve their problems with a product).

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: to like a particular sports team, watch their games, etc.
examples: Which team do you support?
Who do you support?

definitions.description: to help or encourage something to be successful by giving it money
examples: The project was supported by grants from various charities.
A number of famous actors actively supported the campaign.
Several major companies are supporting the project.

definitions.description: to provide everything necessary, especially money, so that somebody/something can live or exist
examples: He struggles to support his family.
She supported herself through college by working as a waitress in a local bar.
He turned to crime to support his drug habit.
The atmosphere of Mars could not support life.

definitions.description: to help to show that something is true
examples: Current data support this hypothesis.
There is no evidence to support his claims.
The witness's story was not supported by the evidence.
He said the figures were questionable and not well supported.

definitions.description: to hold somebody/something in position; to prevent somebody/something from falling
examples: a platform supported by concrete pillars
Support the baby's head when you hold it.
She walked carefully down the stairs, supported by her grandson.

definitions.description: to perform in a pop or rock concert before the main performer
examples: They were supported by a local Liverpool band.

definitions.description: to allow a particular program, language or device to be used with it
examples: This digital audio player supports multiple formats.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: to think or believe that something is true or possible (based on the knowledge that you have)
examples: Getting a visa isn't as simple as you might suppose.
Prices will go up, I suppose.
I don't suppose for a minute that he'll agree (= I'm sure that he won't).
It's reasonable to suppose that he left the note after he tried to call her.
Why do you suppose he resigned?
I suppose all the tickets have been sold now, have they?
There is no reason to suppose she's lying.
I suppose you think it's funny, do you (= showing anger)?
She had supposed him (to be) very rich.
I had supposed him a younger man.

definitions.description: used to make a statement, request or suggestion less direct or less strong
examples: I could take you in the car, I suppose (= but I don't really want to).
‘Can I borrow the car?’ ‘I suppose so (= Yes, but I'm not happy about it).’
What I’m saying, I suppose, is that she’s not really suitable for the job.
I don’t suppose (that) I could have a look at your newspaper, could I?
Suppose we take a later train?

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: to pretend that something is true; to imagine what would happen if something were true
examples: Suppose flights are fully booked on that day—which other day could we go?
Let us suppose, for example, that you are married with two children.
Let's suppose for a moment that these four points are correct.
The theory supposes the existence of life on other planets.
Suppose him (to be) dead—what then?

definitions.description: an event, a piece of news, etc. that is unexpected or that happens suddenly
examples: What a nice surprise!
I have a surprise for you!
a surprise attack
There are few surprises in this year's budget.
It comes as no surprise to learn that they broke their promises.
Her letter came as a complete surprise.
‘The appointment came as a pleasant surprise to me,’ she says.
The announcements came as something of a surprise to them.
There are lots of surprises in store for visitors to the gallery.
He was there on a surprise visit to the troops.
Life’s full of surprises.
She likes springing surprises on people.
Visitors to the gallery are in for a few surprises.

definitions.description: a feeling caused by something happening suddenly or unexpectedly
examples: a look of surprise
She looked up in surprise.
He gasped with surprise at her strength.
They couldn't conceal their surprise at seeing us together.
I got a surprise when I saw the bill.
To everyone's surprise, the plan succeeded.
Much to my surprise, I passed.
Imagine our surprise when he walked into the room!
When we went inside we got a nasty surprise.
The decision has been greeted with surprise.
They expressed surprise at the outcome.

definitions.description: the use of methods that cause feelings of surprise
examples: A successful campaign should have an element of surprise.

definitions.description: feeling or showing surprise
examples: a surprised look
She looked surprised when I told her.
I was surprised at how quickly she agreed.
I'm surprised at you, behaving like that in front of the kids.
They were surprised to find that he'd already left.
You shouldn’t be surprised (that) he didn’t come.
Don't be surprised if I pretend not to recognize you.
‘Will she cancel the party?’ ‘I wouldn't be surprised.’
You’d be surprised how many people voted for him.
He was pleasantly surprised to discover that he was no longer afraid.
to be a little/a bit/quite surprised
She seemed somewhat surprised at his reaction.

definitions.description: causing surprise
examples: It’s not surprising (that) they lost.
The frequency of such bad weather is hardly surprising given how far north we are.
A surprising number of people came.
We had a surprising amount in common.
It's surprising what people will do for money.
It’s surprising how many people applied for the job.

definitions.description: an investigation of the opinions, behaviour, etc. of a particular group of people, which is usually done by asking them questions
examples: A recent survey showed 75 per cent of those questioned were in favour of the plan.
The survey revealed/found that…
to conduct/carry out/do/complete a survey
According to the survey, many young adults have experimented with drugs of some kind.
Another national survey conducted last year found the same result.
Roughly half of survey respondents express strong interest in additional education.
The results of the survey come as no surprise to us.

definitions.description: the act of examining and recording the measurements, features, etc. of an area of land in order to make a map or plan of it
examples: an aerial survey (= made by taking photographs from a plane, drone, etc.)
A geological survey revealed the presence of oil beneath the ground.

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: an examination of the condition of a house, etc., usually done for somebody who is thinking of buying it
examples: a detailed structural survey

definitions.description: a general study, view or description of something
examples: a comprehensive survey of modern music
a historical survey of children's clothing

definitions.description: containing, or tasting as if it contains, a lot of sugar
examples: a cup of hot sweet tea
sweet food
I had a craving for something sweet.
roast duck with a sweet and sour sauce
sweet sherry
This wine is too sweet for me.
I found the dessert a bit sweet for my taste.

definitions.description: having a pleasant smell
examples: a sweet-smelling rose
The air was sweet with incense.

definitions.description: having a pleasant sound
examples: a sweet voice

definitions.description: pleasant and not containing any harmful substances
examples: the sweet air of a mountain village

definitions.description: making you feel happy and/or satisfied
examples: Goodnight. Sweet dreams.
I can't tell you how sweet this victory is.
He played a sweet shot onto the final green (= in golf).
an act of sweet revenge

definitions.label: (especially British English)
definitions.description: attractive
examples: His sister's a sweet young thing.
You look sweet in this photograph.
We stayed in a sweet little hotel on the seafront.

definitions.description: having or showing a kind character
examples: She gave him her sweetest smile.
He's one of the sweetest people I know.
It was sweet of them to offer to help.
He’s not what you’d call sweet-tempered!

definitions.label: (especially North American English, informal)
definitions.description: used to show that you approve of something
examples: Free tickets? Sweet!

definitions.description: a person, an object, an event, etc. that represents a more general quality or situation
examples: The vase is decorated with religious symbols.
The new school stands as a symbol of hope for a better future.
Mandela became a symbol of the anti-apartheid struggle.

definitions.description: a sign, number, letter, etc. that has a fixed meaning, especially in science, mathematics and music
examples: the mathematical symbol for infinity
Hotels that display this symbol offer activities for children.

definitions.description: an organized set of ideas or theories or a particular way of doing something
examples: reform of the country's education system
the criminal justice system
the healthcare system
the legal/financial/political system
Systems are in place for dealing with complaints.
a system of government

definitions.description: a group of things, pieces of equipment, etc. that are connected or work together
examples: They installed a security system but it failed.
How does the system work?

definitions.description: a set of computer equipment and programs that are used together
examples: to develop a new computer system
We're designing a voice-recognition system.
computerized information systems

definitions.description: a human or an animal body, or a part of it, when it is being thought of as the organs and processes that make it function
examples: Wait until the drugs have passed through your system.
the male reproductive system
Returning to work after a long break can be a terrible shock to the system (= a big change that is difficult to deal with).

definitions.label: (informal, usually disapproving)
definitions.description: the rules or people that control a country or an organization, especially when they seem to be unfair because you cannot change them
examples: You can't beat the system (= you must accept it).
You have to learn how to work the system if you want to succeed.
young people rebelling against the system

definitions.description: a small computer that is easy to carry, with a large touch screen and usually without a physical keyboard
examples: The company has launched its latest 10-inch tablet.
Consumers show a growing preference for tablets and smartphones over PCs and laptops.

definitions.label: (especially British English)
definitions.description: a small round solid piece of medicine that you swallow
examples: Take two tablets with water before meals.
I took the tablets prescribed by my doctor.
The drug is now available in tablet and capsule form.

definitions.description: an amount of a substance in a small, round, solid piece
examples: water purification tablets

definitions.label: (figurative)
definitions.description: a flat piece of stone that has words written on it, especially one that has been fixed to a wall in memory of an important person or event
examples: The school has a memorial tablet engraved with the name of the founder.
We can be very flexible—our entry requirements are not set in tablets of stone (= they can be changed).

definitions.label: (old-fashioned, formal)
definitions.description: a piece of soap

definitions.label: (North American English)
definitions.description: a number of pieces of paper for writing or drawing on, that are fastened together at one edge

definitions.label: (North American English)
definitions.description: a result that you try to achieve
examples: to meet/hit a target
The firm is on track to achieve its growth target for the year.
The university will reach its target of 5 000 students next September.
The department has missed its sales target for the third month running.
Set yourself targets that you can reasonably hope to achieve.
The new sports complex is on target to open in June.
These figures are way off target.
a target date of April 2022
a target audience/market (= the particular audience, area etc. that a product, programme, etc. is aimed at)
The film's target demographic is women aged 18–49 years.
We're using social media to communicate with our target customers.

definitions.label: (figurative)
definitions.description: an object, a person or a place that people aim at when attacking
examples: They attacked military and civilian targets.
Doors and windows are an easy target for burglars.
The children became the target for their father’s aggressive outbursts.
It's a prime target (= an obvious target) for terrorist attacks.
He's become the target of a lot of criticism recently.

definitions.label: (figurative)
definitions.description: an object that people practise shooting at, especially a round board with circles on it
examples: to aim at a target
to hit/miss the target
target practice

definitions.description: a piece of work that somebody has to do, especially a hard or unpleasant one
examples: to accomplish/perform/undertake/complete a task
a difficult/a daunting/an impossible task
Getting hold of this information was no easy task (= was difficult).
a thankless task (= an unpleasant one that nobody wants to do and nobody thanks you for doing)
The first task for the new leader is to focus on the economy.
The new role involves a variety of specific tasks.
Detectives are now faced with the task of identifying the body.
The government now has to take on the task of reconstruction of the country.
We should stop chatting and get back to the task at hand.
You need to concentrate on the task in hand.
It was a challenge to adapt this novel for the screen, but the writer proved himself equal to the task.

definitions.description: an activity that is designed to help achieve a particular learning goal, especially in language teaching
examples: Look at the diagram and then do the task below.
task-based learning

definitions.description: scientific knowledge used in practical ways in industry, for example in designing new machines
examples: science and technology
advances in communications technology
advanced/modern technology
to develop and use new technologies
small businesses that are involved with emerging technologies
the use of the latest digital technology to create a virtual world
This technology enables computers to read handwriting.

definitions.description: machines or equipment designed using technology
examples: The scheme provides access to advanced computer technology in the classroom.
The company has invested in the latest technology.
a wireless technology company
the technology sector/industry

definitions.label: (North American English)
definitions.description: a result that you try to achieve
examples: to meet/hit a target
The firm is on track to achieve its growth target for the year.
The university will reach its target of 5 000 students next September.
The department has missed its sales target for the third month running.
Set yourself targets that you can reasonably hope to achieve.
The new sports complex is on target to open in June.
These figures are way off target.
a target date of April 2022
a target audience/market (= the particular audience, area etc. that a product, programme, etc. is aimed at)
The film's target demographic is women aged 18–49 years.

definitions.label: (figurative)
definitions.description: an object, a person or a place that people aim at when attacking
examples: They attacked military and civilian targets.
Doors and windows are an easy target for burglars.
The children became the target for their father’s aggressive outbursts.
It's a prime target (= an obvious target) for terrorist attacks.
He's become the target of a lot of criticism recently.

definitions.label: (figurative)
definitions.description: an object that people practise shooting at, especially a round board with circles on it
examples: to aim at a target
to hit/miss the target
target practice

definitions.description: scientific knowledge used in practical ways in industry, for example in designing new machines
examples: science and technology
advances in communications technology
advanced/modern technology
to develop and use new technologies
small businesses that are involved with emerging technologies
the use of the latest digital technology to create a virtual world
This technology enables computers to read handwriting.

definitions.description: machines or equipment designed using technology
examples: The scheme provides access to advanced computer technology in the classroom.
The company has invested in the latest technology.
a wireless technology company
the technology sector/industry

definitions.description: between 13 and 19 years old; connected with people of this age
examples: a teenage girl/boy
teenage angst
teenage pregnancy
teen magazines

definitions.description: the measurement in degrees of how hot or cold a thing or place is
examples: high/low temperatures
cold/warm temperatures
a drop/rise in temperature
The temperature has risen (by) five degrees.
Some places have had temperatures in the 40s (= over 40° centigrade).
Chemical reactions take place more slowly at low temperatures.
the water/air/surface temperature
Heat the oven to a temperature of 200°C (= degrees centigrade).
The climate is generally mild, and freezing temperatures are almost unknown.

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: the measurement of how hot somebody’s body is
examples: to take somebody’s temperature (= measure the temperature of somebody’s body using a special instrument)
Does he have a temperature (= is it higher than normal, because of illness)?
He's in bed with a temperature of 40°.
When your body temperature rises, your body tries to compensate.
She's running a temperature (= it is higher than normal).
They used ice packs to bring down her temperature.

definitions.description: a word or phrase used as the name of something, especially one connected with a particular type of language
examples: a technical/legal/generic term
a glossary of terms
a term of abuse
What is the meaning of the term ‘globalization’?
William Gibson coined the term (= invented the term) ‘cyberspace’ in 1984.
‘Old man’ is a slang term for ‘father’.
The term ‘Generation X’ refers to the people born in the 1950s and 1960s.
‘Register’ is the term commonly used to describe different levels of formality in language.
I would describe myself, for want of a better term, as a nerd.

definitions.label: North American English also
definitions.description: (especially in the UK) one of the three periods in the year during which classes are held in schools, universities, etc.
examples: the spring/summer/autumn/fall term
Many students now have paid employment during term.
It's nearly the end of term.
It's nearly the end of the term.

definitions.description: a period of time for which something lasts; a fixed or limited time
examples: during the president’s first term of/in office
a term as president/mayor/governor/prime minister
He was sentenced to a prison/jail term of 25 years for the offence.
She served a five-year term of imprisonment.
The contract was for a fixed term of five years.
to extend the term of a loan
His presidential term expires at the end of May.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: the end of a particular period of time, especially one for which something is expected to last
examples: His life had reached its natural term.
This view of the economy is approaching its term (= it will soon be old-fashioned).
The pregnancy went to full term (= lasted the normal length of time).
Her baby was born at term.

definitions.label: (mathematics)
definitions.description: each of the various parts in a series, an equation, etc.
having a larger distance between opposite sides or surfaces than other similar objects or than normal
examples: a thick slice of bread
a thick book (= one that has a lot of pages)
a thick coat (= one made of heavy cloth)
thick fingers
Everything was covered with a thick layer of dust.
Use fairly thick wads of newspaper.
He wore thick glasses.
a thick carpet of snow

definitions.description: used to ask about or state the distance between opposite sides or surfaces
examples: How thick are the walls?
They're two feet thick.
The silk thread is only slightly thicker than a hair.

definitions.description: growing closely together in large amounts or numbers
examples: thick dark hair
This breed of cattle has a very thick coat.
His eyebrows were thick and bushy.
a thick forest

definitions.description: not flowing very easily
examples: thick soup
The effect will be ruined if the paint is too thick.
I was buried up to my waist in thick mud, unable to move.

definitions.label: (figurative)
definitions.description: difficult to see through; difficult to breathe in
examples: The plane crashed in thick fog.
Thick black smoke rose over the city.
Thick cloud covered the sky.
The air had grown thick and smoky.
The air was thick with dust.
The atmosphere was thick with tension.

definitions.description: having a large number of people or a large amount of something in one place
examples: The beach was thick with sunbathers.

definitions.label: (informal, offensive)
definitions.description: an offensive way to describe somebody who is slow to learn or understand things
examples: I'm not completely thick, you know.

definitions.label: (sometimes disapproving)
definitions.description: easily recognized as being from a particular country or area
examples: a thick Brooklyn accent

definitions.description: deep and not as clear as normal, especially because of illness or emotion
examples: His voice was thick with emotion.

definitions.label: (informal)
definitions.description: very friendly with somebody, especially in a way that makes other people suspect that something wrong, illegal or dishonest is involved in the situation
examples: You seem to be very thick with the boss!

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: a person who steals something from another person or place
examples: a car/jewel thief
a gang of thieves
Thieves stole £70 000 worth of jewellery from his home.
a petty thief (= who steals items of quite low value)
It is the fourth time the shop has been targeted by thieves.

definitions.label: (saying)
definitions.description: used to say that even criminals have standards of behaviour that they respect

definitions.label: (informal)
definitions.description: very friendly, especially in a way that makes other people suspect that something wrong, illegal or dishonest is involved in the situation
having a smaller distance between opposite sides or surfaces than other similar objects or than normal
examples: Cut the vegetables into thin strips.
A number of thin cracks appeared in the wall.
The body was hidden beneath a thin layer of soil.
Palm trees cast long, thin shadows on the lawn.
He knew that the ice was too thin to risk crossing the river.
a thin blouse (= of light cloth)

definitions.label: (sometimes disapproving)
definitions.refer: (of a person or part of the body)
definitions.description: not covered with much fat or muscle
examples: He was tall and thin, with dark hair.
She was looking pale and thin.
How do you stay so thin?
He is as thin as a rake (= very thin).
thin legs

definitions.description: not growing closely together or in large amounts
examples: thin grey hair

definitions.description: containing more liquid than is normal or expected
examples: The sauce was thin and tasteless.
The paint looks a bit thin.

definitions.description: fairly easy to see through
examples: They fought their way through where the smoke was thinner.

definitions.description: containing less oxygen than normal
examples: Humans would not be able to survive in the thin atmosphere of the planet.

definitions.label: (disapproving)
definitions.description: high and weak
examples: Her thin voice trailed off into silence.

definitions.description: not sincere or enthusiastic
examples: He gave a thin smile.

definitions.description: not very bright
examples: the thin grey light of dawn

definitions.description: of poor quality; without an important quality
examples: a thin excuse (= one that people are not likely to believe)
Their arguments all sound a little thin to me.
The general standard of applicants is pretty thin this year.

definitions.description: the process of thinking about something
examples: I had to do some quick thinking.
She believes in encouraging creative thinking in the classroom.
He had some serious thinking to do.
With good, clear thinking one can arrive at an answer.

definitions.description: ideas or opinions about something
examples: What is the current thinking on this question?
I disagree with that kind of thinking.
She explained the thinking behind the campaign.

definitions.description: something that you think of or remember
examples: I couldn't bear the thought of waiting any longer.
The very thought of it makes me feel sick.
I don't like the thought of you walking home alone.
She was struck by the sudden thought that he might already have left.
Thank you for sharing your thoughts on this topic.
I'd like to hear your thoughts on the subject.
He shared his thoughts about the future of technology.
He shuddered at the thought of going to the dentist.
He often expresses his thoughts on social media.

thinking about unpleasant things that have happened or that might happen and therefore feeling unhappy and afraid

Parents very often have to juggle work with their family commitments.
I don't want to take on any more commitments.

definitions.description: a promise to pay for something, especially regularly; a promise to use resources in order to achieve something
examples: Taking on a mortgage is a huge financial commitment.
the commitment of resources to education
Achieving success at this level requires a commitment of time and energy.

definitions.description: an order given to a person or an animal
examples: Begin when I give the command.
You must obey the captain's commands.
He issued the command to retreat.
Police said he ignored their commands to stop.

definitions.description: an instruction given to a computer
examples: The computer executes commands successively in the order they arrive.
What is the startup command for the program?

definitions.description: control and authority over a situation or a group of people
examples: He has 1 200 men under his command.
He has command of 1  200 men.
The police arrived and took command of the situation.
In 1939 he assumed command of all French naval forces.
There were many disagreements over the command of the peacekeeping forces.
Who is in command here?
For the first time in years, she felt in command of her life.
He looked relaxed and totally in command of himself.
the chain of command
a breakdown in the command structure

definitions.description: a part of an army, air force, etc. that is organized and controlled separately; a group of officers who give orders
examples: Bomber Command

definitions.description: your knowledge of something; your ability to do or use something, especially a language
examples: Applicants will be expected to have (a) good command of English.
She has an excellent command of French.

definitions.description: usually; very often; by most people
examples: Christopher is commonly known as Kit.
the sudden increase in the birth rate after the Second World War, commonly referred to as the ‘baby boom’
avian influenza, commonly called bird flu
This is one of the most commonly used methods.
symptoms commonly associated with HIV
These fats are commonly found in processed foods.
one of the most commonly available substances on the planet

definitions.description: measured or judged by how similar or different it is to something else
examples: Then he was living in comparative comfort (= compared with others or with his own life at a previous time).
The company is a comparative newcomer to the software market (= other companies have been in business much longer).

definitions.description: relating to studying things to find out how similar or different they are
examples: a comparative study of the educational systems of two countries
comparative linguistics

definitions.label: (grammar)
definitions.description: relating to adjectives or adverbs that express more in amount, degree or quality, for example better, worse, slower and more difficult
the act or process of finishing something; the state of being finished and complete
examples: the completion of the new hospital building
Satisfactory completion of the course does not ensure you a job.
The project is due for completion in the spring.
The road is nearing completion (= it is nearly finished).
the date of completion/the completion date

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: the formal act of completing the sale of property, for example the sale of a house
examples: The keys will be handed over on completion.
The floorboards were replaced prior to completion of the sale.

definitions.description: made of many different things or parts that are connected; difficult to understand
examples: a complicated issue/process/system
The instructions look very complicated.
The story is extremely complicated.
It's all very complicated—but I'll try and explain.
Things get complicated when the hero becomes the target of a stalker.
Life had become more complicated for them.
Some of the maths questions were far too complicated for your average 10-year-old.

definitions.description: one of several parts of which something is made
examples: the different organizations involved in the design of the various components
Key components of the government’s plan are…
an essential/important component of something
a major/principal/critical component of something
Nitrogen is the main component of air.
The country still lacks the basic components of a real democratic system.
the components of a machine
Individual components for the car can be very expensive.
Trust is a vital component in any relationship.
Component failure was the cause of the accident.

definitions.description: to write music
examples: Mozart composed his last opera shortly before he died.
music specially composed for the occasion

definitions.description: to write a letter, etc. usually with a lot of care and thought
examples: She composed a letter of protest.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: to combine together to form a whole
examples: Ten people compose the committee.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: to manage to control your feelings or expression
examples: Emma frowned, making an effort to compose herself.
I was so confused that I could hardly compose my thoughts.

definitions.description: a person who writes music, especially classical music
examples: Verdi was a prolific composer of operas.

definitions.description: a thing consisting of two or more separate things combined together
examples: compounds derived from rainforest plants
The air smelled like a compound of diesel and petrol fumes.

definitions.label: (chemistry)
definitions.description: a substance formed by a chemical reaction of two or more elements in fixed amounts relative to each other
examples: Common salt is a compound of sodium and chlorine.

definitions.label: (grammar)
definitions.description: a noun, an adjective or a verb made of two or more words or parts of words, written as one or more words, or joined by a hyphen. Travel agent, dark-haired and bathroom are all compounds.
examples: Most compound nouns form their plurals in the usual way.

definitions.description: an area surrounded by a fence or wall in which a factory or other group of buildings stands
examples: life inside the prison compound

definitions.description: including all, or almost all, the items, details, facts, information, etc., that may be involved
examples: a comprehensive list of addresses
a comprehensive study
comprehensive insurance (= covering all risks)

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: designed for students of all abilities in the same school
gained or lost by a large amount
examples: The cricket team finished the season with a comprehensive victory over their rivals.

definitions.description: to have somebody/something as parts or members
examples: The collection comprises 327 paintings.
a book comprising eight short stories
The committee is comprised of representatives from both the public and private sectors.

definitions.description: to be the parts or members that form something
examples: Older people comprise a large proportion of those living in poverty.

definitions.description: that must be done because of a law or a rule
examples: English is a compulsory subject at this level.
compulsory education/schooling
The strikers are protesting against the threat of compulsory redundancies.
It is compulsory for all motorcyclists to wear helmets.

definitions.description: the ability to direct all your effort and attention on one thing, without thinking of other things
examples: This book requires a great deal of concentration.
Tiredness affects your powers of concentration.
One momentary lapse in concentration could prove fatal.
He has a poor concentration span (= cannot concentrate for long).

definitions.description: the process of people directing effort and attention on a particular thing
examples: He stressed the need for greater concentration on environmental issues.
In his concentration on the job in hand, John allowed his normal vigilance to slip.

definitions.description: a lot of something in one place
examples: a concentration of industry in the north of the country

definitions.description: the amount of a substance in a liquid or in another substance
examples: glucose concentrations in the blood

definitions.description: an idea or a principle that is connected with something abstract
examples: the concept of social class
helping students grasp abstract concepts such as leadership and teamwork
basic/fundamental/key/core concepts
the concept that everyone should have equality of opportunity
the concepts behind an artist's work

definitions.description: an idea for something new
examples: a novel/innovative concept
an exciting new concept in city living
a novel marketing concept
a design concept for a new school

definitions.description: to affect somebody/something; to involve somebody/something
examples: Don't interfere in what doesn't concern you.
To whom it may concern… (= used for example, at the beginning of a public notice or of a job reference about somebody’s character and ability)
Please pay attention because this information concerns all of you.
The letter is for both of us, but it mainly concerns you.

definitions.description: to be about something
examples: The story concerns the prince's efforts to rescue Pamina.

definitions.description: to worry somebody
examples: What concerns me is our lack of preparation for the change.

It really concerns me that he doesn't eat properly.

definitions.description: to take an interest in something
examples: He didn't concern himself with the details.

definitions.description: worried and feeling concern about something/somebody
examples: Concerned citizens can have a huge impact.
concerned parents/residents/parents/locals
The president is deeply concerned about this issue.
We are extremely concerned about her.
He didn't seem in the least concerned for her safety.
We were concerned for his welfare.
I told him but he didn't seem overly concerned (= he was not very concerned)

Local residents are concerned over the impact of the project.

a concerned look/glance

definitions.description: affected by something; involved in something
examples: The loss was a tragedy for all concerned.
Where our children's education is concerned, no compromise is acceptable.
The individuals concerned have some explaining to do.
The meetings were often embarrassing for all concerned.

definitions.description: interested in something; dealing with something
examples: The public is increasingly concerned with how food is produced.
Mathematics is concerned essentially with understanding abstract concepts.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: to think it is important to do something
examples: She was concerned to write about situations that everybody could identify with.

definitions.description: made of concrete
examples: a concrete floor

definitions.description: based on facts, not on ideas or guesses
examples: concrete evidence/proposals/proof
‘It's only a suspicion,’ she said, ‘nothing concrete.’
It is easier to think in concrete terms rather than in the abstract.

definitions.description: a concrete object is one that you can see and feel

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: to organize and/or do a particular activity
examples: to conduct an experiment/inquiry/investigation/interview
to conduct a survey/poll/study/review
to conduct a test/trial
to conduct research/business
There are concerns about the way in which the firm conducts its activities.
The battalion had been preparing to conduct operations in the same area.
Police conducted a thorough search of the building.
The negotiations have been conducted in a positive manner.
They conducted a vigorous campaign for a shorter working week.

definitions.description: to direct a group of people who are singing or playing music
examples: a concert by the London Philharmonic Orchestra, conducted by Marin Alsop
He conducted a programme of Sibelius and Tchaikovsky.
He will conduct works by Brahms and Schumann in tonight's concert.
She sang Gluck's Orfeo at Covent Garden, with Sir Thomas Beecham conducting.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: to lead or guide somebody through or around a place
examples: a conducted tour of Athens (= one with a guide, giving information about it)
The guide conducted us around the ruins of the ancient city.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: to behave in a particular way
examples: He conducted himself far better than expected.
The report challenges them to examine how they conduct themselves in the workplace.

definitions.label: (specialist)
definitions.description: to allow heat or electricity to pass along or through it
examples: Copper conducts electricity well.

definitions.description: to admit, especially formally or to the police, that you have done something wrong or illegal
examples: After hours of questioning, the suspect confessed.
She confessed to the murder.
He confessed that he had stolen the money.
She confessed to me that she had known his true identity for some time.
We persuaded her to confess her crime.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: to admit something that you feel ashamed or embarrassed about
examples: She was reluctant to confess her ignorance.
I must confess to knowing nothing about golf.
I confess (that) I know nothing about golf.
‘I know nothing about it,’ he confessed.
