definitions.description: to tell God or a priest about the bad things you have done so that you can say that you are sorry and be forgiven
examples: They had confessed their sins and done their penance.

definitions.description: to hear somebody confess their sins (= the bad things they have done)
the feeling that you can trust, believe in and be sure about the abilities or good qualities of somebody/something
examples: The president's actions hardly inspire confidence.
The players all have confidence in their manager.
He believes his reforms will restore confidence in the financial markets.
The survey revealed a lack of confidence in the government.
She has the utmost confidence in her students' abilities.
Our aim is to increase public confidence in the democratic process.
The university is facing a crisis of confidence about its future role.
The new contracts have undermined the confidence of employees.

definitions.description: a belief in your own ability to do things and be successful
examples: People often lose confidence when they are criticized.
He gained confidence when he went to college.
Receiving compliments from my work colleagues has boosted my confidence.
The course will help you build your confidence and develop your study skills.
She certainly doesn't lack confidence.
He suffers from a lack of confidence.
She answered the questions with confidence.
I didn't have any confidence in myself at school.
Winning the award has given me much more confidence in my writing.
The training programmes have given workers the confidence to take on more responsibility.

definitions.description: the feeling that you are certain about something
examples: He said he wished that he shared her confidence.
They could not say with confidence that he would be able to walk again after the accident.
No one can predict with complete confidence what will happen in the financial markets.
She expressed her confidence that they would win.

definitions.description: a feeling of trust that somebody will keep information private
examples: It took a long time to gain her confidence (= make her feel she could trust me).
Eva told me about their relationship in confidence.
This is in the strictest confidence.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: a secret that you tell somebody
examples: The girls exchanged confidences.
I could never forgive Mike for betraying a confidence.

definitions.description: a situation in which people, groups or countries disagree strongly or are involved in a serious argument
examples: The violence was the result of political conflicts.
a conflict between two cultures
His task will be to resolve potential conflicts between the British and Scottish governments.
The prime minister wants to avoid conflict with the unions.
The government has done nothing to resolve the conflict over nurses' pay.
She found herself in conflict with her parents over her future career.
John often comes into conflict with his boss.
The terms of the will became a source of conflict within the family.
She has received training in conflict resolution.

definitions.description: a violent situation or period of fighting between two countries
examples: armed/military conflict
The country has experienced internal conflict over the last decade.
Hopes of ending the conflict in the region are fading.
international efforts to find a peaceful solution to the conflict
This isolated state faces the risk of another violent conflict with its neighbour.
They are engaged in a bloody conflict over the disputed territory.
A conflict between the two countries could easily spread across the whole region.

definitions.description: a situation in which there are ideas, opinions, feelings or wishes that are opposed to each other; a situation in which it is difficult to choose
examples: Her diary was a record of her inner conflict.
The story tells of a classic conflict between love and duty.
Many of these ideas appear to be in conflict with each other.
He faced a conflict of loyalties.
a serious conflict of opinion

definitions.description: difficult to understand; not clear
examples: The instructions on the box are very confusing.
a confusing situation/experience
confusing messages/signals
a confusing array of options
This is where it all starts to get really confusing.
Beginners may find the terminology confusing.
The new signs will be very confusing for tourists.
All this information can be confusing to the user.
The site is somewhat confusing to navigate.
It would be confusing to have two sets of regulations for a single country.

definitions.description: a state of not being certain about what is happening, what you should do, what something means, etc.
examples: The announcement caused a lot of confusion.
There is some confusion about what the correct procedure should be.
There was a confusion as to what to do next.

definitions.description: the fact of making a mistake about who somebody is or what something is
examples: To avoid confusion, please write the children's names clearly on all their school clothes.
confusion between letters of the alphabet like ‘o’ or ‘a’

definitions.description: a situation in which you feel embarrassed because you do not understand something and are not sure what to do
examples: He looked at me in confusion and did not answer the question.
Sacha felt confusion sweeping over her as she read the letter.

definitions.description: a confused situation in which people do not know what action to take
examples: Fighting had broken out and all was chaos and confusion.
Her unexpected arrival threw us into total confusion.

definitions.description: aware of something; noticing something
examples: She's very conscious of the problems involved.
I am conscious of the fact that there's a limit to what we can achieve here.
He became acutely conscious of having failed his parents.
I was vaguely conscious that I was being watched.

definitions.description: able to use your senses and mental powers to understand what is happening
examples: A patient who is not fully conscious should never be left alone.
She remained conscious throughout the operation.

definitions.description: deliberate; done in a careful way
examples: a conscious choice
to make a conscious decision
I made a conscious effort to get there on time.
a conscious act of cruelty

definitions.description: being particularly interested in something
examples: to be environmentally/politically conscious
the band's socially conscious lyrics
They have become increasingly health-conscious.
an image-conscious reality star

definitions.description: directly under the control of the person concerned
examples: When you go to sleep, it is only the conscious mind that shuts down.

definitions.description: as a result; therefore
examples: This poses a threat to agriculture and the food chain, and consequently to human health.
She failed her exams and was consequently unable to start her studies at college.

definitions.description: the protection of the natural environment
examples: to be interested in wildlife conservation
Road development in the area has been limited by conservation programmes.

definitions.description: the official protection of buildings and objects that have historical or artistic importance
examples: the conservation of ancient monuments/manuscripts/our cultural heritage

definitions.description: the act of preventing something from being lost, wasted, damaged or destroyed
examples: to encourage the conservation of water/fuel
energy conservation
practices that are good for the community, such as water efficiency and resource conservation

definitions.description: opposed to great or sudden social change; showing that you prefer traditional styles and values
examples: the conservative views of his parents
music which is accessible to an audience with extremely conservative tastes
The southern state's inhabitants tend to be socially conservative.
Her style of dress was never conservative.
They were deeply conservative in their outlook.

definitions.description: connected with the British Conservative Party
examples: Conservative members/supporters

definitions.description: lower than what is probably the real amount or number
examples: At a conservative estimate, he'll be earning £50 000.

definitions.description: great in amount, size, importance, etc.
examples: The project wasted a considerable amount of time and money.
Damage to the building was considerable.
Considerable progress has been made in finding a cure for the disease.

definitions.description: much; a lot
examples: The need for sleep varies considerably from person to person.
Interest rates on bank loans have increased considerably in recent years.
Pollution levels have considerably reduced in this time.
Prices are considerably higher than they were a year ago.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: the act of thinking carefully about something
examples: An employer is legally bound to give due consideration to the request.
Careful consideration should be given to issues of health and safety.
Her ideas are worthy of serious consideration.
to merit/deserve/warrant further consideration
After a few moments' consideration, he began to speak.
There needs to be a consideration of the legal issues involved.
The proposals are currently under consideration (= being discussed).
I enclose the report for your consideration.
The group have submitted two resolutions for consideration by shareholders.

definitions.description: something that must be thought about when you are planning or deciding something
examples: The government's decision was obviously motivated by political considerations.
economic/commercial/environmental/practical considerations
Time is another important consideration.

definitions.description: the quality of being sensitive towards others and thinking about their wishes and feelings
examples: Their kindness and consideration will not be forgotten.
They showed no consideration whatsoever for my feelings.
She was shocked by his lack of consideration for others.
Journalists stayed away from the funeral out of consideration for the bereaved family.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: a reward or payment for a service
examples: You can buy the books for a small consideration.
She agreed, for a small consideration, to arrange a meeting with the casting director.

definitions.label: (approving)
definitions.description: always behaving in the same way, or having the same opinions, standards, etc.
examples: a consistent approach to the problem
a consistent pattern of behaviour

definitions.description: in agreement with something; not contradicting something
examples: The results are entirely consistent with our earlier research.

injuries consistent with a fall from an upper storey (= similar to those such a fall would have caused)

definitions.refer: (of an argument or a set of ideas)
definitions.description: having different parts that all agree with each other
examples: a well-thought-out and consistent argument
His argument is not even internally consistent.
Balanced economic growth, full employment and financial stability are mutually consistent objectives.

definitions.label: (approving)
definitions.description: always the same
examples: Her work has been of a consistently high standard.

definitions.description: in a way that does not change and continues for a period of time
examples: We have argued consistently for a change in the law.

definitions.description: in a way that has different parts that all agree with each other
examples: Studies have not consistently demonstrated any benefit.

definitions.description: a secret plan by a group of people to do something harmful or illegal
examples: a conspiracy to overthrow the government

conspiracies against the president
a conspiracy of silence (= an agreement not to talk publicly about something that should be made public)

definitions.description: happening all the time or repeatedly

a constant stream of visitors all day

Babies need constant attention.
This entrance is in constant use.

definitions.description: that does not change
examples: The car was travelling at a constant speed of 50 mph.

definitions.description: all the time; repeatedly
examples: Fashion is constantly changing.
I am constantly reminded how fortunate I am.
We are constantly looking for ways to improve our products.
We are constantly on the lookout for new ideas.
Heat the sauce, stirring constantly.

definitions.description: to build or make something such as a road, building or machine
examples: The building was constructed in 1993.

On the smaller islands, houses are often constructed of local materials.

to construct a theory

a well-constructed novel
his carefully constructed public image
the socially constructed nature of gender roles

definitions.label: (geometry)
definitions.description: to draw a line or shape according to the rules of mathematics
examples: to construct a triangle

construction work/workers
a construction company/firm
construction projects/costs/materials

definitions.description: the way that something has been built or made

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: a thing that has been built or made
examples: The summer house was a simple wooden construction.

definitions.description: the way in which words are used together and arranged to form a sentence, phrase, etc.
examples: grammatical constructions

definitions.description: the creating of something from ideas, opinions and knowledge
examples: the construction of a new theory
changes in the social construction of marriage

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: the way in which words, actions, statements, etc. are understood by somebody
examples: What construction do you put on this letter (= what do you think it means)?
ruling on the proper construction to be given to section 78 of the Act
a strict construction of the clause

examples: If the pain continues, consult your doctor.

a consulting engineer (= one who has expert knowledge and gives advice)

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: a hospital doctor of the highest rank who is a specialist in a particular area of medicine
examples: a consultant in obstetrics

definitions.label: (figurative)

definitions.label: (old-fashioned)
definitions.description: a serious disease of the lungs
belonging to the same time
examples: We have no contemporary account of the battle (= written near the time that it happened).

definitions.description: belonging to the present time
examples: contemporary society/culture
contemporary art/music/dance
contemporary architecture/literature/painting/politics/history

definitions.description: following modern ideas in style or design
examples: Try some contemporary colours on your kitchen walls.

examples: a writer of great wisdom and depth
His ideas lack depth.
She has the ability to treat big subjects with breadth and depth.
a job that doesn’t require any great depth of knowledge
Younger students cannot be expected to have great depth of understanding.

definitions.description: the deepest, most extreme or serious part of something
examples: the depths of the ocean
to live in the depths of the country (= a long way from a town)
in the depths of winter (= when it is coldest)

definitions.description: the strength of a colour
examples: Strong light will affect the depth of colour of your carpets and curtains.

definitions.label: (specialist)

to do something or show qualities that mean a particular reaction, reward or punishment is appropriate
examples: You deserve a rest after all that hard work.
The report deserves careful consideration.
This idea deserves more attention.

definitions.label: (informal)

examples: She deserves a medal for teaching those 5-year-olds all day!

definitions.label: (informal)
definitions.description: used to say that you think somebody has earned the bad things that happen to them
examples: He did wrong, and he got what he deserved.

definitions.label: (saying)

definitions.label: (formal)

definitions.description: a person or thing that is wished for

definitions.description: in a way that shows you have little hope and are ready to do anything without worrying about danger to yourself or others
examples: She looked desperately around for a weapon.

definitions.description: extremely, especially when talking about bad situations

definitions.description: very much, especially when talking about difficult or bad situations
examples: They desperately wanted a child.

examples: the destruction of the rainforests
a tidal wave bringing death and destruction in its wake

a detailed analysis/examination/study
a detailed account/discussion/explanation/investigation

definitions.label: (formal)

definitions.label: (British English)

definitions.label: (British English)

definitions.label: (formal)

examples: Holy cow! What was that?

definitions.description: great respect for somebody
examples: the guest of honour (= the most important one)
the seat/place of honour (= given to the most important guest)
They stood in silence as a mark of honour to her.
This biography does great honour to the poet's achievements.

definitions.description: something that you are very pleased or proud to do because people are showing you great respect
examples: It was a great honour to be invited here today.
It is a great honour to represent my country at the Olympics.
It was my honour and privilege to be Helen's friend.
The city has the dubious honour (= something that does not make you pleased or proud) of being the road rage capital of Europe.
She shared the honour of being the season's top scorer with Khadija Shaw.

definitions.description: the quality of knowing and doing what is morally right
examples: a man of honour
Proving his innocence has become a matter of honour.

definitions.description: a good reputation; respect from other people
examples: upholding the honour of your country
The family honour is at stake.

definitions.description: a person or thing that causes others to respect and admire something/somebody
examples: She is an honour to the profession.

definitions.description: an award, official title, etc. given to somebody as a reward for something that they have done
examples: the New Year’s Honours list (= in Britain, a list of awards and titles given on January 1 each year)
to receive/win the highest honour
to bestow an honour on somebody
She received nearly every honour bestowed upon a poet.
He received numerous honours, including the OBE in 1961.
He was buried with full military honours (= with a special military service as a sign of respect).
He wears his scars like badges of honour (= rewards that you can see).

definitions.label: (North American English)
definitions.description: a university course that is of a higher level than a basic course (in the US also used to describe a class in school that is at a higher level than other classes)
examples: an honours degree/course
a First Class Honours degree
I took an honors class in English.

definitions.description: if you pass an exam or graduate from a university or school with honours, you receive a special grade for having achieved a very high standard
examples: He passed with second-class honours.

definitions.description: a title of respect used when talking to or about a judge or a US mayor
examples: No more questions, Your Honour.

definitions.description: the cards that have the highest value
all the people living together in a house or flat
examples: Most households now own at least one car.
The average household spends more on housing than on food.
young people from low-income households
a one-parent/single-parent/two-parent household
families with a male/female head of household
Household incomes have remained stagnant.
Who does most of the household chores?
Packaging makes up about a third of household waste.

definitions.description: houses, flats, etc. that people live in, especially when referring to their type, price or condition
examples: rental/student housing
temporary/permanent housing
low-cost/cheap housing
There is an urgent need to build more affordable housing.
We must find a way to solve the city's housing crisis.
The study linked poor housing conditions to a variety of health problems.
How severe is the housing shortage in Hong Kong?
the housing market (= the activity of buying and selling houses, etc.)
The low interest rate has triggered a housing bubble (= a period of time when house prices increase quickly, but which is unlikely to last long).

definitions.description: the job of providing houses, flats, etc. for people to live in
examples: Tenants may only keep pets with the written consent of the housing department.
They discussed how the council's housing policy could be changed to deal with the growing housing crisis.

definitions.description: a hard cover that protects part of a machine
examples: a car’s rear axle housing

definitions.description: funny; showing a sense of humour
examples: He gave a humorous account of their trip to Spain.
It's a humorous look at the world of fashion.
The show offers a humorous take on family life.
He had a wide mouth and humorous grey eyes.

definitions.description: the quality in something that makes it funny; the ability to laugh at things that are funny
examples: It was a story full of gentle humour.
She ignored his feeble attempt at humour.
They failed to see the humour of the situation.
I can't stand people with no sense of humour.
to have a dry/keen/wicked/wry sense of humour
She smiled with a rare flash of humour.
She has her very own brand of humour.
The film is only funny if you appreciate French humour (= things that cause French people to laugh).

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: the state of your feelings or mind at a particular time
examples: to be in the best of humours
The meeting dissolved in ill humour.
to be out of humour (= in a bad mood)
The remarks were made in good humour.

definitions.label: (old use)
definitions.description: one of the four liquids that were thought in the past to be in a person’s body and to influence health and character
the state of not having enough food to eat, especially when this causes illness or death
examples: Around fifty people die of hunger every day in the camp.
The organization works to alleviate world hunger and disease.

definitions.description: the feeling caused by a need to eat
examples: If you feel hunger pangs between meals, eat some fruit or nuts.
I felt faint with hunger.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: a strong desire for something
examples: She has an insatiable hunger for knowledge.
Nothing seemed to satisfy their hunger for truth.

definitions.description: going after and killing wild animals as a sport or for food
examples: He goes hunting every weekend.
Since 1977 otter hunting has been illegal.
In 1966, the commercial hunting of blue whales was banned.
In the tiger, evolution has produced a perfect hunting machine.

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: a sport in which foxes are hunted by specially trained dogs and by people on horses. Fox hunting with dogs is now illegal in the UK.
the process of looking for something
examples: How's the job-hunting going?
Archaeologists have called for a ban on treasure hunting in the region.

definitions.description: an idea or explanation of something that is based on a few known facts but that has not yet been proved to be true or correct
examples: to formulate/confirm a hypothesis
a hypothesis about the function of dreams
There is little evidence to support these hypotheses.

definitions.description: guesses and ideas that are not based on certain knowledge
examples: It would be pointless to engage in hypothesis before we have the facts.

definitions.description: a small symbol on a computer or smartphone screen that represents a program or a file
examples: Click on the printer icon with the mouse.
Tap the app icon on your phone to open it.

definitions.description: a famous person or thing that people admire and see as a symbol of a particular idea, way of life, etc.
examples: Madonna and other pop icons of the 1980s
a feminist/gay icon (= somebody that feminists/gay people admire)
Sandra has become a style icon, for the fashion world particularly.

definitions.description: a painting or statue of a holy person that is also thought of as a holy object
the part of the unconscious mind where many of a person’s basic needs, feelings and desires are supposed to exist
similar in every detail
examples: a row of identical houses
The two pictures are similar, although not identical.
Her dress is almost identical to mine.
The name on the ticket should be identical with the one in the passport.

definitions.description: the same
examples: This is the identical room we stayed in last year.

definitions.description: a false idea or belief, especially about somebody or about a situation
examples: She's under the illusion that (= believes wrongly that) she'll get the job.
The new president has no illusions about the difficulties facing her country (= she knows that the country has serious problems).
I have no illusions about her feelings for me (= I know the truth is that she does not love me).
He could no longer distinguish between illusion and reality.
I don’t want to have my illusions shattered!

definitions.description: something that seems to exist but in fact does not, or seems to be something that it is not
examples: Mirrors in a room often give an illusion of space.
The idea of absolute personal freedom is an illusion.

definitions.description: to use pictures, photographs, diagrams, etc. in a book, etc.
examples: She illustrated her own books.
His lecture was illustrated with photos taken during the expedition.

definitions.description: to make the meaning of something clearer by using examples, pictures, etc.
examples: To illustrate my point, let me tell you a little story.
Last year's sales figures are illustrated in Figure 2.
He is showing these silent films to help illustrate his story of survival.
Each topic is illustrated with concrete examples of economic practice.
Here's an example to illustrate what I mean.

definitions.description: to show that something is true or that a situation exists
examples: The incident illustrates the need for better security measures.
This story illustrates how little has changed.
These data illustrate that many parents are not aware of the risks.

definitions.description: a drawing or picture in a book, magazine, for decoration or to explain something
examples: 50 full-colour illustrations
detailed illustrations of animals, birds and plants
a volume of Chaucer with illustrations by Edward Burne-Jones
He produced illustrations for children's books.

definitions.description: the process of illustrating something
examples: the art of book illustration

definitions.description: a story, an event or an example that clearly shows the truth about something
examples: The statistics are a clear illustration of the point I am trying to make.
I use this case as an illustration.
Let me, by way of illustration, quote from one of her poems.

definitions.label: (informal)
definitions.description: the ability to create pictures in your mind; the part of your mind that does this
examples: a vivid/fertile imagination
He has no imagination.
It doesn't take much imagination to guess what she meant.
I won't tell you his reaction—I'll leave that to your imagination.
Don't let your imagination run away with you (= don't use too much imagination).
The new policies appear to have captured the imagination of the public (= they find them interesting and exciting)
His stories really stretch children’s imaginations.
Nobody hates you—it's all in your imagination.
This is an image which persists in the popular imagination.
Use your imagination! (= used to tell somebody that they will have to guess the answer to the question they have asked you, usually because it is obvious or embarrassing)

definitions.description: something that you have imagined rather than something that exists
examples: She was no longer able to distinguish between imagination and reality.
Is it my imagination or have you lost a lot of weight?

definitions.label: (approving)
definitions.description: the ability to have new and exciting ideas
examples: His writing lacks imagination.
With a little imagination, you could turn this place into a palace.
We are looking for someone with ingenuity and imagination.

definitions.description: the process of coming to live permanently in a different country from the one you were born in; the number of people who do this
examples: legal/illegal immigration
We are strongly supportive of immigration and multiculturalism.
laws restricting immigration into the US
There was an increase in immigration from Eastern Europe.
immigration policy/reform

definitions.description: the place at a port, an airport, etc. where the passports and other documents of people coming into a country are checked
examples: We landed at Heathrow and went through customs and immigration.
immigration officers
The men were interviewed by immigration officials.

definitions.description: that cannot catch or be affected by a particular disease or illness
examples: Adults are often immune to German measles.

definitions.description: not affected by something, especially something that you might expect to be harmful
examples: You'll eventually become immune to criticism.
Few people are immune to her charms.
Our business is far from immune to economic conditions.

definitions.description: protected from something and therefore able to avoid it
examples: No one should be immune from prosecution.
Not even the monarch was immune from criticism by the press.

definitions.description: annoyed by somebody/something, especially because you have to wait for a long time
examples: I'd been waiting for twenty minutes and I was getting impatient.
The children were growing impatient.
Try not to be too impatient with her.
Sarah was becoming increasingly impatient at their lack of interest.
An impatient driver behind me sounded his horn.
She waved them away with an impatient gesture.

definitions.description: wanting to do something soon; wanting something to happen soon
examples: She was clearly impatient to leave.
impatient for change

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: unable or unwilling to accept something unpleasant
examples: impatient of criticism

definitions.description: to make something that has been officially decided start to happen or be used
examples: to implement changes/decisions/policies/reforms
A new work programme for young people will be implemented.

definitions.description: a possible effect or result of an action or a decision
examples: They failed to consider the wider implications of their actions.
The development of the site will have implications for the surrounding countryside.

definitions.description: something that is suggested or indirectly stated (= something that is implied)
examples: I resent the implication that I don't care about my father.
He criticized the Director and, by implication, the whole of the organization.

definitions.description: the fact of being involved, or of involving somebody, in something, especially a crime
examples: He resigned after his implication in a sex scandal.

definitions.description: to suggest that something is true or that you feel or think something, without saying so directly
examples: Are you implying (that) I am wrong?
His silence seemed to imply agreement.
High-yield bonds, as the name implies, offer a high rate of interest.
It was implied that we were at fault.

definitions.description: to make it seem likely that something is true or exists
examples: The survey implies (that) more people are moving house than was thought.
It was implied in the survey that…
Popularity does not necessarily imply merit.
The fact that she was here implies a degree of interest.

definitions.description: to make something necessary in order to be successful
examples: The project implies an enormous investment in training.
Sustainable development implies a long-term perspective.

definitions.description: to introduce a new law, rule, tax, etc.; to order that a rule, punishment, etc. be used
examples: The UN Security Council imposed sanctions in 1992.
to impose a penalty/fine/sentence/ban
A new tax was imposed on fuel.

definitions.description: to force somebody/something to have to deal with something that is difficult or unpleasant
examples: He described the limitations imposed by his disease.
This system imposes additional financial burdens on many people.
to impose restrictions/constraints/obligations on somebody/something
The time limits are imposed on us by factors outside our control.

definitions.description: to make somebody accept the same opinions, wishes, etc. as your own
examples: She didn't want to impose her values on her family.
It was noticeable how a few people managed to impose their will on the others.

definitions.description: to expect somebody to do something for you or to spend time with you, when it may not be convenient for them
examples: ‘You must stay for lunch.’ ‘Well, thanks, but I don’t want to impose…’
Everyone imposes on Dave's good nature.

definitions.description: to make somebody/something accept or be aware of your presence or ideas
examples: European civilization was the first to impose itself across the whole world.

definitions.description: if a person or thing impresses you, you admire them or it
examples: We interviewed a number of candidates but none of them impressed us.
The Grand Canyon never fails to impress people.
The Grand Canyon never fails to impress.
His sincerity impressed her.
He impressed her with his sincerity.
It impressed me that she remembered my name.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: to make somebody understand how important, serious, etc. something is by emphasizing it
examples: He impressed on us the need for immediate action.
Their responsibilities are impressed on them during training.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: to have a great effect on something, especially somebody’s mind, imagination, etc.
examples: Her words impressed themselves on my memory.

definitions.description: if a person or thing impresses you, you admire them or it
examples: We interviewed a number of candidates but none of them impressed us.

The Grand Canyon never fails to impress.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: to make somebody understand how important, serious, etc. something is by emphasizing it
examples: He impressed on us the need for immediate action.
Their responsibilities are impressed on them during training.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: to have a great effect on something, especially somebody’s mind, imagination, etc.
examples: Her words impressed themselves on my memory.

definitions.description: something that encourages you to do something
examples: There is no incentive for people to save fuel.
There is an added incentive for you to buy from our new range—a free gift with every purchase.

definitions.description: a payment or concession (= a reduction in the amount of money that has to be paid) that encourages somebody to do something
examples: tax incentives to encourage savings

definitions.description: a unit for measuring length or height, equal to 2.54 centimetres. There are 12 inches in a foot.
examples: She's a few inches taller than me.
a laptop with a 15-inch screen
Each image measures 46 x 28 inches.
a fat envelope about half an inch thick
The snow is about one and a half inches deep.
1.14 inches of rain fell last night.
Every square inch of available land has been built on.
a metal tube about three inches in diameter
They feed on leaves and may grow to two inches in length.
Since I started jogging I've lost three and a half inches from my waistline.
Babies focus best on objects ten inches from their eyes.

definitions.description: a small amount or distance
examples: He escaped death by an inch.
The car missed us by inches.
She was within an inch of being killed.
They beat him (to) within an inch of his life (= very severely).
Her face was only inches from mine.
He was just inches away from scoring.

definitions.description: something that happens, especially something unusual or unpleasant
examples: His bad behaviour was just an isolated incident.
The most recent incident occurred last January.
She couldn't have been more than five years old when the incident happened.
One particular incident sticks in my mind.
The hot-headed tennis star became involved in an incident with the umpire.

definitions.description: a serious or violent event, such as a crime, an accident or an attack
examples: a violent/serious incident
There was a shooting incident near here last night.
She reported the incident to the police.
He said that the authorities would investigate the incident.
A 36-year-old man and a 25-year-old woman were stabbed in separate incidents.
The demonstration passed off without incident.
It was an alleged incident with a cleaner in this hotel that led to his dismissal.
There had been a number of incidents of violence against staff.

definitions.description: a disagreement between two countries, often involving military forces
examples: a border/diplomatic incident

definitions.label: (informal)
definitions.description: the money that a person, a region, a country, etc. earns from work, from investing money, from business, etc.
examples: Average household income fell slightly.
a weekly disposable income (= the money that you have left to spend after tax, etc.) of £400

a rise in national income

Tourism is a major source of income for the area.
Both higher- and lower-income groups will be paying more tax from next year.

definitions.description: to include something so that it forms a part of something
examples: The new car design incorporates all the latest safety features.

definitions.label: (business)

examples: The company was incorporated in 2008.

definitions.description: not accurate or true
examples: incorrect information/spelling

definitions.description: speaking or behaving in a way that does not follow the accepted standards or rules
more and more all the time
examples: Tourism is playing an increasingly important role in the region's economy
increasingly difficult/popular
It is becoming increasingly clear that this problem will not be easily solved.
It is looking increasingly likely that no agreement will be reached.
Doctors are growing increasingly concerned about his condition.
Increasingly, training is taking place in the office rather than outside it.

definitions.description: freedom from political control by other countries
examples: Argentina gained independence from Spain in 1816.

definitions.description: the time when a country gains freedom from political control by another country
examples: independence celebrations
the first elections since independence

definitions.description: the freedom to organize your own life, make your own decisions, etc. without needing help from other people
examples: He values his independence.

definitions.description: a list of names or topics that are referred to in a book, etc., usually arranged at the end of a book in alphabetical order or listed in a separate file or book
examples: Look it up in the index.

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: a box of cards with information on them, arranged in alphabetical order
a system that shows the level of prices and wages, etc. so that they can be compared with those of a previous date
examples: the cost-of-living index

stock market indices
house price indexes

definitions.description: a number giving a measurement of something compared with a particular standard
examples: White bread has a high glycaemic index.
pain management index scores

definitions.description: a sign or measure that something else can be judged by
examples: The number of new houses being built is a good index of a country's prosperity.

definitions.label: (computing)
definitions.description: a list of the records in a computer file with information about where each is located
examples: Search the index to find the address of the data file.
The index of a search engine is like a library.

definitions.label: (mathematics)
definitions.description: the small number written above a larger number to show how many times that number must be multiplied by itself. In the equation 42 = 16, the number 2 is an index.
a remark or sign that shows that something is happening or what somebody is thinking or feeling
examples: They gave no indication of how the work should be done.
He shows every indication (= clear signs) of wanting to accept the post.

All the indications are that the deal will go ahead as planned.

definitions.label: (medical)
definitions.description: a symptom that suggests that particular medical treatment is necessary
examples: There was no clinical indication for such a test.

definitions.description: connected with industry
examples: an industrial dispute
industrial unrest
an industrial accident

policy with regard to future industrial development
India has a large industrial sector.
a huge industrial complex
the country's industrial base

definitions.description: used by industries
examples: industrial chemicals

definitions.description: having many industries
examples: an industrial city/town
an industrial society
the world’s leading industrial nations

definitions.description: very great in extent or amount
examples: They had made industrial quantities of food.
They were guilty of fraud on an industrial scale.

definitions.description: that you cannot avoid or prevent
examples: It was an inevitable consequence of the decision.

A rise in interest rates seems inevitable.

definitions.label: (often humorous)
definitions.description: happening so often that you always expect it
examples: the English and their inevitable cups of tea

definitions.description: something that is certain to happen
examples: You have to accept the inevitable.
The inevitable happened—I forgot my passport.

definitions.description: as is certain to happen
examples: Inevitably, the press exaggerated the story.

definitions.label: (often humorous)
definitions.description: as you would expect
examples: Inevitably, it rained on the day of the wedding.

definitions.description: the act or process of causing or getting a disease
examples: to cause/prevent infection

The drugs slow down the progression of HIV infection.
Bacterial infection of the wound may occur.
to increase the risk of infection
The rate of infection is highest in the north-west of the country.
Birds are susceptible to infection by the virus.
Infection with malaria parasites may result in a wide variety of symptoms.

definitions.description: an illness that is caused by bacteria or a virus and that affects one part of the body
examples: an ear/a chest infection
a respiratory infection
a viral/bacterial infection
a media campaign to raise awareness about sexually transmitted infections
to cause an infection
Sneezing is the most common way of spreading an infection.
a fungal infection of the skin

definitions.description: to reach an opinion or decide that something is true on the basis of information that is available
examples: Much of the meaning must be inferred from the context.
Readers are left to infer the killer’s motives.
It is reasonable to infer that the government knew about these deals.

definitions.label: (non-standard)
definitions.description: to suggest indirectly that something is true
examples: Are you inferring (that) I’m not capable of doing the job?

definitions.description: a fall in the value of money and a general increase in prices; the rate at which this happens
examples: the fight against rising inflation
to control/curb inflation
to reduce/bring down inflation
a high/low rate of inflation
an inflation rate of 3%
Wage increases must be in line with inflation.
Inflation is currently running at 3%.
rapid/runaway/galloping inflation

definitions.label: (disapproving)
definitions.description: a general rise in the level of something that is awarded
examples: the gross inflation of executive salaries

definitions.description: the act or process of filling something with air or gas
examples: life jackets with an automatic inflation device

definitions.label: (informal)
definitions.description: information
examples: For more info, click here.
I couldn't find any contact info for the company.
Have you had any more info about the job yet?
Let us know if you get any more info.

definitions.description: connected with information
examples: an infosheet
We send all potential clients an infopack.

definitions.description: to tell somebody about something, especially in an official way
examples: The government took this decision without consulting Parliament or informing the public.
Have the police been informed?
Please inform us of any changes of address.
He went to inform them of his decision.
The leaflet informs customers about healthy eating.
I have been reliably informed (= somebody I trust has told me) that the couple will marry next year.
I am pleased to inform you that you have won first prize in this month’s competition.
‘He's already left,’ she informed us.
I have not been informed when the ceremony will take place.
Inform me at once if there are any changes in her condition.

definitions.description: to find out information about something
examples: We need time to inform ourselves thoroughly of the problem.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: to have an influence on something
examples: Religion informs every aspect of their lives.
These guidelines will be used to inform any future decisions.

definitions.description: the basic systems and services that are necessary for a country or an organization to run smoothly, for example buildings, transport and water and power supplies
a person or an animal that lives in a particular place
examples: the oldest inhabitant of the village
It is a town of about 10 000 inhabitants.

definitions.description: to receive money, property, etc. from somebody when they die
examples: She inherited a fortune from her father.
He will inherit the title on the death of his uncle.
Does he know that she stands to inherit?

definitions.description: to have qualities, physical features, etc. that are similar to those of your parents, grandparents, etc.
examples: He has inherited his mother's patience.
Is this an inherited disease?
How many of these traits are genetically inherited?
She inherited a passion for music from her grandfather.

definitions.description: if you inherit a particular situation from somebody, you are now responsible for dealing with it, especially because you have replaced that person in their job
examples: policies inherited from the previous administration
I inherited a number of problems from my predecessor.

definitions.description: happening at the beginning; first
examples: There is an initial payment of £60 followed by ten instalments of £25.
The government will make an initial investment of $ 4.7 billion in the company.
in the initial stages (= at the beginning) of the campaign
an initial phase/period
an initial assessment/investigation/report
My initial reaction was to decline the offer.
Her initial response was one of anger.

definitions.description: at the beginning
examples: Initially, the system worked well.
More people had been infected than was initially thought.
He was initially reluctant to join the project.
The scientific work will be conducted, at least initially, at our laboratories.

definitions.description: a new plan for dealing with a particular problem or for achieving a particular purpose
examples: a United Nations peace initiative
Most policy initiatives come from the White House.
to launch an initiative
The money was intended to support initiatives in bilingual education.
new initiatives to improve animal welfare
a government initiative to combat unemployment
a joint initiative by the Scottish and UK governments
an initiative for peace and human rights

definitions.description: the ability to decide and act on your own without waiting for somebody to tell you what to do
examples: He said I was lazy and had no initiative.
You won't get much help. You'll have to use your initiative.
She needs to show more initiative if she wants to succeed.
Too much bureaucracy represses creativity and initiative.
She did it on her own initiative (= without anyone telling her to do it).

definitions.description: the power or opportunity to act and gain an advantage before other people do
examples: to seize/regain the initiative
It was up to the US to take the initiative in repairing relations.

definitions.description: (in some states of the US) a process by which ordinary people can suggest a new law by signing a petition
examples: a ballot initiative to establish a local minimum wage

definitions.description: coloured liquid for writing, drawing and printing
examples: written in ink
different coloured inks

definitions.description: a tattoo or tattoos (= pictures or designs marked permanently on a person's skin)
examples: She likes to wear clothes that show off her ink.
He lifted up his shirt so that we could see his two new inks.

definitions.description: inside; towards or close to the centre of a place
examples: an inner courtyard
inner London

definitions.description: private and secret; not expressed or shown to other people
examples: She doesn't reveal much of her inner self.
the inner workings of the mind
An inner voice told him that what he was doing was wrong.
He has to fight an inner turmoil even to step onto a plane.
a character who makes us wish to know more about his inner life
It's time to get in touch with your inner geek (= the part of you that likes geeky things, even though you pretend not to).

definitions.description: the introduction of new things, ideas or ways of doing something
examples: an age of technological innovation
The company is very interested in product design and innovation.

I'm still owed three days' leave.
He owes more money than he can afford to pay.
Exactly how much do we owe?
She still owes £3 000 to her father.
The country owes billions of dollars to foreign creditors.
Most hospitals owe money to pharmaceutical companies for medicines and equipment.
How much do I owe you for the groceries?

definitions.description: to feel that you ought to do something for somebody or give them something, especially because they have done something for you
examples: I owe a debt of gratitude to all my family.
You owe it to your staff to be honest with them.
I owe a duty to my family.
You owe me a favour!
Thanks for sticking up for me—I owe you one (= I owe you a favour).
I think you owe us an explanation.
I think we're owed an apology.

definitions.description: to exist or be successful because of the help or influence of somebody/something
examples: He owes his success to hard work.
The play owes much to French tragedy.
I owe everything to him.
The town owes its existence to the minerals that lie below the mountains.
I owe him everything.
I knew that I owed the surgeon my life.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: to have to obey and support somebody who is in a position of authority or power
examples: All serfs owed allegiance to a lord.

definitions.description: Police and Criminal Evidence Act
a straight tree with a mass of long leaves at the top, growing in tropical countries. There are several types of palm tree, some of which produce fruit.
examples: a date palm
a coconut palm
palm leaves/fronds/groves

definitions.description: the inner surface of the hand between the wrist and the fingers
examples: He held the bird gently in the palm of his hand.
sweaty palms
to read somebody’s palm (= to say what you think will happen to somebody by looking at the lines on their palm)

definitions.description: a square or rectangular piece of wood, glass or metal that forms part of a larger surface such as a door or wall
examples: One of the glass panels in the front door was cracked.
wooden fence panels
The central panel depicts St George.
You need to remove the roof panel to remove the side panels.

definitions.description: a flat board in a vehicle or on a machine where the controls and instruments are fixed
examples: an instrument/a display panel
A red light flashed on the control panel.

definitions.description: a piece of metal that forms part of the outer frame of a vehicle
examples: A rear body panel needed replacing after the accident.

definitions.description: a piece of cloth that forms part of a piece of clothing
examples: The trousers have double thickness knee panels for extra protection.

definitions.description: a group of specialists who give their advice or opinion about something; a group of people who discuss topics of interest on television or radio
examples: an advisory panel
a judging panel
a panel of experts/judges
We have two politicians on tonight's panel.
a panel discussion
The budget increase was recommended by an independent panel.
She is a member of the medical advisory panel.
The interview panel wants/want to find out as much as possible about each candidate's abilities.

definitions.description: a sudden feeling of great fear that cannot be controlled and prevents you from thinking clearly
examples: a moment of panic
They were in a state of panic.
Office workers fled in panic as the fire took hold.
There's no point getting into a panic about the exams.
a panic attack (= a condition in which you suddenly feel very anxious, causing your heart to beat faster, etc.)
a panic decision (= one that is made when you are in a state of panic)
A look of panic crossed his face.
The mere thought of flying fills me with panic.

definitions.description: a situation in which people are made to feel very anxious or frightened, causing them to act quickly and without thinking carefully
examples: News of the losses caused (a) panic among investors.
Careful planning at this stage will help to avoid a last-minute panic.
There's no panic (= we do not need to rush), we've got plenty of time.
panic buying/selling (= the act of buying/selling things quickly and without thinking carefully because you are afraid that a particular situation will become worse)

definitions.description: a public celebration of a special day or event, usually with bands in the streets and decorated vehicles
examples: the Lord Mayor’s parade
St Patrick’s Day parade in New York

definitions.label: (figurative)
definitions.description: a formal occasion when soldiers march or stand in lines so that they can be inspected (= looked at and approved) by their officers or other important people
examples: a military parade
They held a parade to mark the soldiers' return.
They stood as straight as soldiers on parade.
The latest software will be on parade at the exhibition.

definitions.description: a series of things or people
examples: Each generation passes through a similar parade of events.

definitions.label: (especially British English)
definitions.description: a street with a row of small shops
examples: a shopping parade

definitions.label: (often disapproving)
definitions.description: an obvious display of something, particularly in order to impress other people
examples: Social media is a constant parade of wealth, happiness, success and vanity.

definitions.description: two or more lines that are parallel to each other are the same distance apart at every point
examples: parallel lines
The road and the canal are parallel to each other.

definitions.description: very similar or taking place at the same time
examples: parallel trends
Though still a committed painter, in 1978 she launched a parallel career as a photographer.
Two poisonings have been reported recently in London and now there has been a parallel case in the Netherlands.

definitions.label: (computing)
definitions.description: involving several computer operations at the same time
examples: parallel processing

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: the group of people who are elected to make and change the laws of a country
examples: The German parliament is called the ‘Bundestag’.
The Scottish parliament is expected to vote in favour of a ban.
The exit polls predicted a hung parliament (= in which no political party has more elected members than all the other parties added together).

definitions.description: the parliament of some countries, including the United Kingdom. In the UK, Parliament consists of the House of Commons and the House of Lords
examples: a Member of Parliament
an Act of Parliament
The issue was debated in Parliament.
to win a seat in Parliament
The party is set to win a majority in Parliament (= the most votes) in October's election.
to be elected to Parliament
He practised law briefly before standing for Parliament (= becoming a candidate in an election).
The plans are included in a bill currently before Parliament (= that is being discussed in Parliament).

definitions.description: a particular period during which a parliament is working; Parliament as it exists between one general election and the next
examples: We are now into the second half of the parliament.
to dissolve Parliament (= formally end its activities) and call an election
The legislation is expected to be introduced early in the next session of parliament.

definitions.description: for part of the day or week in which people work
examples: She's looking for a part-time job.
to study on a part-time basis
part-time workers
I'm only part-time at the moment.
Liz works part-time from 10 till 2.

definitions.description: a person who is taking part in an activity or event
examples: The average age of study participants was 48 years.
workshop/conference/seminar participants
He has been an active participant in the discussion.
The child must be a willing participant in the therapy.
Participants in the study completed a short questionnaire.

definitions.description: the act of taking part in an activity or event
examples: a show with lots of audience participation
A back injury prevented active participation in any sports for a while.

definitions.description: to some extent; not completely
examples: Some people are unwilling to attend the classes partly because of the cost involved.
These low prices were partly due to excess supply.
He was only partly responsible for the accident.
The story is partly based on fact.
It was partly my fault.
Two factors at least partly explain her success.
Her eyes were partly open.

definitions.description: the state of being a partner in business
examples: to be in/to go into partnership
He developed his own program in partnership with an American expert.

definitions.description: a relationship between two people, organizations, etc.; the state of having this relationship
examples: Marriage should be an equal partnership.
the school’s partnership with parents
a partnership between the United States and Europe

definitions.description: a business owned by two or more people who share the profits
examples: a junior member of the partnership

definitions.description: a long narrow area with walls on either side that connects one room or place with another
examples: A dark narrow passage led to the main hall.
a secret underground passage

definitions.description: a tube in the body through which air, liquid, etc. passes
examples: blocked nasal passages

definitions.label: (US English)
definitions.description: a short section from a book, piece of music, etc.
examples: Read the following passage and answer the questions below.
I have quoted this passage at length.
a passage from the Bible

definitions.label: (literary)
definitions.description: the process of time passing
examples: Her confidence grew with the passage of time.
rituals which mark the passage of the seasons

definitions.description: the process of discussing a bill in a parliament so that it can become law
examples: The bill is now guaranteed an easy passage through the House of Representatives.

definitions.description: a journey from one place to another by ship
examples: Her grandfather had worked his passage (= worked on a ship to pay for the journey) to America.

definitions.description: a way through something
examples: The officers forced a passage through the crowd.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: the action of going across, through or past something
examples: Large trees may obstruct the passage of light.

definitions.description: the permission to travel across a particular area of land
examples: We were promised (a) speedy passage through the border.
If the law were passed, EU nationals would no longer enjoy free passage through member states.

definitions.description: having or showing strong feelings of sexual love or of anger, etc.
examples: to have a passionate nature

definitions.description: having or showing strong feelings of enthusiasm for something or belief in something
examples: a passionate interest in music
a passionate defender of civil liberties

definitions.description: a series of letters, numbers, etc. that you must type into a computer or computer system in order to be able to use it
examples: Enter a username and password to get into the system.

definitions.description: a secret word or phrase that you need to know in order to be allowed into a place
examples: You must give the password before they'll let you in.

definitions.description: the ability to stay calm and accept a delay or something annoying without complaining
examples: She has little patience with (= will not accept or consider) such views.
People have lost patience with (= have become annoyed about) the slow pace of reform.
I have run out of patience with her.
My patience is wearing thin (= I do not have much patience left).
Teaching children with special needs requires patience and understanding.

definitions.description: the ability to spend a lot of time doing something difficult that needs a lot of attention and effort
examples: It takes time and patience to photograph wildlife.
I don't have the patience to do jigsaw puzzles.
Our patience was finally rewarded and we got the band's autographs.

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: a card game for only one player
to stop talking or doing something for a short time before continuing
examples: Anita paused for a moment, then said: ‘All right’.
The woman spoke almost without pausing for breath (= very quickly).
I paused at the door and looked back.
Pausing only to pull on a sweater, he ran out of the house.

definitions.description: to stop a video, etc. for a short time using the pause button
examples: She paused the movie to go and answer the door.

definitions.description: a person who is the same age or who has the same social status as you
examples: She enjoys the respect of her peers.
A peer review system is being introduced to help teachers who are experiencing difficulty.
Children are worried about failing in front of their peers.
Peer pressure is strong among young people (= they want to be like other people of the same age).

definitions.description: (in the UK) a member of the nobility or the House of Lords
examples: MPs and peers from all parties met to discuss the issue.

definitions.description: a punishment for breaking a law, rule or contract
examples: to impose a penalty
Assault carries a maximum penalty of seven years' imprisonment.
The penalty for travelling without a ticket is £200.
Contractors who fall behind schedule incur heavy financial penalties.
Harsher penalties are being imposed for crimes involving firearms.
a penalty clause in a contract
You can withdraw money from the account at any time without penalty.
The Romans prohibited the teaching of the Torah on penalty of death.

definitions.description: a disadvantage suffered as a result of something
examples: One of the penalties of fame is loss of privacy.

definitions.description: a disadvantage given to a player or a team when they break a rule
examples: He incurred a ten-second penalty in the first round.

definitions.refer: (in football (soccer) and some other similar sports)
definitions.description: a chance to score a goal or point without any defending players, except the goalkeeper, trying to stop it; the goal or point that is given if it is successful. This chance is given because the other team has broken the rules.
examples: Two minutes later Ford equalized with a penalty.
We were awarded a penalty after a late tackle.
I volunteered to take the penalty (= be the person who tries to score the goal/point).
He missed a penalty in the last minute of the game.

definitions.label: (often ironic)
definitions.description: an amount of money paid regularly by a government or company to somebody who has retired from work
examples: to receive a retirement pension
The party promised to increase the basic state pension by £15 a week.
a disability pension
to take out a pension
a workplace/an occupational pension
She was struggling to live on a small pension.
I've been paying into a private pension for years.
a pension fund
a pension scheme/plan

definitions.description: to understand or think of somebody/something in a particular way
examples: This discovery was perceived as a major breakthrough.
I do not perceive myself as an expert.
A science degree and artistic interests are often perceived as incompatible.
They were widely perceived to have been unlucky.

definitions.description: to notice or become aware of something
examples: I perceived a change in his behaviour.
She perceived that all was not well.
The patient was perceived to have difficulty in breathing.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: an idea, a belief or an image you have as a result of how you see or understand something
examples: a campaign to change public perception of the police
There is a general public perception that standards in schools are falling.

definitions.label: (specialist or formal)
definitions.description: the way you notice things, especially with the senses
examples: Everyone's perception of reality is slightly different.
visual perception

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: the ability to understand the true nature of something
examples: She showed great perception in her assessment of the family situation.
They have little perception of how ordinary people live their lives.

definitions.description: lasting for a long time or for all time in the future; existing all the time
examples: She was unable to find a permanent job.
Holiday camps employ only a very small number of permanent staff.
They are now living together on a permanent basis.
The accident has not done any permanent damage.
a permanent fixture (= a person or an object that is always in a particular place)
a permanent resident of the United States
She doesn't intend to make London her permanent home.
The gallery hosts various exhibitions and a permanent collection.
We decided to make the arrangement permanent.

definitions.description: in a way that lasts for a long time or for all time in the future; in a way that exists all the time
examples: The stroke left his right side permanently damaged.
She had decided to settle permanently in France.
This door is kept permanently locked.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: to allow somebody to do something or to allow something to happen
examples: Mobile phones are not permitted in the examination room.
We were not permitted any contact with each other.
Visitors are not permitted to take photographs.
The owners have been unwilling to permit the use of their land.
There are fines for exceeding permitted levels of noise pollution.
Jim permitted himself a wry smile.
The bill was designed to permit new fathers to take time off work.
She would not permit herself to look at them.
Permit me to offer you some advice.

definitions.description: to make something possible
examples: We hope to visit the cathedral, if time permits.
I'll come tomorrow, weather permitting (= if the weather is fine).
The password permits access to all files on the hard disk.
The length of the report does not permit a detailed discussion of the problems.
Cash machines permit you to withdraw money at any time.

definitions.description: a particular attitude towards something; a way of thinking about something
examples: a global perspective
A historical perspective may help us understand the issue.
Recent events seem less serious when put into an international perspective.
The aim is to offer a fresh perspective.
Try to see the issue from a different perspective.
a report that looks at the education system from the perspective of deaf people
The exhibition provides us with a unique perspective on her work.

definitions.description: the ability to think about problems and decisions in a reasonable way without making them seem worse or more important than they really are
examples: She was aware that she was losing all sense of perspective.
Try to keep these issues in perspective.
Talking to others can often help to put your own problems into perspective.
It is important not to let things get out of perspective.

definitions.description: the art of creating an effect of depth and distance in a picture by representing people and things that are far away as being smaller than those that are nearer the front
examples: The artist plays with perspective to confuse the eye.
We learnt how to draw buildings in perspective.
The tree on the left is out of perspective.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: a view, especially one in which you can see far into the distance
examples: a perspective of the whole valley

definitions.description: a stage in a process of change or development
examples: during the initial/final phase
the construction/development/design phase
the testing phase of the project
This technology is still in an early phase of development.
an important phase in your career
The wedding marked the beginning of a new phase in Emma's life.
His anxiety about the work was just a passing phase.
During his stay in Spain, his work entered a new phase.
She's going through a difficult phase.
The semester was divided into three phases of study.

definitions.description: each of the shapes of the moon as we see it from the earth at different times of the month
examples: the phases of the moon

definitions.description: a fact or an event in nature or society, especially one that is not fully understood
examples: cultural/natural phenomena
the global phenomenon of climate change
Globalization is a phenomenon of the 21st century.
Early retirement is a relatively new phenomenon in Britain.
We were hoping science could somehow explain this strange phenomenon.

definitions.label: North American English
definitions.description: a person or thing that is very successful or impressive
examples: This young pianist is a phenomenon.
The movie has become a bona fide cult phenomenon.

definitions.description: the study of the nature and meaning of the universe and of human life
examples: the philosophy of science
a professor of philosophy
a degree in philosophy

definitions.description: a particular set or system of beliefs resulting from the search for knowledge about life and the universe
examples: Buddhist/Eastern/Hindu philosophy
the philosophy of Aristotle
the development of different philosophies

definitions.description: a set of beliefs or an attitude to life that guides somebody’s behaviour
examples: Her philosophy of life is to take every opportunity that presents itself.
a furniture-maker's design philosophy

definitions.description: a number of things that have been placed on top of each other
examples: a pile of clothes/paper

The hats were stacked in neat piles.
I've sorted the books into three separate piles.

definitions.description: a mass of something that is high in the middle and wider at the bottom than at the top
examples: piles of dirty washing
The house was reduced to a pile of rubble.
He threw the remaining stones onto the pile.

definitions.label: (informal)
definitions.description: a lot of something
examples: He made a pile of cash on the sale of his house.
He walked out leaving a pile of debt behind him.
I have got piles of work to do.

definitions.description: the short threads, pieces of wool, etc. that form the soft surface of carpets and some types of cloth such as velvet
examples: a deep-pile carpet
Corduroy is the poor man’s velvet; its pile is made of cotton rather than silk or satin.

definitions.description: a large wooden, metal or stone post that is fixed into the ground and used to support a building, bridge, etc.

definitions.label: (formal or humorous)
definitions.description: a large impressive building
examples: a Victorian pile built as a private hospital
her family's ancestral pile

definitions.label: (informal)
definitions.description: a small flat round piece of medicine that you swallow whole, without biting it
examples: a vitamin pill
Take three pills daily after meals.
pill-popping (= the act of taking too many pills or using illegal drugs)
The doctor prescribed her some pills to help her sleep.
I was on various pills for my heart condition.

definitions.description: a pill that some women take to prevent them becoming pregnant
examples: the contraceptive pill
to be/go on the pill
Her doctor put her on the pill at 16.

definitions.label: (North American English)
definitions.description: an annoying person

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: an area of ground specially prepared and marked for playing a sports game
examples: a football pitch
a cricket/rugby/hockey pitch
an artificial pitch

definitions.description: how high or low a sound is, especially a musical note
examples: A basic sense of rhythm and pitch is essential in a music teacher.

definitions.description: the degree or strength of a feeling or activity; the highest point of something
examples: a frenetic pitch of activity

to reach a high pitch of excitement

definitions.description: talk or arguments used by a person trying to sell something or persuade people to do something
examples: an aggressive sales pitch
the candidate’s campaign pitch
Each company was given ten minutes to make its pitch.

definitions.label: especially British English
definitions.description: an act of throwing the ball; the way in which it is thrown
a black sticky substance made from oil or coal, used on roofs or the wooden boards of a ship to stop water from coming through

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: a place in a street or market where somebody sells things, or where somebody performs in order to entertain people outdoors

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: a place in a campsite where you can put up one tent or park one caravan, etc.
examples: Pitches to rent from only £15 per night.

definitions.label: (specialist)
definitions.description: the movement of a ship up and down in the water or of an aircraft in the air

definitions.label: (specialist)
definitions.description: the degree to which a roof slopes
examples: The pitch of the roof is 45 degrees.

definitions.description: used to show that you are disappointed about something
examples: It's a pity that you can't stay longer.

What a pity that she didn't tell me earlier.
This dress is really nice. Pity it's so expensive.
Oh, that's a pity.
It would be a great pity if you gave up now.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: a sad feeling caused by the pain and troubles of others
examples: I took pity on her and lent her the money.

I don't want your pity.
a look/feeling/surge of pity

definitions.description: the act of finding somebody a suitable job or place to live
examples: a job placement service
placement with a foster family

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: a job, often as part of a course of study, where you get some experience of a particular kind of work
examples: The course includes a placement in Year 3.

definitions.description: the act of placing something somewhere

definitions.label: (informal)

definitions.description: without marks or a pattern on it

It is all very plain to me.
It was plain that she wanted to leave.

What is quite plain from the evidence before me is (that) the figures are false.

definitions.label: (especially North American English)
definitions.description: not trying to trick anyone; honest and direct
examples: The plain fact is that nobody really knows.
a politician with a reputation for plain speaking
a plain, straightforward sort of man

definitions.description: used to emphasize that something is very ordinary, not special in any way
examples: You don't need any special skills for this job, just plain common sense.

definitions.description: not beautiful or attractive
examples: I've always had quite a plain face.

definitions.description: describing a simple stitch used in knitting
used when the two numbers or amounts mentioned are being added together
examples: Two plus five is seven.

definitions.description: as well as something/somebody; and also

definitions.description: having a sharp end

definitions.description: one part of something larger

examples: a generous portion of meat

definitions.description: a part of something that is shared with other people

definitions.description: to create a threat, problem, etc. that has to be dealt with
examples: to pose a threat/risk/challenge/danger

to pose a hazard/obstacle/barrier

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: to ask a question, especially one that needs serious thought
examples: The new play poses some challenging questions.

definitions.description: to sit or stand in a particular position in order to be painted, drawn or photographed

definitions.description: to pretend to be somebody in order to trick other people
examples: The gang entered the building posing as workmen.

definitions.label: (disapproving)
definitions.description: to dress or behave in a way that is intended to impress other people
examples: I saw him out posing in his new sports car.

definitions.label: (literary)
definitions.description: to have a powerful effect on somebody and control the way that they think, behave, etc.
examples: A terrible fear possessed her.

definitions.description: to make somebody do something that seems strange or unreasonable
examples: What possessed him to say such a thing?

definitions.description: that can develop into something or be developed in the future
examples: potential customers/buyers/investors/clients

the potential benefits of European integration
potential risks
a potential threat
the potential impact of the latest surge in oil prices

a potential prime minister
a potential source of conflict

definitions.description: used to say that something may develop into something
examples: a potentially dangerous situation

definitions.label: less frequent

Critics heaped/lavished/showered praise on her latest movie.
to deserve/earn/garner praise

definitions.description: the expression of thanks to or respect for God
examples: hymns/songs of praise
joyous singing and praise to God

definitions.description: to happen before something or come before something/somebody in order
