She preceded me in the job.
in the moments which immediately preceded the earthquake

definitions.description: to go in front of somebody
examples: She preceded him out of the room.

definitions.description: to do or say something to introduce something else
examples: She preceded her speech with a vote of thanks to the committee.

definitions.description: rare and worth a lot of money

definitions.description: valuable or important and not to be wasted
examples: Clean water is a precious commodity in that part of the world.
You're wasting precious time!

definitions.description: loved or valued very much
examples: precious memories/possessions

definitions.label: (informal)

definitions.label: (disapproving)

definitions.label: (figurative)
definitions.description: to buy something
examples: Please ensure that you purchase your ticket in advance.
to purchase an item/a product
to purchase a property/home
We recently purchased a home just outside Las Vegas.
The equipment can be purchased from your local supplier.
The tickets can only be purchased in advance from our website.
They purchased the land for $1 million.
Victory was purchased (= achieved) at too great a price.

definitions.description: not mixed with anything else; with nothing added
examples: pure gold
ties made of pure silk
These shirts are 100% pure cotton.
The patient was given pure oxygen to breathe.
Classical dance in its purest form requires symmetry and balance.
One movie is classified as pure art, the other as entertainment.
The metal needs to be very pure.

definitions.description: clean and not containing any harmful substances
examples: a bottle of pure water
The air was sweet and pure.
Much of the population still does not have access to pure drinking water.

definitions.description: complete and total
examples: They met by pure chance.
She laughed with pure joy.
That woman is pure evil.
These reports are pure speculation (= there is no evidence that they are true).
It was a pure accident. I'm not blaming anybody.
It was pure coincidence that all the absences occurred at the same time.

definitions.description: very clear; perfect
examples: beaches of pure white sand
a pure voice

definitions.label: (literary)
definitions.description: without evil thoughts or actions, especially sexual ones; morally good
examples: to lead a pure life
His motives were pure.
to be pure in body and mind

definitions.description: about increasing knowledge of the subject rather than using knowledge in practical ways
examples: pure mathematics
technology as opposed to pure science subjects

definitions.description: not mixed with any other type of animal or plant
examples: These cattle are one of the purest breeds in Britain.

definitions.description: only; completely
examples: I saw the letter purely by chance.
The charity is run on a purely voluntary basis.
She took the job purely and simply for the money.
The fireplace in the bedroom is purely decorative.

definitions.description: to do something or try to achieve something over a period of time
examples: to pursue a goal
to pursue an aim/objective
How can we most effectively pursue these aims?
We intend to pursue this policy with determination.
She wishes to pursue a medical career.
I was determined to pursue my dream of becoming an actor.
Many communities are aggressively pursuing plans to preserve open spaces.
I wasn't sure I wanted to pursue dance as a career.
He continues to pursue a soft policy on crime.

definitions.description: to continue to discuss, find out about or be involved in something
examples: to pursue an agenda/a strategy/a claim
to pursue legal action
The Crown Prosecution Service is unwilling to pursue the case.
We have decided not to pursue the matter.
She wanted the freedom to pursue her own interests.
He was still pursuing his studies.
Other companies are pursuing the same course.
The government has actively pursued a campaign against the militants.
‘But’, he pursued, ‘you still haven't answered the question.’

definitions.description: to follow or go after somebody/something, especially in order to catch them
examples: She left the theatre, hotly pursued by the press.
Police pursued the car at high speed.
Jake has been pursuing her (= trying to have a relationship with her) for months.

definitions.description: the act of looking for or trying to get something
examples: the pursuit of happiness/knowledge/profit
She travelled the world in pursuit of her dreams.

definitions.description: the act of following or going after somebody, especially in order to catch them
examples: We drove away with two police cars in pursuit (= following).
I galloped off on my horse with Rosie in hot pursuit (= following quickly behind).

definitions.description: something that you give your time and energy to, that you do as a hobby
examples: outdoor/leisure/artistic pursuits

definitions.description: a game, etc. that you have to think about carefully in order to answer it or do it
examples: a crossword puzzle
a book of puzzles for children

definitions.description: something that is difficult to understand or explain
examples: The deeper meaning of the poem remains a puzzle.
The detectives were beginning to solve the murder. All the pieces of the puzzle were falling neatly into place.

definitions.label: (especially North American English)
definitions.description: a picture printed on cardboard (= very thick, stiff card) or wood, that has been cut up into a lot of small pieces of different shapes that you have to fit together again

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: a written list of questions that are answered by a number of people so that information can be collected from the answers
examples: to fill in a questionnaire
to fill out a questionnaire
Local companies were asked to complete a questionnaire about their exports.

definitions.description: happening or existing between people of different races
examples: racial hatred/prejudice/tension/violence
racial equality
They have pledged to end racial discrimination in areas such as employment.

definitions.description: connected with a person’s race
examples: racial minorities
a person’s racial origin
The community has a religious rather than a racial identity.
There is growing sensitivity about sexual and racial stereotypes in children's literature.

definitions.description: the unfair treatment of people who belong to a different race; violent behaviour towards them
examples: a victim of racism
ugly outbreaks of racism
the urgent need to address institutional racism within the organization
It is important to identify root causes that perpetuate systemic racism in the city.
structural/casual racism
Half a million people held a mass protest against racism last night.

definitions.description: the belief that there are different races of people with different characteristics and abilities, and that some races are better than others; a general belief about a whole group of people based only on their race
examples: irrational racism
Many 19th-century scientific theories were underpinned by racism.

definitions.description: having the belief that some races of people are better than others or having general beliefs about other people based only on their race; showing this through violent or unfair treatment of people of other races
examples: racist attitudes/remarks
racist thugs/attacks
It's a bit racist to assume I only eat Chinese food.

definitions.description: powerful and very dangerous rays that are sent out from radioactive substances
examples: high levels/doses of radiation that damage cells
the link between exposure to radiation and childhood cancer
a radiation leak from a nuclear power station
radiation sickness
the radiations emitted by radium

definitions.description: heat, energy, etc. that is sent out in the form of rays
examples: ultraviolet radiation
electromagnetic radiation from power lines
The ozone layer absorbs solar radiation.

definitions.description: the treatment of cancer and other diseases using radiation
a wooden or metal bar placed around something as a barrier or to provide support
examples: She leaned on the ship's rail and gazed out to sea.

definitions.description: a bar fixed to the wall for hanging things on
examples: a curtain rail

definitions.description: each of the two metal bars that form the track that trains run on
examples: The train thundered along the rails.

definitions.description: railways as a means of transport
examples: to travel by rail
rail travel/services/fares
a rail link/network

definitions.label: (informal)
definitions.description: done, chosen, etc. without somebody deciding in advance what is going to happen, or without any regular pattern
examples: the random killing of innocent people
a random sample/selection (= in which each thing has an equal chance of being chosen)
The information is processed in a random order.
I find and play a lot of random stuff—Bach, blues, bebop.
He grabbed a random pair of jeans and an old red shirt.
She dodged the random items that were on the concrete floor.

definitions.label: (informal)
definitions.description: not known or not identified
examples: Some random guy gave me a hundred bucks.
You don’t want some random dude telling you how to live your life.

definitions.label: (informal)
definitions.description: a thing or person that is random is strange and does not make sense, often in a way that interests you or makes you laugh
examples: Mum, you are so random!
The humour is great because it's just so random and unhinged from reality.

definitions.description: a small animal with a long tail, that looks like a large mouse, usually considered a pest (= an animal which is disliked because it destroys food or spreads disease)
examples: rat poison
The police are all over town. He’s caught, like a rat in a trap.

definitions.label: (informal, disapproving)
definitions.description: an unpleasant person, especially somebody who treats their partner or friends badly, for example by leaving them or cheating them
examples: You mean he just walked out on her after fifteen years? What a rat!

definitions.description: a measurement of how good, popular, important, etc. somebody/something is, especially in relation to other people or things
examples: Education has been given a high-priority rating by the new administration.
‘The Big Bang Theory’ was the network show with the highest rating.

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: a set of figures that show how many people watch or listen to a particular television or radio programme, used to show how popular a programme is
examples: The show has gone up in the ratings.
The BBC is currently ahead in the ratings war.
Bringing her on the show was a cynical attempt to boost the ratings.
His new sitcom was a ratings success.
It has been ousted from top spot in the TV ratings.
The network's prime-time ratings are up 150 per cent.
The programme's ratings have dipped sharply.
The ratings went shooting up overnight.
The show continues to garner high ratings.

definitions.description: a number or letter that shows which groups of people a particular film is suitable for
examples: The film was given a 15 rating by British censors.
The movie carries an R rating.

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: a sailor in the navy who is not an officer
accepting in a sensible way what it is actually possible to do or achieve in a particular situation
examples: a realistic assessment/approach/view
We have to be realistic about our chances of winning.
It is not realistic to expect people to spend so much money.
It would not be realistic for the Government to demand a pay freeze in the sector at this point.

definitions.description: sensible and appropriate; possible to achieve
examples: a realistic prospect/chance/possibility
a realistic alternative/option
The important thing is to have realistic expectations about what you can and can't accomplish.
We must set realistic goals.
a realistic target
If you want to retain good employees, you have to pay a realistic salary.

definitions.description: representing things as they are in real life
examples: a realistic portrayal/depiction/picture
She made a very realistic drawing of a horse.
We try to make these training courses as realistic as possible.
The realistic graphics really bring the game to life.

definitions.description: fair, practical, and sensible
examples: It is reasonable to assume that he knew beforehand that this would happen.
As life expectancy increases, it is reasonable to expect that the retirement age will increase too.
It seems reasonable to conclude that their claims are unfounded.
Is it not reasonable for the government to look for savings and efficiencies?
Be reasonable! We can't work late every night.
The prosecution has to prove beyond (a) reasonable doubt that he is guilty of murder.
We have reasonable grounds for believing that you are responsible.
Any reasonable person would have done exactly as you did.
You must take all reasonable steps to ensure that the information that you provide is correct.
It seems a perfectly reasonable request to make.
If companies expect work during personal time, it's only reasonable to allow personal time at work.
I considered the evidence in order to decide what is fair and reasonable in the circumstances.

definitions.description: acceptable and appropriate in a particular situation
examples: The police apparently thought this explanation perfectly reasonable.
The judge said they had a reasonable expectation of privacy relating to the information concerned.
He made us a reasonable offer for the car.
You must submit your claim within a reasonable time.
It can even be done as a class project in a reasonable amount of time.
The adviser must take reasonable care to ensure that the information is correct

definitions.description: not too expensive
examples: We sell good-quality food at reasonable prices.
He believes NASA can reach Mars at a reasonable cost.
If the price is reasonable, we'll buy it.

definitions.description: fairly good, but not very good
examples: Most people here have a reasonable standard of living.
The hotel was reasonable, I suppose (= but not excellent).
There's a reasonable chance that he'll come.
The furniture is in reasonable condition.

definitions.description: to a degree that is fairly good but not very good
examples: The instructions are reasonably straightforward.
She seems reasonably happy in her new job.

definitions.description: in a logical and sensible way
examples: We tried to discuss the matter calmly and reasonably.

definitions.description: in a fair way
examples: He couldn't reasonably be expected to pay back the loan all at once.
The apartments are reasonably priced (= not too expensive).

definitions.description: to build or put something together again
examples: After the earthquake, the people set about rebuilding their homes.
He rebuilt the engine using parts from cars that had been scrapped.
It could take ten years for the area to completely rebuild after the hurricane.

definitions.description: to make something/somebody complete and strong again
examples: When she lost her job, she had to rebuild her life completely.
attempts to rebuild the shattered post-war economy
After the divorce, it took me a long time to rebuild my confidence.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: to remember something
examples: She could not recall his name.
Many years later Muir recalled his days at Glasgow University.

‘I may have; I don't recall,’ she said.

I can't recall meeting her before.
I vaguely recall seeing the film.
I seem to recall receiving an email from a reader a while ago.
I seem to recall him mentioning a brother once.
He recalled that she always came home late on Wednesdays.
She later recalled that she had met him once.
Can you recall exactly what happened?
I can vividly recall where and when I saw them.
‘It was on a Thursday in March,’ he recalled.

definitions.description: to make somebody think of something
examples: The poem recalls Eliot's ‘The Waste Land’.

definitions.description: to order somebody to return
examples: Both countries recalled their ambassadors.
He was recalled to military duty.
They have both been recalled to the Welsh squad (= selected as members of the team after a time when they were not selected).

definitions.description: to ask for something to be returned, often because there is something wrong with it
examples: The company has recalled all the faulty hairdryers.

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: the part of a phone that you hold close to your mouth and ear
examples: to pick up/lift/put down/replace the receiver

definitions.description: a piece of radio or television equipment that changes broadcast signals into sound or pictures
examples: a satellite/GPS receiver
To change channel, select the desired number on the receiver unit.

definitions.label: British English also
definitions.description: a person who is chosen by a court to be in charge of a company that is bankrupt
examples: They had to lay off 200 staff and call in the receivers.
The company has been put in the hands of the receiver.
A receiver was appointed by the court to handle the company’s affairs.
The company remained in the hands of the receiver.

definitions.description: a person who receives something
examples: Molly's more of a giver than a receiver.

definitions.description: a person who buys or accepts stolen goods, knowing that they have been stolen
a player who plays in a position in which the ball can be caught when it is being passed forward
a difficult time for the economy of a country, when there is less trade and industrial activity than usual and more people are unemployed
examples: How do you assess the impact of the current recession on manufacturing?
The economy is in deep recession.
policies to pull the country out of recession
These industries have been hard hit by recession.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: the movement backwards of something from a previous position
examples: the gradual recession of the floodwater

definitions.label: (especially British English, informal)
definitions.description: to think something or have an opinion about something
examples: I reckon (that) I’m going to get that job.
He'll be famous one day. What do you reckon (= do you agree)?
It's worth a lot of money, I reckon.
‘They'll never find out.’ ‘You reckon?’ (= I think you may be wrong about that)

definitions.description: to be generally considered to be something
examples: Children are reckoned to be more sophisticated nowadays.
It was generally reckoned a success.

definitions.label: (British English, informal)
definitions.description: to expect to do something
examples: We reckon to finish by ten.
He wasn’t reckoning to pay so much.

definitions.description: to calculate an amount, a number, etc.
examples: I could see him reckoning the cost as I spoke.
The age of the earth is reckoned at about 4.6 billion years.
My debts were reckoned at $12 000.
They reckon (that) their profits are down by at least 20%.

The journey was reckoned to take about two hours.
The trip was reckoned to take over two days.

definitions.description: to get well again after being ill, hurt, etc.
examples: He's still recovering from his operation.
She spent many weeks in hospital recovering from her injuries.
He has fully recovered from the shoulder surgery.
She remains in serious condition, but is expected to recover.
The victim is recovering well at home.

definitions.description: to return to a normal state after an unpleasant or unusual experience or a period of difficulty
examples: It can take many years to recover from the death of a loved one.
The economy is at last beginning to recover.

definitions.description: to get back the same amount of money that you have spent or that is owed to you
examples: He is unlikely to ever recover his legal costs.

definitions.description: to get back or find something that was lost, stolen or missing
examples: The police eventually recovered the stolen paintings.
Six bodies were recovered from the wreckage.

definitions.description: to win back a position, level, status, etc. that has been lost
examples: The team recovered its lead in the second half.

definitions.description: to get back the use of your senses, control of your emotions, etc.
examples: It took her a few minutes to recover consciousness.
to recover your sight
She seemed upset but quickly recovered herself.

definitions.description: an act of making something less or smaller; the state of being made less or smaller
examples: Some staff received wage rises, while others experienced a reduction.

a drastic reduction in costs

There has been some reduction in unemployment.
a significant/substantial reduction in spending

definitions.description: an amount of money by which something is made cheaper
examples: price reductions

a sale with massive reductions on selected items

definitions.description: a copy of a photograph, map, picture, etc. that is made smaller than the original one

definitions.label: (chemistry)
definitions.description: the fact of adding one or more electrons to a substance or of removing oxygen from a substance
a sauce made by boiling a liquid until it becomes thick
examples: a red wine reduction
a reduction of chicken stock, wine and cream

definitions.description: to think about somebody/something in a particular way
examples: They regarded people outside their own town with suspicion.

He regards himself as a patriot.
Capital punishment was regarded as inhuman and immoral.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: to look at somebody/something, especially in a particular way
examples: He regarded us suspiciously.

definitions.description: of or relating to a region
examples: services available at a local and regional level
the conflict between regional and national interests
a regional assembly/council/government
a regional director/manager
national initiatives for regional development
a regional office/centre/agency

definitions.description: to record your/somebody’s/something’s name on an official list
examples: You can also register online.
to register a birth/marriage/death
to register a company/trademark

a registered charity

The ship was registered in Panama.
Six other families were also registered at the same address.
to register at a hotel
She is officially registered disabled.

to register with a doctor/dentist
All childminders should be registered with the local authority.
About 700 people registered for the conference.

More than 5 000 people registered to take part in the contest.
78 per cent reported that they were registered to vote.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: to make your opinion known officially or publicly
examples: Many saw the vote as a way to register a protest.

examples: The thermometer registered 32°C.

The stock exchange has registered huge losses this week.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: to show or express a feeling
examples: Her face registered disapproval.

definitions.description: to notice something and remember it; to be noticed
examples: He barely registered our presence.
I told her my name, but it obviously didn't register.

definitions.description: to send something by mail, paying extra money to protect it against loss or damage
examples: Can I register this, please?
a registered letter

definitions.description: the act of making an official record of something/somebody
examples: the registration of letters and parcels
the registration of students for a course
registration fees
the registration of a child’s birth

definitions.description: a document showing that an official record has been made of something
examples: my Democratic party registration
the information on the registration roll
I traced my family history using the civil registration records.

definitions.label: (both British English)
definitions.description: the series of letters and numbers that are shown on a number plate at the front and back of a vehicle to identify it
examples: The police are looking for a black car with German registration plates.

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: the time when a teacher looks at the list of students on the class register and checks that the students are present
to feel sorry about something you have done or about something that you have not been able to do
examples: If you don't do it now, you'll only regret it.
The decision could be one he lives to regret.

I never regretted dropping out of college.
I deeply regret what I said.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: used to say in a polite or formal way that you are sorry or sad about a situation
examples: The airline regrets any inconvenience.
The president said that his country deeply regretted the incident.
The United States regrets the loss of innocent civilian lives.
I regret that I am unable to accept your kind invitation.
I very much regret that I cannot be with you this evening.
We regret to inform you that your application has not been successful.
I regret to say that we cannot let you have the picture.

definitions.description: to control something by means of rules
examples: The department is responsible for regulating the insurance industry.
The activities of credit companies are regulated by law.
The government accepts whaling in principle as long as it is carefully regulated.
It is up to the regulating authority to put the measures into effect.

definitions.description: to control the speed, pressure, temperature, etc. in a machine or system
examples: This valve regulates the flow of water.

definitions.description: an official rule made by a government or some other authority
examples: too many rules and regulations
fire/building regulations
the strict regulations governing the sale of weapons
To comply with government hygiene regulations, there must be a separate sink for hand washing.
It's against safety regulations to fix these doors open.
Under the new regulations spending on office equipment will be strictly controlled.

definitions.description: controlling something by means of rules
examples: the voluntary regulation of the press

definitions.description: to make a feeling, an idea, etc. stronger
examples: The experience reinforced my sense of loss.
Such jokes tend to reinforce gender stereotypes.
The climate of political confusion has only reinforced the country's economic decline.
Success in the talks will reinforce his reputation as an international statesman.

definitions.description: to make a structure or material stronger, especially by adding another material to it
examples: All buildings are now reinforced to withstand earthquakes.
reinforced plastic/steel/concrete
The door was built of oak, heavily reinforced with iron.

definitions.description: to send more people or equipment in order to make an army, etc. stronger
examples: The UN has undertaken to reinforce its military presence along the borders.

definitions.description: to a fairly large degree, especially in comparison to something else
examples: relatively large/small/high/low

These students had a relatively simple task.

definitions.description: used when you are comparing something with all similar things
examples: Relatively speaking, these jobs provide good salaries.

definitions.description: closely connected with the subject you are discussing or the situation you are in
examples: relevant information/facts/documents/factors

definitions.description: the fact of being valuable and useful to people in their lives and work
examples: Her novel is still relevant today.

definitions.description: the feeling of happiness that you have when something unpleasant stops or does not happen
examples: I felt a huge sense of relief when I heard they were all OK.
We all breathed a sigh of relief when he left.
Much to my relief the car was not damaged.
News of their safety came as a great relief.
She sighed with relief.
He smiled in relief as he saw them both.
She had gone through hell and there was no relief in sight for her.
This was a great relief to him.

It was a relief to her to realize that she was not the only one with this problem.
His mother spoke of her relief that he was now safely home.
It is actually a relief that it's finally happened.
She expressed relief at the outcome of the investigation.
He described his relief at securing his freedom.
What a relief!

definitions.description: the act of removing or reducing pain, worry, etc.
examples: modern methods of pain relief
the relief of symptoms/suffering/poverty/pain

Massage can bring some relief from tension.

definitions.description: food, money, medicine, etc. that is given to help people in places where there has been a war or natural disaster
examples: disaster relief
relief efforts/operations
relief organizations/supplies/work

definitions.description: financial help given by the government to people who need it

examples: relief on mortgage interest payments

definitions.description: something that is interesting or fun that replaces something boring, difficult or unpleasant for a short period of time
examples: a few moments of light relief in an otherwise dull performance

definitions.description: a person or group of people that replaces another when they have finished working for the day or when they are sick
examples: The next crew relief comes/come on duty at 9 o'clock.

definitions.description: the act of freeing a town, etc. from an enemy army that has surrounded it
examples: the relief of Mafeking

definitions.description: a way of decorating wood, stone, etc. by cutting designs into the surface of it so that some parts stick out more than others; a design that is made in this way
examples: The column was decorated in high relief (= with designs that stick out a lot) with scenes from Greek mythology.
The bronze doors are covered with sculpted reliefs.

definitions.description: the effect of colours, light, etc. that makes an object easier to notice than others around it
examples: The snow-capped mountain stood out in sharp relief against the blue sky.

definitions.description: the quality of a particular situation, problem, etc. that makes it easier to notice than before
examples: Their differences have been thrown into sharp relief by the present crisis.

definitions.description: to remove or reduce an unpleasant feeling or pain
examples: to relieve the symptoms of a cold
to relieve anxiety/guilt/stress
Being able to tell the truth at last seemed to relieve her.

definitions.description: to make a problem less serious
examples: efforts to relieve poverty

definitions.description: to make something less boring, especially by introducing something different
examples: We played cards to relieve the boredom of the long wait.

definitions.description: to replace somebody at the end of their period of duty
examples: to relieve a sentry

definitions.description: to free a town, etc. from an enemy army that has surrounded it

examples: I had to relieve myself behind a bush.

definitions.description: feeling happy because something unpleasant has stopped or has not happened; showing this
examples: She sounded relieved.

definitions.description: something that you say or write which expresses an opinion, a thought, etc. about somebody/something
examples: to make a remark

definitions.description: to fight back when attacked; to use force to stop something from happening

definitions.label: (British English also)

examples: seaside/mountain resorts

definitions.label: (formal)

definitions.description: the act of limiting or controlling somebody/something

She was super (= very kind) when I was having problems.

definitions.description: a doctor who is trained to perform surgery (= medical operations that involve cutting open a person’s body)
examples: a brain/heart surgeon
Surgeons performed two operations on him yesterday.

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: medical treatment of injuries or diseases that involves cutting open a person’s body and often removing or replacing some parts; the branch of medicine connected with this treatment
examples: major/minor surgery
to undergo heart/knee/shoulder surgery
He will require surgery on his left knee.
The doctor had to perform emergency surgery to the patient's head.
She's a specialist in reconstructive and cosmetic surgery.
The president is to undergo minor surgery to remove a small growth from his hand.

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: a place where a doctor, dentist or vet sees patients
examples: a doctor’s/dentist’s/vet's surgery

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: the time during which a doctor, dentist or vet is available to see patients
examples: morning/afternoon/evening surgery
surgery hours
Is there a surgery this evening?
He holds surgery from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m.

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: a time when people can meet their Member of Parliament to ask questions and get help
examples: a constituency surgery

definitions.description: to be all around something/somebody
examples: Tall trees surround the lake.
the membranes surrounding the brain
The garden is surrounded by a wall.
As a child I was surrounded by love and kindness.
I loved being surrounded by enthusiastic young people.
The lake is surrounded with trees.

definitions.description: to move into position all around somebody/something, especially so as to prevent them from escaping; to move somebody/something into position in this way
examples: Police surrounded the building.
They've surrounded the building with police.

definitions.description: to be closely connected with something/somebody
examples: publicity surrounding the divorce
the controversy/circumstances surrounding his death
The report explores the issues surrounding the case.

definitions.description: to choose to have particular people or things near you all the time
examples: I like to surround myself with beautiful things.

definitions.description: that is near or around something
examples: Oxford and the surrounding area
From the top of the hill you can see all the surrounding countryside.
the immediately surrounding area
The college tries to respond to the needs of the surrounding community.

definitions.description: the state of continuing to live or exist, often despite difficulty or danger
examples: the struggle/battle/fight for survival
His only chance of survival was a heart transplant.
Exporting is necessary for our economic survival.
Continued trade in these products is a threat to the survival of the species.

definitions.description: something that has continued to exist from an earlier time
examples: The ceremony is a survival from pre-Christian times.

definitions.description: a person who continues to live, especially despite being nearly killed or experiencing great danger or difficulty
examples: the sole/only survivor of the massacre
The plane crashed in an area of dense jungle. There were no survivors.
There are only a few survivors from the original team (= members who remain in it while others have been replaced).
She'll cope. She's one of life's great survivors (= somebody who deals very well with difficult situations).
A movie has been made about the last remaining survivor of the tribe.

definitions.description: to have an idea that something is probably true or likely to happen, especially something bad, but without having definite proof
examples: As I had suspected all along, he was not a real policeman.
If you suspect a gas leak, do not strike a match or even turn on an electric light.
Suspecting nothing, he walked right into the trap.
I didn’t want the neighbours suspecting anything.
I began to suspect (that) they were trying to get rid of me.
I strongly suspect (that) this whole story is fictional.
She had no reason to suspect (that) Sylvia had not been telling the truth.
I suspect (that) she might be lying.
It was suspected that the drugs had been brought into the country by boat.
She suspected him to be an impostor.

definitions.description: to have an idea that somebody is guilty of something, without having definite proof
examples: He resigned after being suspected of theft.
He is not suspected of any involvement in the recent attacks.
He was wrongly suspected of the crime.
They arrested four men suspected of links to an extremist group.
I suspected her of damaging the equipment.
The drug is suspected of causing over 200 deaths.
Whom do the police suspect?

definitions.description: to feel that something is not completely right, legal or honest, without having any proof; to not trust something
examples: I suspected her motives in offering to help.
He dealt through a broker whose honesty he had no reason to suspect.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: to hang something from something else
examples: A lamp was suspended from the ceiling.
Her body was found suspended by a rope.
A boat was suspended on wires from the rafters.

definitions.description: to officially stop something for a time; to prevent something from being active, used, etc. for a time
examples: Production has been suspended while safety checks are carried out.
The constitution was suspended as the fighting grew worse.
In the theatre we willingly suspend disbelief (= temporarily believe that the characters, etc. are real).

definitions.description: to officially delay something; to arrange for something to happen later than planned
examples: The introduction of the new system has been suspended until next year.
to suspend judgement (= delay forming or expressing an opinion)

definitions.description: to officially prevent somebody from doing their job, going to school, etc. for a time, as a punishment or while a complaint against them is investigated
examples: The police officer was suspended while the complaint was investigated.
She was suspended from school for a week.

definitions.label: (specialist)
definitions.description: to float in liquid or air without moving
examples: Small droplets are held suspended in the atmosphere.

definitions.description: involving the use of natural products and energy in a way that does not harm the environment
examples: sustainable forest management
an environmentally sustainable society
This type of farming is simply not sustainable any more.

definitions.description: that can continue or be continued for a long time
examples: sustainable economic growth
Unfortunately, this level of output is not sustainable.

definitions.description: to make food, drink, etc. go down your throat into your stomach
examples: Always chew food well before swallowing it.
I had a sore throat and it hurt to swallow.
The pills should be swallowed whole.

definitions.description: to move the muscles of your throat as if you were swallowing something, especially because you are nervous
examples: She swallowed hard and told him the bad news.

definitions.description: to take somebody/something in or completely cover them/it so that they/it cannot be seen or exist separately any longer
examples: I watched her walk down the road until she was swallowed by the darkness.
Large areas of countryside have been swallowed up by towns.

definitions.description: to use up something completely, especially an amount of money
examples: Most of my salary gets swallowed (up) by the rent and bills.

definitions.description: to accept that something is true; to believe something
examples: I found her excuse very hard to swallow.
He told her a pack of lies, but she swallowed it whole.

definitions.description: to hide your feelings
examples: to swallow your doubts
You're going to have to swallow your pride and ask for your job back.

definitions.description: to accept offensive remarks, criticisms, etc. without complaining or protesting
examples: I was surprised that he just sat there and swallowed all their remarks.

definitions.description: to use rude or offensive language, usually because you are angry
examples: She fell over and swore loudly.
I don't like to hear children swearing.
He heard her swear under her breath.
She was shouting, swearing, and acting in an aggressive manner towards the staff
Why did you let him swear at you like that?

definitions.description: to make a serious promise to do something
examples: He swore revenge on the man who had killed his father.
I solemnly swear (that) it will never happen again.
I swear (that) I’ll never leave you.
He swore solemnly that he would never hit her again.
She made him swear not to tell anyone.
He left, swearing never to return.

definitions.description: to promise that you are telling the truth
examples: She swore (that) she’d never seen him before.
I could have sworn (= I am sure) I heard the phone ring.
I swear to God I had nothing to do with it.

definitions.description: to make a public or official promise, especially in court
examples: Witnesses were required to swear on the Bible.
Are you willing to stand up in court and swear that you don't recognize him?
Remember, you have sworn to tell the truth.
Barons had to swear an oath of allegiance to the king.
I swear by Almighty God to tell the truth.
They refused to swear allegiance to the new ruler.

definitions.description: to make somebody promise not to tell something to anyone
examples: Everyone was sworn to secrecy about what had happened.

definitions.description: to clean a room, surface, etc. using a broom (= a type of brush on a long handle)
examples: to sweep the floor
Chimneys should be swept regularly.
I don't have to sweep and mop every day.
Don't just stand around—grab a broom and sweep up.
The showroom had been emptied and swept clean.

definitions.description: to remove something from a surface using a brush, your hand, etc.
examples: She swept the crumbs into the wastebasket.
He swept the leaves up into a pile.
She swept the clothes onto the floor and invited him to sit down.

definitions.description: to move or push somebody/something suddenly and with a lot of force
examples: The little boat was swept out to sea.
Their tent was swept away in the storm.
She let herself be swept along by the crowd.

definitions.description: to move suddenly and/or with force over an area or in a particular direction
examples: Rain swept in through the broken windows.
A fire swept through the store on Tuesday night.
Strong winds regularly sweep the islands.

definitions.label: (figurative)
definitions.description: to move quickly and/or smoothly, especially in a way that impresses or is intended to impress other people
examples: Without another word she swept out of the room.
Two police motorcycles swept through the village.
A pair of golden eagles swept across the sky.
She swept past the photographers without a glance.
He swept into the lead with an almost perfect performance.

definitions.description: to move something, especially your hand or arm, quickly and smoothly in a particular direction
examples: He rushed to greet her, sweeping his arms wide.

definitions.description: to suddenly affect somebody strongly
examples: A wave of tiredness swept over her.
Memories came sweeping back.

definitions.description: to spread quickly
examples: Rumours of his resignation swept through the company.
the latest craze sweeping the nation

definitions.description: to move over an area, especially in order to look for something
examples: His eyes swept around the room.
The car headlights swept across the front of the building.
Searchlights swept the sky.
She swept the crowd with her binoculars.

definitions.description: to move, or move something, over a surface, touching it lightly
examples: Her dress swept the ground as she walked.

definitions.description: to brush, comb, etc. your hair in a particular direction
examples: Her hair was swept back from her face.

definitions.description: to form a long, smooth curve
examples: The hotel gardens sweep down to the beach.

definitions.label: (North American English)
definitions.description: to win all the games in a series of games against another team or all the parts of a contest
examples: The Blue Jays have a chance to sweep the series.
New Jersey swept Detroit last season.

definitions.description: kind to somebody who is hurt or sad; showing that you understand and care about their problems
examples: a sympathetic listener
a sympathetic response
She was very sympathetic when I was sick.
I did not feel at all sympathetic towards Kate.
I'm here if you need a sympathetic ear (= somebody to talk to about your problems).

definitions.description: showing that you approve of somebody/something or that you share their views and are willing to support them
examples: He was speaking to a highly sympathetic audience.
to be sympathetic to the party’s aims
Russian newspapers are largely sympathetic to the president.

definitions.description: easy to like
examples: a sympathetic character in a novel
I don't find her a very sympathetic person.
The character's faults actually make him more sympathetic.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: the feeling of being sorry for somebody; showing that you understand and care about somebody’s problems
examples: to express/feel sympathy for somebody
I have no sympathy for Jan—it's all her own fault.
I wish he'd show me a little more sympathy.
Our heartfelt sympathy goes out to the victims of the war.
Shops were closed out of sympathy for the victims.
May we offer our deepest sympathies on the death of your wife.
I would like to extend our sincere sympathies to his family at this sad time.

definitions.description: the act of showing support for or approval of an idea, a cause, an organization, etc.
examples: The seamen went on strike in sympathy with (= to show their support for) the dockers.
Her sympathies lie with the anti-abortion lobby.

definitions.description: friendship and understanding between people who have similar opinions or interests
examples: There was no personal sympathy between them.
He has a total lack of sympathy for young people.

definitions.description: to make a determined effort to deal with a difficult problem or situation
examples: The government is determined to tackle inflation.
I think I'll tackle the repairs next weekend.
Firefighters tackled a blaze in a garage last night.

definitions.description: to speak to somebody about a problem or difficult situation
examples: I tackled him about the money he owed me.

definitions.description: to try and take the ball from an opponent
examples: He was tackled just outside the penalty area.

definitions.description: to make an opponent fall to the ground in order to stop them running
examples: He can run fast and tackle hard.

definitions.description: to deal with somebody who is violent or threatening you
examples: He tackled a masked intruder at his home.

definitions.description: a small piece of paper, cloth, plastic, etc. attached to something to identify it or give information about it
examples: He put name tags on all his shirts.
a gift tag (= tied to a present)

definitions.description: an electronic device that can be attached to a person, animal or object so that police, researchers, etc. know where the person, etc. is
examples: The police use electronic tags to monitor the whereabouts of young offenders on probation.

definitions.description: a name or phrase that is used to describe a person or thing in some way
examples: They are finally ready to drop the tag ‘the new Beatles’.
The ‘lucky’ tag stuck for years.
The president made several jokes in an attempt to shake off his ‘humourless’ tag.

definitions.label: (linguistics)
definitions.description: a word or phrase that is added to a sentence for emphasis, for example I do in Yes, I do

definitions.label: (computing)
definitions.description: a set of letters or symbols that are put before and after a piece of text or data in order to identify it or show that it is to be treated in a particular way
a short quotation or saying in a foreign language
examples: the Latin tag ‘Si vis pacem, para bellum.’ (= if you want peace, prepare for war)

definitions.label: British English also
definitions.description: a children’s game in which one child runs after the others and tries to touch one of them
a symbol or name used by a graffiti writer and painted in a public place
a story created using the imagination, especially one that is full of action and adventure
examples: a coming-of-age/morality tale
The story is a classic tale of love and betrayal.
Dickens’ ‘A Tale of Two Cities’
His latest book is a delightful children’s tale about talking animals.

definitions.description: an exciting spoken description of an event, which may not be completely true
examples: I love listening to his tales of life at sea.
I've heard tales of people seeing ghosts in that house.
She regaled us with tales of her wild youth.
The team's tale of woe continued on Saturday (= they lost another match).
Her experiences provide a cautionary tale (= a warning) for us all.

definitions.description: a large container for holding liquid or gas
examples: a fuel/water/storage tank
a fish tank (= for keeping fish in)
He uses an oxygen tank to breathe.

definitions.description: the contents of a tank or the amount it will hold
examples: We drove there and back on one tank of fuel.

definitions.description: a military vehicle covered with strong metal and armed with guns. It can travel over very rough ground using wheels that move inside metal belts.
examples: Tanks rolled in to end the siege.
He's six feet tall and built like a tank (= has a solid, strong body).

definitions.label: (Indian English)
definitions.description: an artificial pool, lake or reservoir
to hit somebody/something quickly and lightly
examples: Someone tapped at the door.
He was busy tapping away at his computer.
Ralph tapped me on the shoulder.
Tap the icon to open the app.

definitions.description: if you tap your fingers, feet, etc. or they tap, you hit them gently against a table, the floor, etc., for example to the rhythm of music
examples: He kept tapping his fingers on the table.
The music set everyone's feet tapping.

definitions.description: to make use of a source of energy, knowledge, etc. that already exists
examples: We need to tap the expertise of the people we already have.
The movie seems to tap into a general sentimentality about animals.

definitions.label: (especially British English)
definitions.description: to fit a device to a phone so that somebody’s calls can be listened to secretly
examples: He was convinced his phone was being tapped.

definitions.description: to cut into a tree in order to get liquid from it

definitions.label: (North American English)
definitions.description: to choose somebody to do a particular job
examples: Richards has been tapped to replace the retiring chairperson.

definitions.label: (phonetics)
definitions.description: to produce a tap (6)
to damage something by pulling it apart or into pieces or by cutting it on something sharp; to become damaged in this way
examples: I tore my jeans on the fence.
I tore a hole in my jeans.
He tore the letter in two.
I tore the picture into pieces.
The letter had been torn to shreds.
His clothes were badly torn.
Careful—the fabric tears very easily.
I tore the package open.
I tore open the package.

definitions.description: to make a hole in something by force
examples: The blast tore a hole in the wall.

definitions.description: to remove something from something else by pulling it roughly or violently
examples: The storm nearly tore the roof off.
I tore another sheet from the pad.

definitions.description: to pull yourself/somebody away by force from somebody/something that is holding you or them
examples: She tore herself from his grasp.
He tore himself free.
One error and he would have been torn loose and hurled overboard by the squalling wind.

definitions.description: to injure a muscle, etc. by stretching it too much
examples: a torn ligament/muscle
She's torn a ligament in her right hand.
She tore a calf muscle playing squash.

definitions.description: to move somewhere very quickly or in an excited way
examples: He tore off down the street.

definitions.description: very badly affected or damaged by something
examples: to bring peace to a strife-torn country
a strike-torn industry

definitions.description: connected with technology
examples: technological advances
technological change
a major technological breakthrough

definitions.description: the years of a person’s life when they are between 13 and 19 years old
examples: She began writing poetry in her teens.
to be in your early/late teens

definitions.label: (North American English)
definitions.description: a building used for religious worship, especially in religions other than Christianity
examples: the Temple of Diana at Ephesus
a Buddhist/Hindu/Sikh temple
to go to temple (= to a service in a synagogue, where Jewish people worship)

definitions.description: each of the flat parts at the sides of the head, at the same level as the eyes and higher
examples: He had black hair, greying at the temples.
There was a throbbing in her temples.

definitions.description: in a way that lasts or is intended to last or be used only for a short time; in a way that is not permanent
examples: We regret this service is temporarily unavailable.
The company announced that it would be temporarily closing the factory because of the global downturn.

definitions.description: lasting or intended to last or be used only for a short time; not permanent
examples: to hire temporary workers
They had to move into temporary accommodation.
Volunteers built temporary shelters for the survivors.
temporary relief from pain
a temporary fix/measure/solution
More than half the staff are temporary.

definitions.description: if somebody/something has a particular tendency, they are likely to behave or act in a particular way
examples: to display artistic tendencies
I have a tendency to talk too much when I'm nervous.
This material has a tendency to shrink when washed.
There is a tendency for this disease to run in families.
She has a strong natural tendency towards caution.

definitions.description: a new custom that is starting to develop
examples: There's a growing tendency for women to marry later.
Industry showed a tendency towards increasingly centralized administration.

definitions.label: (British English)

examples: a growing separatist tendency within the Anglo-Irish community

examples: There is mounting tension along the border.
international/racial/political tensions

The incident has further increased tension between the two countries.

definitions.description: a situation in which the fact that there are different needs or interests causes difficulties
examples: There is often a tension between the aims of the company and the wishes of the employees.

definitions.description: a feeling of worry and stress that makes it impossible to relax

Walking and swimming are excellent for releasing tension.
a tension headache

definitions.description: the feeling of fear and excitement that is created by a writer or a film director
examples: dramatic tension

definitions.description: the state of being stretched tight; the extent to which something is stretched tight

definitions.description: a place, building or set of buildings where journeys by train, bus or boat begin or end
examples: a railway/bus/ferry terminal

definitions.label: (computing)

examples: Internet terminals have been installed at most libraries.

definitions.label: (specialist)
definitions.description: a point at which connections can be made in an electric circuit
examples: a positive/negative terminal

definitions.description: the conditions that people offer, demand or accept when they make an agreement, an arrangement or a contract
examples: peace terms

These are the terms and conditions of your employment.

definitions.description: conditions that you agree to when you buy, sell, or pay for something; a price or cost
examples: to buy something on easy terms (= paying for it over a long period)

definitions.description: a way of expressing yourself or of saying something
examples: We wish to protest in the strongest possible terms (= to say we are very angry).
I'll try to explain in simple terms.
The letter was brief, and couched in very polite terms.
She spoke of you in glowing terms (= expressing her admiration of you).

definitions.label: (especially British English)
definitions.description: very
examples: I'm terribly sorry—did I hurt you?

I’m not terribly interested in politics.

definitions.description: very much; very badly

examples: Flying terrifies her.

examples: These street gangs have become the terror of the neighbourhood.
The terrors of the night were past.
Death holds no terrors for (= does not frighten or worry) me.

definitions.description: violent action or the threat of violent action that is intended to cause fear, usually for political purposes

terror tactics/groups

examples: an act of terrorism
the fight against terrorism

examples: The terrorists are threatening to blow up the plane.

testing and assessment in education

examples: a speech therapist
a beauty therapist

a long piece of writing completed by a student as part of a university degree, based on their own research

examples: Wash the fruit thoroughly before use.
