The expedition was widely hailed as a success.
Teenager Matt Brown is being hailed a hero for saving a young child from drowning.
Union leaders hailed the socialists’ victory as a huge step forward.

definitions.description: to signal to a taxi or a bus, in order to get the driver to stop
examples: to hail a taxi/cab

definitions.label: (literary)
definitions.description: to call to somebody in order to say hello to them or attract their attention
examples: A voice hailed us from the other side of the street.
We soon came within hailing distance of (= fairly close to) the others.

definitions.description: when it hails, small balls of ice fall like rain from the sky
examples: It's hailing!

definitions.description: at an equal distance between two points; in the middle of a period of time
examples: I got the ball on the halfway line.

definitions.description: part of the way towards doing or achieving something
examples: the halfway point/stage

definitions.description: to stop; to make somebody/something stop
examples: She walked towards him and then halted.
‘Halt!’ the Major ordered (= used as a command to soldiers).
The police were halting traffic on the parade route.
The trial was halted after the first week.

definitions.label: (figurative)
definitions.description: to suddenly make somebody stop by frightening or surprising them; to suddenly stop because something has frightened or surprised you
examples: The question stopped Alice in her tracks.
Suddenly he stopped dead in his tracks: what was he doing?
The disease was stopped in its tracks by immunization programmes.

definitions.description: the amount of something that can be held in one hand
examples: a handful of rice
She scooped up handfuls of loose earth.

definitions.description: a small number of people or things
examples: Only a handful of people came.
They cannot hope to win more than a handful of seats at the next election.

definitions.label: (informal)
definitions.description: a person or an animal that is difficult to control
examples: Her children can be a real handful.

definitions.description: the way that somebody deals with or treats a situation, a person, an animal, etc.
examples: I was impressed by his handling of the affair.
This horse needs patient handling.
Why is he being so polite, as if I need tactful handling?

definitions.description: the action of touching, feeling or holding something with your hands
examples: toys that can stand up to rough handling
In the manufacturing industries heavy materials handling is often done by robots.
hygienic food handling practice

definitions.description: the action of organizing or controlling something
examples: data handling on computer

definitions.description: the cost of dealing with an order, delivering goods, booking tickets, etc.
examples: a small handling charge
The cost is $11 plus $5 for shipping and handling.

definitions.description: the way in which a vehicle can be controlled by the driver
examples: a car designed for easy handling

definitions.label: British English also
definitions.description: the act or cost of transporting goods from one place to another
easy to use or to do
examples: a handy little tool
handy hints/tips for removing stains
a handy-sized dictionary

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: located near to somebody/something; located or stored in a convenient place
examples: Always keep a first-aid kit handy.
Have you got a pen handy?
Our house is very handy for the station.

definitions.description: able to use your hands or tools to make or repair things well
examples: to be handy around the house
to be handy with a sewing machine
Lucy is quite handy with a drill!

definitions.description: the act of annoying or worrying somebody by putting pressure on them or saying or doing unpleasant things to them
examples: sexual/racial harassment
workplace/street harassment (= that happens at work/in the street)

definitions.description: the act of making repeated attacks on an enemy
examples: guerrilla harassment of the enemy

definitions.label: (computing)
definitions.description: the machines and electronic parts in a computer or other electronic system
examples: We supply computer hardware to businesses.

definitions.label: also British English, old-fashioned
definitions.description: tools and equipment that are used in the house and garden
examples: a hardware shop/store

definitions.description: the equipment, machines and vehicles used to do something
examples: tanks and other military hardware

definitions.label: (approving)
definitions.description: a state of peaceful existence and agreement
examples: social/racial harmony
They lived together in perfect harmony.
the need to be in harmony with our environment

definitions.label: (music)
definitions.description: the way in which different notes that are played or sung together combine to make a pleasant sound
examples: to sing in harmony
They began to sing in perfect four-part harmony.
passionate lyrics and stunning vocal harmonies

definitions.label: (approving)
definitions.description: an attractive combination of related things
examples: the harmony of colour in nature
The designer’s aim is to produce a harmony of shape and texture.

definitions.description: cruel, severe and unkind
examples: The punishment was harsh and unfair.
The minister received some harsh criticism.
the harsh treatment of prisoners
He regretted his harsh words.
We had to face up to the harsh realities of life sooner or later.
It may seem harsh to criticize him after his death.
‘She's just totally useless!’ ‘That's a bit harsh.’

definitions.description: very difficult and unpleasant to live in
examples: a harsh winter/wind/climate
the harsh conditions of poverty which existed for most people at that time

definitions.description: too strong and bright; ugly or unpleasant to look at
examples: harsh colours
She was caught in the harsh glare of the headlights.
the harsh lines of concrete buildings

definitions.description: unpleasant to listen to
examples: ‘Stop it!’ she said in a harsh voice.

definitions.description: too strong and rough and likely to damage something
examples: harsh detergents
Ordinary soap can be too harsh for delicate skin.

definitions.description: the time of year when the crops are gathered in on a farm, etc.; the act of cutting and gathering crops
examples: harvest time
Farmers are extremely busy during the harvest.

definitions.label: (figurative)
definitions.description: the crops, or the amount of crops, cut and gathered
examples: the grain harvest
a good/bad harvest (= a lot of crops or few crops)
The appeal produced a rich harvest of blankets, medicines and clothing.
Plum growers say they are expecting a bumper harvest (= a large amount of produce) this year.

definitions.description: a very strong feeling of dislike for somebody/something
examples: He looked at me with intense hatred.
There was fear and hatred in his voice.
She felt nothing but hatred for her attacker.
a profound hatred of war
feelings of hatred towards the bombers
racial hatred (= hatred for people from a different race)
The debate simply revived old hatreds.

definitions.description: if the ghost of a dead person haunts a place, people say that they have seen it there
examples: A headless rider haunts the country lanes.
I’ll come back to haunt you!

definitions.description: if something unpleasant haunts you, it keeps coming to your mind so that you cannot forget it
examples: The memory of that day still haunts me.
For years she was haunted by guilt.

definitions.description: to continue to cause problems for somebody for a long time
examples: That decision came back to haunt him.
She has been haunted by her past during her career.

definitions.description: something that can be dangerous or cause damage
examples: a fire/safety hazard
The island group is particularly vulnerable to natural hazards.
Growing levels of pollution represent a serious health hazard to the local population.
Everybody is aware of the hazards of smoking.

definitions.description: if a feeling or an effect heightens, or something heightens it, it becomes stronger or increases
examples: Tension has heightened after the recent bomb attack.
The campaign is intended to heighten public awareness of the disease.
His breakdown was followed by a period of heightened activity.
Fears of a pandemic were heightened by rising case numbers.
The drug is said to give users a heightened sense of well-being.

definitions.description: the history, traditions, buildings and objects that a country or society has had for many years and that are considered an important part of its character
examples: Spain’s rich cultural heritage
The building is part of our national heritage.

definitions.description: a person's ethnic or religious background; the countries, cultures, religious groups, etc. that a person's parents or ancestors come from
examples: What's your heritage?
Her heritage is Chinese and Vietnamese.
She made a conscious attempt to explore her Jewish heritage.

definitions.description: used to describe a traditional product, brand, type of animal or plant variety, especially one that is old-fashioned, rare and of high quality
examples: Cotswold sheep are considered a heritage breed in Canada.
Heritage carrots are not always orange in colour.
They work with some of Britain's oldest heritage brands, including Jaguar, Harrods and the BBC.

definitions.description: a system, especially in a society or an organization, in which people are organized into different levels of importance from highest to lowest
examples: the social/political hierarchy
She's quite high up in the management hierarchy.

definitions.description: the group of people in control of a large organization or institution
examples: It was on orders from the party hierarchy that she dropped the investigation.
The hierarchy has/have remained silent on this issue.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: a system that ideas or beliefs can be arranged into according to their importance
examples: a hierarchy of needs

definitions.description: receiving or involving a lot of attention and discussion in the media
examples: a high-profile campaign

definitions.description: something that you say or do in an indirect way in order to show somebody what you are thinking
examples: He gave a broad hint (= one that was obvious) that he was thinking of retiring.
Should I drop a hint (= give a hint) to Matt?
He resented any hint that he might be to blame.

definitions.description: something that suggests what will happen in the future
examples: At the first hint of trouble, they left.
The opening scene gives us a hint of things to come.

definitions.description: a small amount of something
examples: a hint of a smile
There was more than a hint of sadness in his voice.
The walls were painted white with a hint of peach.
Gail searched his face for the slightest hint of regret.

definitions.description: a small piece of practical information or advice
examples: handy hints on saving money
The teacher’s book gives useful hints on how to develop reading skills.

definitions.description: the country where a person was born
examples: Many refugees have been forced to flee their homeland.

definitions.description: (in the Republic of South Africa under the apartheid system in the past) one of the areas with some self-government that were intended for a group of black African people to live in
examples: the Transkei homeland

definitions.description: a curved piece of metal, plastic or wire for hanging things on, catching fish with, etc.
examples: a picture/curtain/coat hook
a fish hook
Hang your towel on the hook.
The key was hanging from a hook.
Your coat’s hanging on a hook behind the door.

definitions.description: a short hard hit that is made with the elbow bent
examples: a left hook to the jaw

definitions.description: a way of hitting the ball so that it curves to the side instead of going straight ahead (usually by mistake in golf, but deliberately in cricket)
a thing that is used to make people interested in something
examples: The images are used as a hook to get children interested in science.
Well-chosen quotations can serve as a hook to catch the reader’s interest.

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: believing that something you want will happen
examples: I feel hopeful that we'll find a suitable house very soon.
He is not very hopeful about the outcome of the interview.
She is hopeful of returning to work soon.

definitions.description: showing hope
examples: a hopeful smile

definitions.description: making you believe that something you want will happen; bringing hope
examples: The latest trade figures are a hopeful sign.
The future did not seem very hopeful.

definitions.label: British English
definitions.description: people in general
examples: He was found guilty of crimes against humanity.
He believed in serving the greater good of humanity.
We are talking about nothing less than the survival of humanity.

definitions.description: the state of being a person rather than a god, an animal or a machine
examples: The story was used to emphasize the humanity of Jesus.
united by a sense of common humanity

definitions.description: the quality of being kind to people and animals by making sure that they do not suffer more than is necessary; the quality of being humane
examples: The judge was praised for his courage and humanity.

definitions.description: the subjects of study that are about the way people think and behave, for example literature, language, history and philosophy
examples: The college offers a wide range of courses in the arts and humanities.

definitions.description: showing you do not think that you are as important as other people
examples: Be humble enough to learn from your mistakes.
my humble tribute to this great man

definitions.label: (ironic or humorous)
definitions.description: used to suggest that you are not as important as other people, but in a way that is not sincere or not very serious
examples: In my humble opinion, you were in the wrong.
My humble apologies. I did not understand.

definitions.description: having a low rank or social position
examples: a man of humble birth/origins
a humble occupation
the daughter of a humble shopkeeper

definitions.description: not large or special in any way
examples: a humble farmhouse
The company has worked its way up from humble beginnings to become the market leader.
Most of us have never considered the humble potato as a precious gift from nature.

definitions.description: a chemical element. Hydrogen is a gas that is the lightest of all the elements. It combines with oxygen to form water.
the process of showing, proving or recognizing who or what somebody/something is
examples: The identification of the crash victims was a long and difficult task.
Accurate identification of these birds is difficult.
Each product has a number for easy identification.
The vehicle's identification number is stamped on the engine.
Biometric identification methods include fingerprints and facial recognition scanners.
Only one witness could make a positive identification.
The hospital had mixed up the patients' identification tags.

definitions.description: the process of recognizing that something exists, or is important
examples: The early identification of children with special educational needs is very important.

definitions.description: official papers or a document that can prove who you are
examples: Can I see some identification, please?
To vote, Florida law requires a photo identification with a signature.

definitions.description: a strong feeling of sympathy, understanding or support for somebody/something
examples: her emotional identification with the play’s heroine
their increasing identification with the struggle for independence

definitions.description: the process of making a close connection between one person or thing and another
examples: the voters’ identification of the Democrats with high taxes

definitions.description: based on or connected with an ideology
examples: ideological differences
This was rejected for ideological reasons.
His agenda has been purely ideological.

definitions.description: a set of ideas that an economic or political system is based on
examples: Marxist/capitalist ideology

definitions.description: a set of beliefs, especially one held by a particular group, that influences the way people behave
examples: the ideology of gender roles
alternative ideologies

definitions.label: (informal)
definitions.description: a rude way to refer to somebody who you think is very stupid
examples: When I lost my passport, I felt such an idiot.
What idiot pressed the switch?

definitions.label: (old-fashioned, offensive)
definitions.description: a word for a person with very low intelligence that is now considered offensive
a lack of knowledge or information about something
examples: They fought a long battle against prejudice and ignorance.
I hate to admit my ignorance, but how does it work?
He showed a remarkable ignorance of the facts.
widespread ignorance about the disease
They were kept in ignorance of their government's activities.
Children often behave badly out of ignorance.
Many lives are lost through ignorance.

definitions.description: the state of not knowing about something and so being unable to worry about it
examples: We preferred to remain in blissful ignorance of what was going on.

definitions.label: (saying)
definitions.description: if you do not know about something, you cannot worry about it
examples: Some doctors believe ignorance is bliss and don't give their patients all the facts.

definitions.label: (US English)
definitions.description: language that produces pictures in the minds of people reading or listening
examples: poetic imagery

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: pictures, photographs, etc.
examples: satellite imagery (= for example, photographs of the earth taken from space)

definitions.description: extremely large or great
examples: There is still an immense amount of work to be done.
The benefits are immense.
a project of immense importance
To my immense relief, he didn’t notice my mistake.

definitions.description: likely to happen very soon
examples: the imminent threat of invasion
The system is in imminent danger of collapse.
An announcement about his resignation is imminent.
An attack seems imminent.

definitions.description: the act of making something that has been officially decided start to happen or be used
examples: the implementation of the new system

definitions.label: (figurative)
definitions.description: to put somebody in a prison or another place from which they cannot escape
examples: They were imprisoned for a crime they didn't commit.
I feel imprisoned in my own home.

definitions.description: the act of putting somebody in a prison or another place from which they cannot escape; the state of being there
examples: to be sentenced to life imprisonment for murder

definitions.description: the fact of not being able to do something
examples: the government’s inability to provide basic services
Some families go without medical treatment because of their inability to pay.

definitions.description: not enough; not good enough
examples: inadequate supplies
The system is inadequate for the tasks it has to perform.
The food supplies are inadequate to meet the needs of the hungry.

definitions.description: not able, or not confident enough, to deal with a situation
examples: I felt totally inadequate as a parent.

definitions.description: not suitable or appropriate in a particular situation
examples: inappropriate behaviour/language
It would be inappropriate for me to comment.
clothes inappropriate to the occasion

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: the extent to which something happens or has an effect
examples: an area with a high incidence of crime

definitions.label: (physics)
definitions.description: the way in which light meets a surface
examples: the angle of incidence

definitions.description: wanting to do something
examples: She was inclined to trust him.
He writes only when he feels inclined to.
There'll be time for a swim if you feel so inclined.

definitions.description: tending to do something; likely to do something
examples: He's inclined to be lazy.
They'll be more inclined to listen if you don't shout.

definitions.description: used when you are expressing an opinion but do not want to express it very strongly
examples: I'm inclined to agree with you.
I'm half inclined to believe him.

definitions.description: having a natural ability for something; preferring to do something
examples: musically/academically inclined children
The club was a notorious hang-out for the criminally inclined.

definitions.description: sloping; at an angle
the fact of including somebody/something; the fact of being included
examples: His inclusion in the team is in doubt.

definitions.description: a person or thing that is included
examples: There were some surprising inclusions in the list.

definitions.description: the fact or policy of providing equal opportunities and resources for people who might otherwise not get them, for example people who are disabled or belong to minority groups
examples: The company is actively promoting diversity and inclusion.
The internet promotes the social inclusion of groups such as people with disabilities.

definitions.description: if you incur something unpleasant, you are in a situation in which you have to deal with it
examples: She had incurred the wrath of her father by marrying without his consent.

definitions.description: if you incur costs, you have to pay them
examples: You risk incurring bank charges if you exceed your overdraft limit.

definitions.description: a sign that shows you what something is like or how a situation is changing
examples: The economic indicators are better than expected.
These atmospheric waves are a reliable indicator of weather changes.

definitions.description: a device on a machine that shows speed, pressure, etc.
examples: a depth indicator

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: a light on a vehicle that flashes to show that the vehicle is going to turn left or right
examples: Her right-hand indicator was flashing.
He flicked on his indicator light and passed the lorry.

definitions.description: a sign that a system, society, etc. is very bad or very wrong
examples: The poverty in our cities is a damning indictment of modern society.
This research is a terrible indictment on the medical profession.

definitions.label: (especially North American English)
definitions.description: an official statement accusing somebody of a crime
examples: She was convicted on an indictment for conspiracy.
The federal district court dismissed the indictment.
The government announced a federal indictment against him.
They issued an indictment against them.
Two men were named in the indictment.
War crimes indictments were handed down by a UN-backed court.
an indictment charging theft
There is sufficient evidence against him to support an indictment for murder.

definitions.label: (especially North American English)
definitions.description: the act of officially accusing somebody of a crime
examples: This led to his indictment on allegations of conspiracy.
He faces indictment for perjury.

definitions.description: coming from a particular place and having lived there for a long time before other people came there; relating to, belonging to or developed by these people
examples: the indigenous peoples/languages of an area
Indigenous Australians/Canadians
indigenous land/territory
She campaigns for indigenous rights.

definitions.description: having originally developed in a particular place, rather than having been brought there from somewhere else
examples: The kangaroo is indigenous to Australia.
The reserve supports a wide range of indigenous species.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: to persuade or influence somebody to do something
examples: Nothing would induce me to take the job.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: to cause something
examples: drugs that induce sleep
a drug-induced coma
Hearing loss is often induced by exposure to loud noise.

definitions.label: (medical)
definitions.description: to make a woman start giving birth to her baby by giving her special drugs; to make a baby start being born by giving the mother special drugs
examples: an induced labour
We'll have to induce her.
I was admitted and the baby was induced at 35 weeks.

definitions.description: to allow yourself to have or do something that you like, especially something that is considered bad for you
examples: They went into town to indulge in some serious shopping.
She has never been one to indulge in gossip.
He was free to indulge in a little romantic daydreaming.
I indulged myself with a long hot bath.
For a special treat, indulge yourself with one of these luxury desserts.

definitions.description: to satisfy a particular desire, interest, etc.
examples: The inheritance enabled him to indulge his passion for art.
In the closing lines, the poet indulges his sense of irony.

definitions.description: to be too generous in allowing somebody to have or do whatever they like
examples: She did not believe in indulging the children with presents.
His questions were annoying but it was easier to indulge him than try and protest.
Her father had always indulged her every whim.

definitions.description: to take part in an activity, especially one that is illegal
the unfair difference between groups of people in society, when some have more wealth, status or opportunities than others
examples: We need to tackle inequality of opportunity wherever we find it.
economic inequalities between different areas
Gender and racial inequality are still widespread throughout society.

definitions.label: (humorous)
definitions.description: well known for being bad or evil
examples: a general who was infamous for his brutality
the most infamous concentration camp
the infamous British sandwich

definitions.label: (formal or specialist)
definitions.description: a baby or very young child
examples: a nursery for infants under two
their infant son
She was seriously ill as an infant.
Mozart was an infant prodigy (= a young child with unusual ability).

definitions.description: a child at school between the ages of four and seven
examples: The majority of infant teachers are women.
I've known her since we were in the infants (= at infant school).

definitions.description: to make a disease or an illness spread to a person, an animal or a plant
examples: It is not possible to infect another person through kissing.
people infected with the virus

definitions.description: to make a substance contain harmful bacteria that can spread disease
examples: The eggs were infected with salmonella.

definitions.description: to make a computer virus spread to another computer or program
to make somebody share a particular feeling
examples: She infected the children with her enthusiasm for music.
The whole room was soon infected by his laughter.

definitions.label: (humorous)
definitions.description: to make somebody/something suffer something unpleasant
examples: They inflicted a humiliating defeat on the home team.
Heavy casualties were inflicted on the enemy.
Do you have to inflict that music on us?
They surveyed the damage inflicted by the storm.
The rodent’s sharp teeth can inflict a nasty bite.
When someone deliberately inflicts damage, it is a matter for the police.

definitions.description: having a lot of influence on somebody/something
examples: a highly influential book
His conversation with the manager was influential in his decision to join United.
She is one of the most influential figures in local politics.
The committee was influential in formulating government policy on employment.

definitions.description: that is a basic or permanent part of somebody/something and that cannot be removed
examples: the difficulties inherent in a study of this type
Violence is inherent in our society.
an inherent weakness in the design of the machine

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: to prevent something from happening or make it happen more slowly or less frequently than normal
examples: A lack of oxygen may inhibit brain development in the unborn child.
Financial considerations are inhibiting access to higher education.
Alcohol significantly inhibits the action of the drug.

definitions.description: to make somebody nervous or embarrassed so that they are unable to do something
examples: The managing director's presence inhibited them from airing their problems.
The fear of dismissal inhibited employees from raising problems.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: to make something begin
examples: to initiate legal proceedings against somebody
The government has initiated a programme of economic reform.

definitions.description: to explain something to somebody and/or make them experience it for the first time
examples: She was initiated into classical music by her mother.
His uncle initiated him into the pleasures of sailing.

definitions.description: to make somebody a member of a particular group, especially as part of a secret ceremony
examples: Hundreds are initiated into the sect each year.

definitions.description: to put a drug or other substance into a person’s or an animal’s body using a syringe
examples: Adrenaline was injected into the muscle.
The anaesthetic is injected locally.
She has been injecting herself with insulin since the age of 16.
The animals were injected with small amounts of the chemical.
She ran courses to train other beauticians how to inject.

definitions.description: to put a liquid or other substance into something using a syringe or similar instrument
examples: The fruit is injected with chemicals to reduce decay.
Chemicals are injected into the fruit to reduce decay.
Foam is injected into the walls where it expands and provides insulation.

definitions.description: to add a particular quality to something
examples: His comments injected a note of humour into the proceedings.
They are hoping a change of leader will inject new energy into the movement.
trying to inject some new life into their marriage

definitions.description: to give money to an organization, a project, etc. so that it can function
examples: They are refusing to inject any more capital into the industry.

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: an act of injecting somebody with a drug or other substance
examples: to give somebody an injection
He was treated with penicillin injections.
daily injections of insulin
An anaesthetic was administered by injection.
In some US states execution is by lethal injection.

definitions.description: a large sum of money that is spent to help improve a situation, business, etc.
examples: The theatre faces closure unless it gets an urgent cash injection.

definitions.description: an act of forcing a liquid or other substance into something
examples: a 2-litre direct injection engine

definitions.description: the fact of a situation being unfair and of people not being treated equally; an unfair act or an example of unfair treatment
examples: We are committed to fighting against poverty and injustice.
a burning sense of injustice
Social and political injustice seemed to be getting worse rather than better.
She was enraged at the injustice of the remark.
The report exposes the injustices of the system.

definitions.description: to judge yourself/somebody unfairly
examples: We may have been doing him an injustice. This work is good.
Perhaps I'm doing you an injustice.

definitions.description: one of the people living in an institution such as a prison or a psychiatric hospital
examples: The jail has 500 inmates.
He was attacked by a fellow inmate.

definitions.description: the act of putting something inside something else; a thing that is put inside something else
examples: An examination is carried out before the insertion of the tube.
Acupuncture involves the insertion of needles into specific points of the body.

definitions.description: a thing that is added to a book, piece of writing, etc.; the act of adding something
examples: the insertion of an extra paragraph

definitions.description: a person who knows a lot about a group or an organization, because they are part of it
examples: The situation was described by one insider as ‘absolute chaos’.
an insider’s view of the movie industry

definitions.description: to look closely at something/somebody, especially to check that everything is as it should be
examples: The teacher walked around inspecting their work.
Make sure you inspect the goods before signing for them.
The plants are regularly inspected for disease.

definitions.description: to officially visit a school, factory, etc. in order to check that rules are being obeyed and that standards are acceptable
examples: Public health officials were called in to inspect the premises.
The Tourist Board inspects all recommended hotels at least once a year.

definitions.description: an official visit to a school, factory, etc. in order to check that rules are being obeyed and that standards are acceptable
examples: Regular inspections are carried out at the prison.
The head went on a tour of inspection of all the classrooms.

definitions.description: the act of looking closely at something/somebody, especially to check that everything is as it should be
examples: The documents are available for inspection.
Engineers carried out a thorough inspection of the track.
Following an 8 a.m. pitch inspection by the referee, today's game has been called off due to a waterlogged pitch.
On closer inspection, the notes proved to be forgeries.

definitions.description: the process that takes place when somebody sees or hears something that causes them to have exciting new ideas or makes them want to create something, especially in art, music or literature
examples: Dreams can be a rich source of inspiration for an artist.
Both poets drew their inspiration from the countryside.
Her work lacks inspiration (= it does not contain any exciting new ideas).
Looking for inspiration for a new dessert? Try this recipe.
She had the time and the inspiration to develop her talent.

definitions.description: a person or thing that is the reason why somebody creates or does something
examples: He says my sister was the inspiration for his heroine.
Clark was the inspiration behind Saturday's victory.

definitions.description: a person or thing that makes you want to be better, more successful, etc.
examples: His charity work is an inspiration to us all.
She became an inspiration and a role model for a new generation of women.

definitions.description: a sudden good idea
examples: He had an inspiration: he'd give her a dog for her birthday.
It came to me in a flash of inspiration.

definitions.description: a natural quality that makes people and animals tend to behave in a particular way using the knowledge and abilities that they were born with rather than thought or training

definitions.description: to surprise or shock somebody so much that they cannot think clearly or speak
examples: Her words stunned me—I had no idea she felt that way.
The guests were stunned into silence.
The company stunned investors with its third profits warning in five months.

definitions.description: to impress somebody very much
examples: They were stunned by the view from the summit.

definitions.description: the act of accepting that somebody has defeated you and that you must obey them
examples: a gesture of submission
to beat/force/starve somebody into submission
His response was one of resistance, not submission.

definitions.description: the act of giving a document, proposal, etc. to somebody in authority so that they can study or consider it; the document, etc. that you give
examples: When is the final date for the submission of proposals?
They prepared a report for submission to the council.
The deadline is 1 October and late submissions will not be marked.
Many diploma courses require the submission of a project.

definitions.label: (law)
definitions.description: a statement that is made to a judge in court
examples: All parties will have the opportunity to make submissions relating to this case.
The judge upheld the defendant's submission and quashed his conviction.

definitions.description: a person who pays money, usually once a year, to receive regular copies of a magazine or newspaper or have access to it online
examples: subscribers to ‘New Scientist’
Subscribers to the magazine can take advantage of this special offer.

definitions.description: a person who pays to receive a service
examples: subscribers to cable television

definitions.description: a person who gives money regularly to help the work of an organization such as a charity
examples: subscribers to Oxfam

definitions.description: an amount of money that you pay regularly to receive a service, be a member of a club, support a charity or receive regular copies of a newspaper or magazine; the act of paying this money
examples: an annual subscription
a subscription to Netflix
a monthly subscription to Oxfam
to take out a subscription to ‘Newsweek’
to cancel/renew a subscription
Copies are available by subscription.
Subscriptions are due annually by the end of January.

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: the act of people paying money for something to be done
examples: A statue in his memory was erected by public subscription.

definitions.label: (North American English)
definitions.description: money that is paid by a government or an organization to reduce the costs of services or of producing goods so that their prices can be kept low
examples: agricultural subsidies
to reduce the level of subsidy

definitions.description: large in amount, value or importance
examples: substantial sums of money
a substantial change
Substantial numbers of people support the reforms.
He ate a substantial breakfast.
There are substantial differences between the two groups.
Their share of the software market is substantial.
We were able to see a substantial improvement.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: large and solid; strongly built
examples: a substantial house
a street of substantial Victorian villas

definitions.description: very much; a lot
examples: The costs have increased substantially.
The plane was substantially damaged in the crash.
The company’s profits have been substantially lower this year.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: mainly; in most details, even if not completely
examples: What she says is substantially true.

definitions.description: a person or thing that you use or have instead of the one you normally use or have
examples: a meat substitute
a substitute family
Paul's father only saw him as a substitute for his dead brother.
The course teaches you the theory but there's no substitute for practical experience.
The local bus service was a poor substitute for their car.

definitions.label: informal
definitions.description: a player who replaces another player in a sports game
examples: He was brought on as (a) substitute after half-time.

definitions.description: an act of using one person or thing in the place of another
examples: Two substitutions were made during the game.
the substitution of low-fat spreads for butter
the substitution of butter with low-fat spreads

definitions.description: to make a claim against a person or an organization in court about something that they have said or done to harm you
examples: They threatened to sue if the work was not completed.
to sue somebody for breach of contract
to sue somebody for $10 million (= in order to get money from somebody)
to sue somebody for damages
He threatened to sue the company for negligence.
The water authority was successfully sued over his illness.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: to formally ask for something, especially in court
examples: to sue for divorce
The rebels were forced to sue for peace.

definitions.description: the act of killing yourself deliberately
examples: to commit suicide
an attempted suicide (= one in which the person survives)
a suicide bomber (= who expects to die while trying to kill other people with a bomb)

definitions.description: a course of action that is likely to destroy your career, position in society, etc.
examples: It would have been political suicide for him to challenge the allegations in court.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: a person who commits suicide
a set of rooms, especially in a hotel
examples: a hotel/private/honeymoon suite
a suite of rooms/offices

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: a set of matching pieces of furniture
examples: a bathroom/bedroom suite
a three-piece suite with two armchairs and a sofa

definitions.description: a piece of music made up of three or more related parts, for example pieces from an opera
examples: Stravinsky’s Firebird Suite

definitions.label: (computing)
definitions.description: a set of related computer programs
examples: a suite of software development tools

definitions.label: (figurative)
definitions.description: the highest point of something, especially the top of a mountain
examples: We reached the summit at noon.
This path leads to the summit.
the summit of his career

definitions.label: (US English)
definitions.description: an official meeting or series of meetings between the leaders of two or more governments at which they discuss important matters
examples: a summit in Moscow
a summit conference

definitions.description: excellent; of very good quality
examples: a superb player
The car's in superb condition.
His performance was absolutely superb.
You look superb.

definitions.description: better in quality than somebody/something else; greater than somebody/something else
examples: vastly superior
superior intelligence
Liverpool were clearly the superior team.
This model is technically superior to its competitors.
She felt socially superior to most of her neighbours.
The enemy won because of their superior numbers (= there were more of them).

definitions.description: higher in rank, importance or position
examples: my superior officer
superior status
a superior court of law

definitions.label: (disapproving)
definitions.description: showing by your behaviour that you think you are better than others
examples: a superior manner
He always looks so superior.

definitions.description: of very good quality; better than other similar things
examples: superior apartments
The hotel offers superior accommodation and leisure facilities.

definitions.description: to be in charge of somebody/something and make sure that everything is done correctly, safely, etc.
examples: to supervise building work
Who is supervising?
She supervised the children playing near the pool.

definitions.description: the work or activity involved in being in charge of somebody/something and making sure that everything is done correctly, safely, etc.
examples: Very young children should not be left to play without supervision.
The drug should only be used under medical supervision.

definitions.description: a meeting between a student and their tutor or supervisor that involves teaching and discussion of the student's work
examples: I have weekly supervisions.

definitions.description: a person who supervises somebody/something
examples: I have a meeting with my supervisor about my research topic.
All work is done under the guidance of a supervisor.

definitions.description: a thing that is added to something else to improve or complete it
examples: vitamin/dietary supplements (= vitamins and other foods eaten in addition to what you usually eat)
Industrial sponsorship is a supplement to government funding.

definitions.description: an extra separate section, often in the form of a magazine, that is sold with a newspaper
examples: the Sunday colour supplements
Our special supplement is packed with ideas for healthy hair.

definitions.description: a book or a section at the end of a book that gives extra information or deals with a special subject
examples: the supplement to the Oxford English Dictionary
a supplement to the main report
You can use these books as supplements to the basic English course.

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: an amount of money that you pay for an extra service or item, especially in addition to the basic cost of a holiday
examples: There is a £10 supplement for a single room.
There is a supplement on rooms with a sea view.
Safety deposit boxes are available at a supplement.

definitions.description: encouraging somebody or giving them help or sympathy
examples: a supportive family
She was very supportive during my father's illness.
a mutually supportive relationship
He was strongly supportive of my career.

definitions.description: according to what is generally thought or believed but not known for certain
examples: The novel is supposedly based on a true story.
a poem supposedly written by Shakespeare
Police have found the supposedly stolen car.

definitions.label: (usually disapproving)
definitions.description: to put an end, often by force, to a group or an activity that is believed to threaten authority
examples: The rebellion was brutally suppressed.

definitions.label: (usually disapproving)
definitions.description: to prevent something from being published or made known
examples: The police were accused of suppressing vital evidence.
This information had been deliberately suppressed.

definitions.description: to prevent yourself from having or expressing a feeling or an emotion
examples: to suppress a smile
She was unable to suppress her anger.
He had suppressed the painful memories of his childhood.
He could hardly suppress his surprise.
Her face was charged with barely suppressed anger.
She was unable to suppress a giggle.
The disloyal thought was instantly suppressed.
He couldn't suppress the excitement in his voice.

definitions.description: to prevent something from growing, developing or continuing
examples: drugs that suppress the appetite

definitions.description: highest in rank or position
examples: the Supreme Commander of the armed forces
the supreme champion
It is an event in which she reigns supreme.

definitions.description: very great or the greatest in degree
examples: to make the supreme sacrifice (= die for what you believe in)
a supreme effort
She smiled with supreme confidence.

definitions.description: a sudden increase of a strong feeling
examples: She felt a sudden surge of anger.
a surge of excitement

definitions.description: a sudden increase in the amount or number of something
examples: a surge in consumer spending
We are having trouble keeping up with the recent surge in demand.
A last-minute surge in ticket sales saved the show from closure.
After an initial surge of interest, there has been little call for our services.

definitions.description: a sudden, strong movement forward or upwards
examples: a tidal surge
A surge of people poured through the gates.
Police struggled to control the sudden surge forward by the demonstrators.

definitions.description: a sudden increase in the flow of electrical power through a system
examples: An electrical surge damaged the computer's disk drive.
The National Grid was hit by a huge power surge.

definitions.description: used in or connected with surgery
examples: surgical procedures
a surgical ward (= for patients having operations)

definitions.refer: (especially of a military attack from the air)
definitions.description: very accurate
examples: They launched surgical strikes against enemy targets.
surgical bombing
The quarterback found the wide receiver with a pass of almost surgical precision.

definitions.description: an amount that is extra or more than you need
examples: food surpluses
Wheat was in surplus that year.

definitions.label: (US English)
definitions.description: the amount by which the amount of money received is greater than the amount of money spent
examples: a surplus of £400 million
The balance of payments was in surplus last year (= the value of exports was greater than the value of imports).

definitions.description: to admit that you have been defeated and want to stop fighting; to allow yourself to be caught, taken prisoner, etc.
examples: The rebel soldiers were forced to surrender.
He surrendered voluntarily to his enemies.
The hijackers eventually surrendered themselves to the police.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: to give up something/somebody when you are forced to
examples: He agreed to surrender all claims to the property.
They surrendered their guns to the police.
The defendant was released to await trial but had to surrender her passport.
The dictator surrendered power to Parliament.

definitions.description: the act of carefully watching a person suspected of a crime or a place where a crime may be committed
examples: The police are keeping the suspects under constant surveillance.
surveillance cameras/equipment

definitions.description: the act of officially removing somebody from their job, school, team, etc. for a period of time, usually as a punishment
examples: suspension from school
The two players are appealing against their suspensions.

definitions.description: the act of delaying something for a period of time, until a decision has been taken
examples: These events have led to the suspension of talks.
Many movies require the viewer to engage in a willing suspension of disbelief.

definitions.description: the system of springs, etc. by which a vehicle is supported on its wheels and that makes it more comfortable to ride in when the road surface is not even
examples: the front/rear suspension
The new model is fitted with computer-controlled suspension.

definitions.label: (specialist)
definitions.description: a liquid with very small pieces of solid matter floating in it; the state of such a liquid
examples: The suspension was passed through a filter to separate out the solid particles.
The material carried in suspension by the tide is deposited on the shore.

definitions.description: a feeling that somebody has done something wrong, illegal or dishonest, even though you have no proof
examples: They drove away slowly to avoid arousing suspicion.
He was arrested on suspicion of murder.
I have a sneaking suspicion that she's not telling the truth.
My suspicions were confirmed when police raided the property.
She was reluctant to voice her suspicions.
His resignation seemed only to fuel suspicions.
It’s time to confront him with our suspicions.

definitions.description: a feeling or belief that something is true, even though you have no proof
examples: I have a horrible suspicion that we've come to the wrong station.

definitions.description: the feeling that you cannot trust somebody/something
examples: Their offer was greeted with some suspicion.
Water from shallow wells should be regarded with suspicion, as it may be contaminated.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: a small amount of something
examples: His mouth quivered in the suspicion of a smile.
Wasn’t there even a suspicion of truth in what he said?

definitions.description: feeling that somebody has done something wrong, illegal or dishonest, without having any proof
examples: They became suspicious of his behaviour and contacted the police.
a suspicious look
You have a very suspicious mind (= you always think that people are behaving in an illegal or dishonest way).

definitions.description: making you feel that something is wrong, illegal or dishonest
examples: Didn't you notice anything suspicious in his behaviour?
She died in suspicious circumstances.
Police are not treating the fire as suspicious.
It might look suspicious if we arrived together.
It was all very suspicious.

definitions.description: not willing or able to trust somebody/something
examples: I was suspicious of his motives.
Many were suspicious of reform.

definitions.description: to provide enough of what somebody/something needs in order to live or exist
examples: Which planets can sustain life?
I only had a little chocolate to sustain me on my walk.
The love and support of his family sustained him during his time in prison.
When she lost her job they could no longer sustain their expensive lifestyle.
The soil was so badly eroded it could no longer sustain crop production.

definitions.description: to make something continue for some time without becoming less
examples: She managed to sustain everyone's interest until the end of her speech.
Kangaroos can sustain high speeds over long distances.
the sustaining pedal of a piano (= that allows a note to continue sounding for a long time)
This relationship would be very difficult to sustain.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: to experience something bad
examples: to sustain damage/an injury/a defeat
The company sustained losses of millions of dollars.

definitions.description: to provide evidence to support an opinion, a theory, etc.
examples: The evidence is not detailed enough to sustain his argument.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: to support a weight without breaking or falling
examples: The ice will not sustain your weight.

definitions.label: (law)
definitions.description: to decide that a claim, etc. is true or legally valid
examples: The court sustained his claim that the contract was illegal.
Objection sustained! (= said by a judge when a lawyer makes an objection in court)

definitions.description: to move backwards or forwards or from side to side while hanging from a fixed point; to make something do this
examples: His arms swung as he walked.
As he pushed her, she swung higher and higher (= while sitting on a swing).
A set of keys swung from her belt.
He sat on the stool, swinging his legs.

definitions.description: to move from one place to another by holding something that is fixed and pulling yourself along, up, etc.
examples: The gunshot sent monkeys swinging away through the trees.
He swung himself out of the car.

definitions.description: to move or make something move with a wide curved movement
examples: A line of cars swung out of the palace gates.
He swung his legs over the side of the bed.
The door swung open.
She let the door swing shut behind her.
She swung the door open.

definitions.description: to change or make somebody/something change from one opinion, mood, etc. to another
examples: The state has swung from Republican to Democrat.
His emotions swung between fear and curiosity.
The game could swing either way (= either side could win it).
I managed to swing them round to my point of view.

definitions.description: to turn or change direction suddenly; to make something do this
examples: She swung back to face him.
The bus swung sharply to the left.
He swung the camera around to face the opposite direction.

definitions.description: to try to hit somebody/something
examples: She swung at me with the iron bar.
He swung another punch in my direction.

definitions.label: (informal)
definitions.description: to succeed in getting or achieving something, sometimes in a slightly dishonest way
examples: We're trying to swing it so that we can travel on the same flight.
Is there any chance of you swinging us a couple of tickets?

definitions.description: to have a strong rhythm

definitions.label: (informal)
definitions.description: if a party, etc. is swinging, there are a lot of people there having a good time
a weapon with a long metal blade (= sharp cutting part) and a handle
examples: to draw/sheathe a sword (= to take it out of/put it into its cover)

definitions.description: to be something that has both advantages and disadvantages
examples: Fame is a double-edged sword.

definitions.description: to fight or argue with somebody

definitions.label: (saying)
definitions.description: people who write books, poems, etc. have a greater effect on history and human affairs than soldiers and wars

definitions.label: (old-fashioned or literary)
definitions.description: to kill somebody with a sword
examples: All the men were put to the sword.

definitions.label: (literary)
definitions.description: a bad or unpleasant thing that might happen to you at any time and that makes you feel worried or frightened

definitions.label: (literary)
definitions.description: to stop fighting and return to peaceful activities
containing symbols, or being used as a symbol
examples: He shook his fist in a symbolic gesture of defiance.
The ceremony has a deep symbolic meaning.
The new regulations are largely symbolic (= they will not have any real effect).
The dove is symbolic of peace.

definitions.description: a set of physical conditions that show you have a particular disease or medical problem
examples: PMS or premenstrual syndrome
This syndrome is associated with frequent coughing.
This syndrome mostly affects women in their forties.

definitions.description: a set of opinions or a way of behaving that is typical of a particular type of person, attitude or social problem
examples: With teenagers, be prepared for the ‘Me, me, me!’ syndrome (= they think of themselves first).
This phenomenon has become known as the ‘Californian syndrome’.

definitions.description: the act of combining separate ideas, beliefs, styles, etc.; a mixture or combination of ideas, beliefs, styles, etc.
examples: the synthesis of art with everyday life
a synthesis of traditional and modern values

definitions.label: (specialist)
definitions.description: the natural chemical production of a substance in animals and plants
examples: protein synthesis
the synthesis of nucleic acids

definitions.label: (specialist)
definitions.description: the artificial production of a substance that is present naturally in animals and plants
examples: the synthesis of penicillin

definitions.label: (specialist)
definitions.description: the production of sounds, music or speech by electronic means
done according to a system or plan, in a complete, efficient or determined way
examples: a systematic approach to solving the problem
a systematic attempt to destroy the organization
The prisoner was subjected to systematic torture.
the systematic analysis of the risks involved

definitions.description: the particular method you use to achieve something
examples: They tried all kinds of tactics to get us to go.
This was just the latest in a series of delaying tactics.
The manager discussed tactics with his team.
Confrontation is not always the best tactic.
It's time to try a change of tactic.
They used strong-arm (= aggressive or violent) tactics.

definitions.description: the art of moving soldiers and military equipment around during a battle or war in order to use them in the most effective way
connected with the particular method you use to achieve something
examples: tactical planning
to have a tactical advantage
Telling your boss you were looking for a new job was a tactical error (= it was the wrong thing to do at that time).

definitions.description: carefully planned in order to achieve a particular aim
examples: a tactical decision

definitions.description: used or having an effect over short distances or for a short time
examples: tactical weapons/missiles
tactical nuclear weapons

definitions.description: connected with military tactics
examples: He was given tactical command of the operation.

definitions.description: a person who pays tax to the government, especially on the money that they earn
examples: Hundreds of thousands of pounds of taxpayers' money (= money paid in taxes) have been spent on the project.
The proposals will be popular with higher-rate taxpayers.

definitions.description: to attract somebody or make somebody want to do or have something, even if they know it is wrong
examples: I was tempted by the dessert menu.
Don't tempt thieves by leaving valuables clearly visible.
He was tempted into a life of crime.
I was tempted to take the day off.

definitions.description: to persuade or try to persuade somebody to do something that you want them to do, for example by offering them something
examples: How can we tempt young people into engineering?
Nothing would tempt me to live here.

definitions.label: (especially North American English)
definitions.description: a person who pays rent for the use of a room, building, land, etc. to the person who owns it
examples: They had evicted their tenants for non-payment of rent.
The decorating was done by a previous tenant.
tenant farmers (= ones who do not own their own farms)

definitions.description: kind, gentle and loving
examples: tender words
What he needs now is a lot of tender loving care (= sympathetic treatment).

definitions.description: easy to bite through and cut
examples: This meat is extremely tender.
Boil the beans until they are tender.
four large slices of tender chicken

definitions.description: painful when you touch it
examples: My leg is still very tender where I banged it.
The back of my neck feels very tender.

definitions.description: easily hurt or damaged
examples: tender young plants

definitions.description: the period of time when somebody holds an important job, especially a political one; the act of holding an important job
examples: his four-year tenure as president
She had a long tenure of office.

definitions.description: the right to stay permanently in your job, especially as a teacher at a university
examples: It's still extremely difficult to get tenure.
She has been granted tenure at Leeds University.

definitions.description: the legal right to live in a house or use a piece of land
examples: When you rent a house here, you don’t have security of tenure.

definitions.description: to end; to make something end
examples: Your contract of employment terminates in December.
The agreement was terminated immediately.
to terminate a pregnancy (= to perform or have an abortion)

definitions.description: to end a journey
examples: This train terminates at London Victoria.

definitions.description: used to refer to an area of land when you are mentioning its natural features, for example, if it is rough, flat, etc.
examples: difficult/rough/mountainous terrain
They walked for miles across steep and inhospitable terrain.

definitions.label: (informal)
definitions.description: excellent; wonderful
examples: I feel absolutely terrific today!
She's doing a terrific job.
You look terrific in that dress.
He was really terrific when I was in trouble.
That’s terrific news!
So nobody’s coming. Terrific!

definitions.label: (informal)
definitions.description: very large; very great
examples: I've got a terrific amount of work to do.
We drove along at a terrific speed.

definitions.description: to make a statement that something happened or that something is true, especially as a witness in court
examples: She refused to testify against her husband.
There are several witnesses who will testify for the defence.
He was summoned to testify before a grand jury about his role in the affair.
Evans testified to receiving $200 000 in bribes.
He testified (that) he was at the theatre at the time of the murder.
‘I was approached by a man I did not recognize,’ she testified.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: to say that you believe something is true because you have evidence of it
examples: Too many young people are unable to write or spell well, as employers will testify.

definitions.label: (especially North American English)
definitions.description: to express your belief in God publicly

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: a thing that shows that something else exists or is true
examples: This increase in exports bears testimony to the successes of industry.
The pyramids are an eloquent testimony to the ancient Egyptians' engineering skills.
His thick, swollen fingers bore testimony to a lifetime of toil.

definitions.description: a formal written or spoken statement saying what you know to be true, usually in court
examples: a sworn testimony
Her claim was supported by the testimony of several witnesses.
Can I refuse to give testimony?

definitions.label: (figurative)
definitions.description: the way a surface, substance or piece of cloth feels when you touch it, for example how rough, smooth, hard or soft it is
examples: the soft texture of velvet
She uses a variety of different colours and textures in her wall hangings.
The method used will vary with the soil texture and climate.

definitions.description: the way food or drink tastes or feels in your mouth, for example whether it is rough, smooth, light, heavy, etc.
examples: The two cheeses were very different in both taste and texture.

definitions.description: the way that different parts of a piece of music or literature are combined to create a final impression
examples: the rich texture of the symphony
a piece of music with a dense choral texture

definitions.description: used to show that you are pleased that something good has happened or that something bad has been avoided
examples: There was a fire in the building, but thankfully no one was hurt.
Thankfully, the house was empty when I got home.

definitions.description: in a pleased or grateful way
examples: At the end of a busy day, I just sink thankfully into bed.
I accepted the invitation thankfully.

definitions.description: connected with the theatre
examples: a theatrical agent

definitions.label: (often disapproving)
definitions.description: deliberately attracting attention or creating a particular effect in a way that seems false
examples: a theatrical gesture

definitions.description: the study of religion and beliefs
examples: a degree in theology
a theology student
the rarefied world of academic theology

definitions.description: a set of religious beliefs
examples: the theologies of the East

definitions.description: connected with the ideas and principles on which a particular subject is based, rather than with practice and experiment
examples: a theoretical approach
theoretical physics
The first year provides students with a sound theoretical basis for later study.

definitions.description: that could possibly exist, happen or be true, although this is unlikely
examples: It's a theoretical possibility.

definitions.description: after the time or event mentioned
examples: She married at 17 and gave birth to her first child shortly thereafter.

definitions.description: used to introduce the result of the action or situation mentioned
examples: Regular exercise strengthens the heart, thereby reducing the risk of heart attack.

definitions.description: making people think seriously about a particular subject or issue
examples: a brilliant and thought-provoking play

definitions.description: quiet, because you are thinking
examples: He looked thoughtful.
They sat in thoughtful silence.

definitions.label: (approving)
definitions.description: showing that you think about and care for other people
examples: The hotel manager was very kind and thoughtful.
It was very thoughtful of you to send the flowers.

definitions.description: showing signs of careful thought
examples: a player who has a thoughtful approach to the game

definitions.description: a thin string of cotton, wool, silk, etc. used for sewing or making cloth
examples: a needle and thread
a robe embroidered with gold thread
the delicate threads of a spider’s web
You've pulled a thread in your jumper.

definitions.description: an idea or a feature that is part of something greater; an idea that connects the different parts of something
examples: A common thread runs through these discussions.
The author skilfully draws together the different threads of the plot.
I lost the thread of the argument (= I could no longer follow it).
The speaker lost his thread (= forgot what he wanted to say) halfway through the talk.

definitions.description: a long, thin line of something
examples: A thread of light emerged from the keyhole.
a silvery thread of water
Thin threads of blood glittered on his forehead and cheeks.

definitions.label: (computing)
definitions.description: a series of connected messages on email, social media, etc. that have been sent by different people
the raised line that runs around the length of a screw and that allows it to be fixed in place by twisting

definitions.label: (North American English, old-fashioned, informal)
definitions.description: clothes
the floor or ground at the bottom of a doorway, considered as the entrance to a building or room
examples: He stepped across the threshold.
She stood hesitating on the threshold.

definitions.description: the level at which something starts to happen or have an effect
examples: He has a low boredom threshold (= he gets bored easily).
I have a high pain threshold (= I can suffer a lot of pain before I start to react).
My earnings are just above the tax threshold (= more than the amount at which you start paying tax).

definitions.description: the point just before a new situation, period of life, etc. begins
examples: She felt as though she was on the threshold of a new life.

definitions.label: (British English)
definitions.description: very excited and pleased
examples: ‘Are you pleased?’ ‘I'm thrilled.’
He was thrilled at the prospect of seeing them again.
I'm really thrilled with the results.
I was thrilled to be invited.
She was thrilled to bits (= extremely pleased) that he'd been offered the job.

definitions.description: to become, and continue to be, successful, strong, healthy, etc.
examples: New businesses thrive in this area.
These animals rarely thrive in captivity.

definitions.description: a regular rise and fall in the level of the sea, caused by the pull of the moon and sun; the flow of water that happens as the sea rises and falls
examples: the ebb and flow of the tide
The tide is in/out.

examples: She gets a widow’s pension.

definitions.description: the measurement from one side of something to the other; how wide something is
examples: The terrace runs the full width of the house.
It's about ten metres in width.
The carpet is available in different widths.

definitions.description: a piece of material of a particular width
examples: You'll need two widths of fabric for each curtain.

definitions.description: the distance between the two long sides of a swimming pool
examples: How many widths can you swim?

definitions.description: the quality of being happy and ready to do something
examples: Success in studying depends on a willingness to learn.

definitions.description: to rub something against a surface, in order to remove dirt or liquid from it; to rub a surface with a cloth, etc. in order to clean it
examples: Please wipe your feet on the mat.
He wiped his hands on a clean towel.
She was sniffing and wiping her eyes with a tissue.
He wiped his plate clean with a piece of bread.

definitions.description: to remove dirt, liquid, etc. from something by using a cloth, your hand, etc.
examples: He wiped the sweat from his forehead.
She wiped off her make-up.
Use that cloth to wipe up the mess.

definitions.description: to remove information, sound, images, etc. from a computer, video, etc.
examples: You must have wiped off that programme I recorded.
Somebody had wiped all the tapes.

definitions.description: to deliberately forget an experience because it was unpleasant or embarrassing
examples: I tried to wipe the whole episode from my mind.
You can never wipe out the past.

definitions.description: the ability to say or write things that are both clever and humorous
examples: to have a quick/sharp/dry/ready wit
a woman of wit and intelligence
a book full of the wit and wisdom of his 30 years in politics

definitions.description: a person who has the ability to say or write things that are both clever and humorous
examples: a well-known wit and raconteur

definitions.description: your ability to think quickly and clearly and to make good decisions
examples: He needed all his wits to find his way out.
The game was a long battle of wits.
Kate paused and gathered her wits.
a chance to pit your wits against (= compete with, using your intelligence) our quiz champion

definitions.description: having the type of intelligence mentioned
examples: a quick-witted group of students

definitions.description: the intelligence or good sense to know what is the right thing to do
examples: At least you had the wit to ask for help.
It should not be beyond the wit of man to resolve this dispute.

definitions.label: (informal)
definitions.description: the act of taking an amount of money out of your bank account
examples: You can make withdrawals of up to $250 a day.
She made a withdrawal of £250 from her bank account.

definitions.description: the act of moving or taking something away or back
examples: the withdrawal of support
the withdrawal of the UN troops from the region
the withdrawal of a product from the market

definitions.description: the act of no longer taking part in something or being a member of an organization
examples: his withdrawal from the election
Britain’s withdrawal from the EU

definitions.description: the period of time when somebody is getting used to not taking a drug that they have become addicted to, and the unpleasant effects of doing this
examples: I got withdrawal symptoms after giving up smoking.
She was still suffering withdrawal from nicotine.

definitions.description: the act of saying that you no longer believe that something you have previously said is true
examples: The newspaper published a withdrawal the next day.

definitions.label: (psychology)
definitions.description: the behaviour of somebody who wants to be alone and does not want to communicate with other people
examples: She is showing signs of withdrawal and depression.

definitions.description: a period of physical exercise that you do to keep fit
examples: She does a 20-minute workout every morning.
The team had a hard workout this morning.
When I do a good workout, I feel fine.

definitions.description: the practice of showing respect for God or a god, by saying prayers, singing with others, etc.; a ceremony for this
examples: an act/a place of worship
morning/evening worship (= a church service in the morning/evening)
The tradition of ancestor worship stretches back thousands of years.

definitions.description: a strong feeling of love and respect for somebody/something
examples: What she feels for him is akin to worship.

definitions.label: (British English, formal)
definitions.description: a polite way of addressing or referring to a magistrate or mayor
important, pleasant, interesting, etc.; worth spending time, money or effort on
examples: It was in aid of a worthwhile cause (= a charity, etc.).
a worthwhile discussion/job
The smile on her face made it all worthwhile.
We all felt we had done something worthwhile for the local community.
High prices in the UK make it worthwhile for buyers to look abroad.
It is worthwhile to include really high-quality illustrations.
It didn't seem worthwhile writing it all out again.

definitions.label: (formal)
definitions.description: having the qualities that deserve somebody/something
examples: Very few of his ideas are worthy of further attention.
A number of the report's findings are worthy of note.
No composer was considered worthy of the name until he had written an opera.
a worthy champion (= one who deserved to win)
He felt he was not worthy of her.

definitions.description: having qualities that deserve your respect or attention
examples: The money we raise will be going to a very worthy cause.
a worthy member of the team
We thought it was a worthy enough objective.

definitions.description: having good qualities but not very interesting or exciting
examples: her worthy but dull husband
He's a very worthy man, I suppose, but he's very dull.

definitions.description: typical of what a particular person or thing might do, give, etc.
examples: He gave a speech that was worthy of Martin Luther King.

definitions.description: deserving, or suitable for, the thing mentioned
examples: trustworthy
roadworthy

definitions.description: to shout loudly, for example because you are angry, excited, frightened or in pain
examples: He yelled at the other driver.
She yelled at the child to get down from the wall.
They yelled with excitement.
She yelled out in pain.
‘Be careful!’ he yelled.
The crowd yelled encouragement at the players.
He yelled out her name.
He yelled for help.

definitions.description: the total amount of crops, profits, etc. that are produced
examples: a high crop yield
a reduction in milk yield
This will give a yield of 10% on your investment.
